metadata.summary: This multidisciplinary guideline addresses assessment, acute treatment, rehabilitation, and postacute follow-up for adults and children with traumatic brain injury. It covers triage, imaging and biomarkers, neurologic monitoring, medical and surgical care, complications, prognosis, and outcome assessment. It also offers guidance for implementing these practices within trauma centers while emphasizing individualized clinical judgment.

target_population: Adults with suspected or confirmed TBI
Children with suspected or confirmed TBI
therapeutic_areas: Intracranial pressure monitoring and tiered treatment

toxicities.event: Secondary brain injury associated with hypotension
prevention: Avoid hypotension during TBI care and general anesthesia.
Avoid hypotension when administering barbiturates.
Monitor for hypotension during beta blocker treatment.

recognition: PaO2 > 100 mm Hg when brain oximetry does not guide treatment
prevention: Initially target PaO2 of 80–100 mm Hg and avoid PaO2 > 100 mm Hg unless brain oximetry guides treatment.
Consider the potential harm of hyperoxia when escalating treatment for brain tissue hypoxia, particularly at Tier Three.

toxicities.event: Reduced cerebral blood flow with profound hyperventilation
prevention: Do not routinely lower PaCO2 below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa.
Reserve PaCO2 less than 30 mm Hg for brief rescue treatment of refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation while other interventions are arranged.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Use profound hyperventilation for the shortest possible period when employed as rescue treatment.

prevention: Do not routinely use therapeutic hypothermia below 35°C for intracranial hypertension in severe TBI because of systemic complications.

toxicities.event: Adverse drug reactions and drug interactions with phenytoin
prevention: Monitor phenytoin concentrations, albumin, and free phenytoin concentrations to guide dosing.
Therapeutic drug monitoring is usually performed 24 hours after the initial dose and once more during the 7 days of TBI prophylaxis.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Guide dosing adjustments using albumin and free phenytoin concentrations; corrected total phenytoin concentrations may be calculated if free phenytoin assays are unavailable.

toxicities.event: Behavioral adverse drug reactions with levetiracetam
recognition: Behavioral adverse drug reactions in pediatric and adult patients, particularly those with TBI
prevention: Pyridoxine 50–100 mg daily supplementation may reduce behavioral adverse drug reactions.

toxicities.event: Increased risk of death with valproic acid used for early posttraumatic seizure prophylaxis
prevention: Do not use valproic acid for early PTS prophylaxis because the guide reports a higher risk of death than with phenytoin.
Monitor for these adverse effects when beta blockers are considered for adrenergic stress or paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.

toxicities.event: Venous thromboembolism risk during anticoagulant reversal
prevention: Balance the benefit of reversal against bleeding and underlying thrombosis risks.
Higher 4PCC doses (> 2000 to 3000 units) were associated with increased VTE risk in patients with nontraumatic ICH; for INR 1.5–1.9, lower doses of 4PCC (10–20 units/kg) are suggested.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Lower doses of 4PCC (10–20 units/kg) are suggested for patients with INR 1.5–1.9.

toxicities.event: Delayed therapeutic effect of restarted warfarin after vitamin K reversal
recognition: High-risk patients who received vitamin K > 2.5 mg may have a delayed return of warfarin's therapeutic effect for several weeks after restarting it.

management.severity: High-risk warfarin patients after reversal with vitamin K > 2.5 mg
management.actions: Use LMWH or unfractionated heparin for anticoagulation until the vitamin K effect has worn off.

toxicities.event: Potential complications associated with reversal of antiplatelet effects
recognition: Adverse effects of platelet transfusions or desmopressin may contribute to complications and worse outcomes.
prevention: Do not routinely transfuse platelets solely because a patient used an antiplatelet agent before injury.
Platelet transfusion and desmopressin are not recommended for patients with TBI who are not candidates for an invasive intervention.
When possible, assess platelet function before transfusion; reversal treatment is not recommended when platelet function is normal or resistance is documented.

recognition: Low serum sodium after desmopressin administration

management.actions: Monitor serum sodium and treat hyponatremia as needed to reach therapeutic sodium concentrations.

prevention: Monitor for hyponatremia if desmopressin is administered.

toxicities.event: Prolonged neurocognitive recovery associated with acute treatment of agitation
prevention: Acute use of benzodiazepines and typical antipsychotic medications for posttraumatic confusion or agitation is not recommended because evidence suggests they may prolong neurocognitive recovery.
Atypical antipsychotics or beta blockers such as propranolol may instead be considered during acute agitation when needed for patient and staff safety.

toxicities.event: Radiation-induced malignancy risk from CT in children
prevention: Use CT judiciously in children because they are more vulnerable to radiation-induced malignancy.
Base indications for emergency head imaging on a validated pediatric decision rule such as PECARN.

toxicities.event: Aspiration and malnutrition associated with dysphagia

management.severity: Dysphagia in older adults with TBI
management.actions: Screen swallowing at the bedside using volume-viscosity testing.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide mechanical prophylaxis on admission regardless of eligibility for pharmacologic prophylaxis.
prophylaxis.target_population: All patients with TBI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Start pharmacologic prophylaxis when follow-up head CT shows no progression of intracranial injury.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with low-risk nonoperative TBI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Start pharmacologic prophylaxis if follow-up head CT shows no progression of intracranial injury.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with moderate- or high-risk nonoperative TBI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider starting or resuming pharmacologic prophylaxis if postoperative CT shows stable ICH.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with TBI after craniotomy or craniectomy

prophylaxis.recommendation: Withhold pharmacologic prophylaxis when CT shows ICH progression until repeat imaging demonstrates stability.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with TBI and progressing ICH
prophylaxis.duration: Repeat imaging usually in another 24 to 48 hours

prophylaxis.recommendation: An ICP monitor alone does not warrant withholding pharmacologic prophylaxis before placement or throughout monitoring; consider continuing it without interruption before monitor removal.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with an ICP monitor and no craniotomy or craniectomy

prophylaxis.recommendation: Prefer LMWH over UFH, including in patients with ICP monitors. The recommended initial enoxaparin regimen for TBI is 30 mg every 12 hours; consider anti-factor Xa activity monitoring for later LMWH dosing. If UFH is selected, best-practice dosing is 5000 units every 8 hours.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with TBI receiving pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use prophylactic inferior vena cava filters, regardless of when pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis begins.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with TBI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Assess VTE risk after admission with an adopted published pediatric trauma risk tool, such as ROCKIT. Low-risk children do not need pharmacologic prophylaxis; begin mechanical prophylaxis on admission for moderate-risk children and reserve pharmacologic prophylaxis for those at high risk. LMWH is preferred when pharmacologic prophylaxis is used, with weight-based dosing in young children.
prophylaxis.target_population: Pediatric trauma patients
prophylaxis.duration: Discontinue when the patient becomes ambulatory if no other thrombogenic factors are present.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider subcutaneous heparin or LMWH during the acute period without therapeutic anticoagulants.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients whose preinjury therapeutic anticoagulation has been interrupted
prophylaxis.duration: During the acute period off anticoagulants

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider ASM to prevent early PTS when risk factors are present. Phenytoin and levetiracetam appear similar in safety and effectiveness for this indication; valproic acid is not recommended because of an increased risk of death compared with phenytoin.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with severe TBI and risk factors for early PTS

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not continue prophylaxis to prevent late PTS when there has been no clinical or EEG seizure activity, or when seizure activity occurred only within the first 24 hours postinjury. Continued ASM may be appropriate if seizure activity begins beyond 24 hours or if the patient previously received treatment for a known seizure disorder.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients receiving ASM after TBI
prophylaxis.duration: No more than 7 days for early PTS prophylaxis in the stated circumstances

prophylaxis.recommendation: Seizure prophylaxis is not recommended.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with TBI without intracranial bleeding or with isolated traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage

prophylaxis.recommendation: Either levetiracetam or (fos)phenytoin is appropriate; the most commonly used levetiracetam dose is 20–40 mg/kg/day divided into two doses per day.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children with TBI for whom early PTS prophylaxis is indicated

prophylaxis.recommendation: Choose the antimicrobial and dose using published guidelines, pharmacist input, and assessment of ICU antibiograms. Cefazolin is preferred in patients without methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or a documented severe beta lactam allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin are alternatives for severe beta lactam allergy.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing surgery after TBI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not give systemic prophylactic antibiotics for EVD or intraparenchymal ICP monitor placement, or during use of parenchymal or ventricular drains, because this may favor drug-resistant organisms.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing EVD or intraparenchymal ICP monitoring

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use perioperative antibiotics with surgical debridement and irrigation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with open or penetrating skull fractures undergoing surgery

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider broad-spectrum antibiotics with high blood-brain barrier penetration.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with open or penetrating skull fractures

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use antibiotic prophylaxis because it may promote growth of drug-resistant organisms.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with traumatic skull-based fractures accompanied by CSF leaks or pneumocephalus

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use antimicrobial-impregnated catheters when available during EVD monitoring, as recommended by the BTF and Neurocritical Care Society guidelines cited in the document.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing EVD monitoring

infection_management.prevention: Establish and follow facility protocols for EVD and intraparenchymal monitor insertion and care. Use antimicrobial-impregnated catheters when available, remove monitors and drains as early as clinically possible, avoid routine manipulation of the closed EVD system and CSF sampling without a clinical indication, and use aseptic technique. An EVD bundle may include insertion, maintenance, dressing-change, and CSF-sampling procedures. A cited meta-analysis reported CSF infection of 3.6% with antimicrobial-impregnated catheters versus 13.7% with standard catheters.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Infection associated with open or penetrating skull fracture
infection_management.prevention: Surgical debridement and irrigation are recommended, with perioperative antibiotics for not more than 24 hours. Broad-spectrum antibiotics with high blood-brain barrier penetration may be considered for a maximum of 3 days.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Pneumonia associated with prolonged ventilation or feeding
infection_management.prevention: Early tracheostomy can reduce pneumonia risk in severe TBI. Postpyloric feeding was associated with lower pneumonia rates in TBI studies, but obtaining that access should not delay initiation of EN.

therapies_index.name: mannitol
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier One treatment of intracranial hypertension by intermittent bolus; pediatric evidence is less supportive than for hypertonic saline.
therapies_index.administration: Intermittent bolus: 0.25–1.0 g/kg. SIBICC recommends sodium and osmolality limits of 155 mEq/L and 320 mEq/L during administration. Non-bolus continuous intravenous infusion is discouraged.
monitoring: Measure serum osmolality when used as an osmotic agent.
Monitor sodium and osmolality during treatment.

therapies_index.name: hypertonic saline
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier One treatment of intracranial hypertension by intermittent bolus.
therapies_index.administration: Administer by intermittent bolus. SIBICC recommends sodium and osmolality limits of 155 mEq/L and 320 mEq/L. Scheduled hyperosmolar infusions are discouraged.
monitoring: Monitor sodium and osmolality during treatment.

therapies_index.name: hypertonic 3% saline
approved_indications: Treatment of intracranial hypertension in children with severe TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Boluses of 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 20 min, or a constant rate of 0.1–1 mL/kg/hour.

approved_indications: The pediatric intracranial hypertension section presents this concentration as a hypertonic saline treatment option.
therapies_index.administration: 0.5 mL/kg (up to 30 mL) over 10 to 20 minutes.

therapies_index.name: pentobarbital
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier Three treatment of intracranial hypertension when a test demonstrates ICP benefit.
therapies_index.administration: Titrate barbiturate coma to ICP control without exceeding the dose that achieves burst suppression; continue only if ICP improves.
key_toxicities: Hypotension is a hazard to avoid during administration.
monitoring: Assess the effect on ICP.
Monitor for hypotension and burst suppression.

therapies_index.name: sodium thiopentone
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier Three treatment of intracranial hypertension when a test demonstrates ICP benefit.
therapies_index.administration: Titrate barbiturate coma to ICP control without exceeding the dose that achieves burst suppression; continue only if ICP improves.
key_toxicities: Hypotension is a hazard to avoid during administration.
monitoring: Assess the effect on ICP.
Monitor for hypotension and burst suppression.

therapies_index.name: propofol
therapies_index.administration: SIBICC discourages high-dose use to attempt burst suppression.

therapies_index.name: furosemide
therapies_index.administration: SIBICC discourages its use for intracranial hypertension in severe TBI.

therapies_index.name: steroids
therapies_index.administration: Routine use for intracranial hypertension in severe TBI is discouraged.

therapies_index.name: enoxaparin
approved_indications: Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in patients with TBI when intracranial bleeding is stable.
therapies_index.administration: The recommended initial TBI regimen is 30 mg every 12 hours; the stated general-trauma regimen is 40 mg every 12 hours.
monitoring: Consider anti-factor Xa activity monitoring to guide subsequent LMWH dosing.
Assess ICH stability on follow-up imaging before prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: dalteparin
approved_indications: LMWH option for pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in patients with TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Use standard dosing; no numerical dalteparin dose is specified.
monitoring: Consider anti-factor Xa activity monitoring to guide subsequent LMWH dosing.

therapies_index.name: LMWH
approved_indications: Preferred pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis for patients with TBI, including those with ICP monitors.
Preferred pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis for pediatric patients at high VTE risk.
An option for interim prophylaxis when therapeutic anticoagulation has been stopped.
therapies_index.administration: Use weight-based dosing in young children.
key_toxicities: Altered renal function in older adults may affect dosing.
monitoring: Consider anti-factor Xa activity to guide subsequent dosing.
Consider renal function in older adults.

therapies_index.name: UFH
approved_indications: Alternative pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis when selected instead of LMWH.
therapies_index.administration: 5000 units every 8 hours for pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: heparin
approved_indications: Bridging IV treatment until INR becomes therapeutic in patients receiving warfarin for cervical arterial dissection in the cited trials.
Subcutaneous VTE prophylaxis may be considered during an acute interruption of therapeutic anticoagulation.
therapies_index.administration: IV for the described warfarin bridging; subcutaneous for the described prophylaxis.
monitoring: Monitor INR when bridging to therapeutic warfarin.

therapies_index.name: warfarin
approved_indications: Anticoagulation option discussed for cervical arterial dissection, including trials not primarily focused on BCVI.
therapies_index.administration: The cited trials usually used bridging IV heparin until INR was therapeutic. After TBI, restarting anticoagulation is individualized according to bleeding and thrombosis risk.
key_toxicities: Anticoagulation in a patient with TBI raises concern for intracranial bleeding or hematoma expansion.
monitoring: Assess INR.
Assess patient-specific bleeding and thrombosis risks when deciding on reversal or restart.

therapies_index.name: aspirin
approved_indications: Antiplatelet treatment for BCVI is discussed, but whether dual antiplatelet therapy is preferable to aspirin alone remains unresolved.
monitoring: Consider platelet function testing when preinjury antiplatelet-associated dysfunction is suspected.

therapies_index.name: clopidogrel
key_toxicities: Its active metabolite is associated with longer antiplatelet activity.
monitoring: Consider point-of-care platelet function testing when preinjury antiplatelet-associated dysfunction is suspected.

therapies_index.name: ticagrelor
key_toxicities: Its active metabolite is associated with longer antiplatelet activity.
monitoring: Consider point-of-care platelet function testing when preinjury antiplatelet-associated dysfunction is suspected.

therapies_index.name: rivaroxaban
monitoring: Determine the drug, dose and time of the last dose when assessing urgent reversal after TBI.

therapies_index.name: apixaban
monitoring: Determine the drug, dose and time of the last dose when assessing urgent reversal after TBI.

therapies_index.name: edoxaban
monitoring: Determine the drug, dose and time of the last dose when assessing urgent reversal after TBI.

therapies_index.name: dabigatran
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies it as a thrombin inhibitor.
monitoring: Determine dose and time of the last dose when assessing urgent reversal.
An activated partial thromboplastin time may be elevated after recent administration, but a normal result does not exclude a clinically relevant concentration.

therapies_index.name: vitamin K
approved_indications: Warfarin reversal in patients with TBI requiring emergent surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Give 2.5–10 mg IV with 4PCC. Recheck INR 6–8 hours after 4PCC; if INR is > 1.4, give another 2.5–10 mg IV.
key_toxicities: A reversal dose > 2.5 mg may delay the therapeutic effect of restarted warfarin for several weeks.
monitoring: Recheck INR 6–8 hours after 4PCC.

therapies_index.name: 4PCC
approved_indications: Reversal of oral anticoagulation in patients with TBI who need emergent surgery.
An alternative for reversal of the listed DOACs when their specific reversal agent is unavailable.
therapies_index.administration: For warfarin, give 15 units/kg IV at INR 1.5–1.9, 25 units/kg IV at INR 2–3.9, 35 units/kg IV at INR 4–6, or 50 units/kg IV at INR > 6; an alternative fixed dose is 1500 units. For the listed Xa inhibitors when andexanet alfa is unavailable, give 25–50 units/kg or a fixed dose of 2000 units. The text also discusses fixed doses of 1500 to 2500 units and suggests 10–20 units/kg when INR is 1.5–1.9.
key_toxicities: Higher doses (> 2000 to 3000 units) were associated with increased VTE risk in patients with nontraumatic ICH.
monitoring: For warfarin reversal, recheck INR 1 hour and 6–8 hours after administration.

therapies_index.name: FFP
approved_indications: Alternative when 4PCC is unavailable for anticoagulant reversal.
An option after warfarin reversal with 4PCC if INR remains > 1.4.
therapies_index.administration: If INR is > 1.4 at the 1-hour recheck after 4PCC, consider 2–4 units. The document states that approximately 8–16 units of FFP are equivalent to approximately 20–50 units/kg of 4PCC.
monitoring: Recheck INR after reversal; the document states that the lowest achievable INR with FFP alone is approximately 1.5–1.7.

therapies_index.name: andexanet alfa
approved_indications: Reversal strategy listed for rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban in patients with TBI needing emergent surgery.
therapies_index.administration: If the last dose was > 7 hours earlier, give a 400 mg IV bolus followed by a 480 mg IV infusion. If the last dose was < 7 hours earlier, give an 800 mg IV bolus followed by a 960 mg IV infusion.

therapies_index.name: idarucizumab
approved_indications: Reversal strategy for dabigatran in patients with TBI needing emergent surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Give two consecutive IV doses of 2.5 g, infusing each over 10 minutes.

therapies_index.name: activated charcoal
approved_indications: Consider after a dose of rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban or dabigatran administered < 2 hours earlier when reversal is needed.

therapies_index.name: platelet transfusion
approved_indications: May be considered before an invasive procedure in a patient taking antiplatelet agents who has a low platelet count and needs procedural hemostasis.
therapies_index.administration: For a patient requiring a neurosurgical procedure, consider one single-donor apheresis unit, described as equivalent to 6 pooled units or 1 random-donor unit per 10 kg of body weight. Routine reversal of antiplatelet effects or postoperative transfusion is not recommended.
key_toxicities: Platelet transfusion for reversal of antiplatelet effects is associated with adverse effects that may cause additional complications and worse outcomes.
monitoring: Perform platelet function testing before transfusion whenever possible.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin
approved_indications: Suggested for consideration, alone or with platelet transfusion, in neurosurgical patients previously given aspirin, clopidogrel or ticagrelor; additional research is needed to establish benefit.
therapies_index.administration: 0.4 mcg/kg IV. It is not recommended for patients with TBI who are not candidates for an invasive intervention.
key_toxicities: Hyponatremia.
Treatments used to reverse antiplatelet effects, including desmopressin, are associated with adverse effects that may cause further complications and worse outcomes.
monitoring: Monitor sodium and treat hyponatremia if it occurs.
Perform platelet function testing before reversal whenever possible.

therapies_index.name: phenytoin
approved_indications: Consider for prevention of early PTS in patients with TBI who have risk factors; prophylaxis beyond 7 days to prevent late PTS is not recommended.
therapies_index.administration: The prophylaxis course discussed is 7 days.
key_toxicities: Numerous drug-drug interactions and potentially severe adverse drug reactions.
monitoring: Check drug concentration, usually 24 hours after initial dosing and once more during the 7 days of prophylaxis.
Monitor albumin and free phenytoin concentrations to guide dose adjustment.

therapies_index.name: (fos)phenytoin
approved_indications: An appropriate option for the recommended 7-day PTS prophylaxis course in children with TBI.
therapies_index.administration: 7-day prophylaxis course.

therapies_index.name: levetiracetam
approved_indications: Consider for prevention of early PTS in patients with TBI who have risk factors.
An appropriate option for the recommended 7-day PTS prophylaxis course in children.
therapies_index.administration: The commonly used pediatric dose is 20–40 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses per day.
key_toxicities: Behavioral adverse drug reactions have been observed in adults and children, particularly those with TBI.
monitoring: Therapeutic drug monitoring is not needed for pediatric PTS prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: valproic acid
therapies_index.administration: Not recommended for early PTS prophylaxis.
key_toxicities: Increased risk of death compared with phenytoin when used for early PTS prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: pyridoxine
approved_indications: Supplementation may limit behavioral adverse drug reactions associated with levetiracetam.
therapies_index.administration: 50–100 mg daily.

therapies_index.name: propranolol
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies it as a nonselective BBK.
approved_indications: May be considered for TBI-related adrenergic stress or paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome.
May be considered as an alternative during acute posttraumatic agitation.
key_toxicities: Potential BBK adverse effects include bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure and bronchospasm.
monitoring: Monitor for bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure and bronchospasm.

therapies_index.name: beta blockers
approved_indications: May be considered for adrenergic stress or paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.
May be considered during acute posttraumatic agitation.
key_toxicities: Bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure and bronchospasm.
monitoring: Monitor for the stated cardiovascular and respiratory adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: benzodiazepines
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Acute use for posttraumatic confusion and agitation is not recommended.
key_toxicities: Acute use for posttraumatic agitation may prolong neurocognitive recovery.

therapies_index.name: opioids
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.
key_toxicities: Drug-related small pupils can make clinical assessment of pupillary reactivity difficult.
monitoring: Quantitative pupillometry can assess reactivity despite drug-related small pupils.

therapies_index.name: alpha-2 agonists
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.

therapies_index.name: gabapentin
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.

therapies_index.name: muscle relaxants
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.

therapies_index.name: baclofen
approved_indications: Listed among agents that can treat symptoms of paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI.

therapies_index.name: atypical antipsychotics
approved_indications: May be considered as an alternative during acute posttraumatic agitation to protect patients and staff.

therapies_index.name: typical antipsychotic medications
therapies_index.administration: Acute use for posttraumatic confusion and agitation is not recommended.
key_toxicities: Acute use may prolong neurocognitive recovery.

therapies_index.name: amantadine
approved_indications: Recommended to accelerate recovery and reduce disability in adults with vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome or minimally conscious state at 4–16 weeks postinjury, after confounding factors have been assessed and treated.
therapies_index.administration: 100–200 mg twice daily.

therapies_index.name: cefazolin
approved_indications: Preferred surgical prophylaxis for patients without methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus unless they have a documented severe beta lactam allergy.
therapies_index.administration: Select dosing using published guidelines with pharmacist consultation.
monitoring: Clarify antibiotic allergy before surgery when possible.

therapies_index.name: clindamycin
approved_indications: Alternative surgical prophylaxis for patients with a severe beta lactam allergy.
therapies_index.administration: Select dosing using published guidelines with pharmacist consultation.
monitoring: Clarify antibiotic allergy before surgery when possible.

therapies_index.name: vancomycin
approved_indications: Alternative surgical prophylaxis for patients with a severe beta lactam allergy.
therapies_index.administration: Select dosing using published guidelines with pharmacist consultation.
monitoring: Clarify antibiotic allergy before surgery when possible.

therapies_index.name: broad-spectrum antibiotics
approved_indications: Consider for open or penetrating skull fractures when the agents have high blood-brain barrier penetration.
therapies_index.administration: Treat for a maximum of 3 days.

therapies_index.name: antibiotic prophylaxis
approved_indications: Use surgical prophylaxis according to published guidelines, with pharmacist consultation and consideration of ICU antibiograms.
Perioperative antibiotics accompany surgical debridement and irrigation of open or penetrating skull fractures.
therapies_index.administration: For the described surgical debridement, give perioperative antibiotics for not more than 24 hours. Prophylaxis for EVD or intraparenchymal ICP monitor placement, skull-based fractures, CSF leaks or pneumocephalus is not recommended.
key_toxicities: Prophylaxis in the discouraged settings may promote growth of drug-resistant bacteria.
monitoring: Assess antibiotic allergy before surgery when possible.
In older adults, consider physiologic and pharmacokinetic changes when selecting the agent and dose.

therapies_index.name: antimicrobial-impregnated catheters
approved_indications: Recommended in cited guidelines to prevent ventriculostomy-related infection during EVD monitoring, subject to availability.
therapies_index.administration: Use during EVD monitoring.

therapies_index.name: fish-oil fortified EN formulas
approved_indications: Consider for enteral feeding after TBI unless contraindicated.
therapies_index.administration: Give as EN.

therapies_index.name: high-protein EN formulations
approved_indications: Preferred enteral formulations to better meet protein targets following TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Give as EN.

therapies_index.name: immune-enhancing enteral formulations
approved_indications: May reduce infectious complications and improve nutritional parameters in patients with TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Give as EN.

therapies_index.name: EN
approved_indications: First-line nutritional support after TBI once the patient is hemodynamically stable.
therapies_index.administration: Ideally initiate within 24–72 hours of injury and achieve full supplementation within 7 days. Postpyloric access is preferred if rapidly available; gastric access is acceptable rather than delaying feeding.
monitoring: Monitor nutritional status, glucose and electrolyte goals.
Indirect calorimetry is described as the optimal way to determine caloric targets.

therapies_index.name: PN
approved_indications: Consider when EN is contraindicated and its initiation is expected to be delayed.
therapies_index.administration: If EN is contraindicated, initiation within 72 hours postinjury is recommended.
monitoring: Monitor glucose and nutritional status.

therapies_index.name: postpyloric feeding
approved_indications: Preferred enteral access if obtainable promptly without delaying EN.
therapies_index.administration: Place postpyloric feeding access when it will not delay initiation of EN.
monitoring: Assess caloric delivery and feeding tolerance.

therapies_index.name: gastric access
approved_indications: Acceptable route for early EN when obtaining postpyloric access would delay feeding.
therapies_index.administration: Initiate EN through gastric access rather than postponing nutrition to obtain postpyloric access.
monitoring: Assess caloric delivery and feeding tolerance.

therapies_index.name: endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
approved_indications: Recommended early for TBI with GCS < 9, severe agitation or loss of airway protective reflexes.
May be indicated with GCS > 8, particularly when thoracic and abdominal injuries are present.
therapies_index.administration: Protect the cervical spine during intubation. Ventilator goals include oxygen saturation at least 94%, PaO2 80–100 mm Hg and, without intracranial hypertension, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg and arterial pH 7.35–7.45.
monitoring: Monitor oxygenation, PaCO2, arterial pH and end-tidal CO2.
Monitor ICP when applying ventilatory measures that may affect it.

therapies_index.name: mild hyperventilation
approved_indications: Suggested SIBICC Tier Two intervention for elevated ICP or neurological worsening.
therapies_index.administration: Target PaCO2 32–35 mm Hg. Reduction below 30 mm Hg may be justified briefly as rescue treatment for refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation while other interventions are arranged; routine reduction below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa is discouraged.
key_toxicities: Profound hyperventilation can cause arterial spasm and reduced CBF.
monitoring: Monitor PaCO2, end-tidal CO2 and ICP; the arterial–end-tidal CO2 gradient varies.

therapies_index.name: neuromuscular paralysis
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier Two option for lowering ICP in adequately sedated patients if effective.
May be attempted to improve PbtO2 in SIBICC II Tier Two.
therapies_index.administration: Begin with a trial dose; proceed to continuous infusion only if it lowers ICP.
monitoring: Assess the ICP response to the trial dose and subsequent treatment.
Assess PbtO2 when treating brain tissue hypoxia.

therapies_index.name: sedation
approved_indications: Tier Zero care to prevent agitation and ventilator asynchrony.
Increase as a SIBICC Tier One intervention to reduce ICP; increased sedation may also be attempted for low PbtO2 in Tier Two.
key_toxicities: Sedative effects can confound neurological examination and brain death assessment.
monitoring: Assess ICP when sedation is increased for intracranial hypertension.
Assess PbtO2 when sedation is used for brain tissue hypoxia.

therapies_index.name: analgesia
approved_indications: Tier Zero treatment of signs of pain.
Increase as a SIBICC Tier One intervention to lower ICP.
key_toxicities: Analgesic medications can confound neurological assessment.
monitoring: Assess signs of pain and the ICP response when analgesia is increased to lower ICP.

therapies_index.name: external ventricular drain (EVD)
therapies_index.mechanism: Allows measurement of ICP and drainage of CSF to reduce intracranial volume.
approved_indications: Gold-standard ICP measurement with an external strain-gauge transducer and therapeutic CSF drainage.
Consider placement for CSF drainage if an intraparenchymal probe was initially used.
key_toxicities: Ventricular catheter-related infection is a potential complication.
monitoring: Continue ICP monitoring during transport outside the ICU when indicated.
Follow facility insertion and maintenance protocols; minimize closed-system manipulation and avoid CSF sampling unless clinically indicated.
Remove the drain as early as clinically possible.

therapies_index.name: intraparenchymal transducer
therapies_index.mechanism: Measures ICP but does not permit CSF drainage.
approved_indications: Alternative method of ICP monitoring in adults and children.
key_toxicities: Infection is a potential complication of invasive ICP monitoring.
monitoring: Continue ICP monitoring during transport outside the ICU when indicated.
Follow facility insertion and maintenance protocols and remove the monitor as early as clinically possible.

therapies_index.name: lumbar CSF drainage
therapies_index.administration: SIBICC discourages its use for intracranial hypertension in severe TBI because sufficient supporting evidence is lacking.

therapies_index.name: MAP challenge
therapies_index.mechanism: Tests cerebral autoregulation by observing ICP and other physiological responses to a temporary rise in MAP.
approved_indications: SIBICC Tier Two assessment to help individualize MAP and CPP targets after inadequate response to initial ICP treatment.
therapies_index.administration: In a euvolemic patient with a closed cranium, initiate or increase a vasopressor infusion to raise MAP by 10–15 mm Hg for no more than 20 minutes. Use direct supervision by an experienced bedside provider and make no other therapeutic adjustments during the challenge.
monitoring: Record MAP, ICP, CPP and PbtO2 before and after the challenge.
Check arterial blood gas before and after if PbtO2 is used to assess autoregulation.

therapies_index.name: decompressive craniectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Leaves or removes the bone flap to allow decompression of a swollen brain.
approved_indications: Primary decompression after evacuation of an acute mass lesion when brain swelling is present.
Secondary decompression for elevated ICP refractory to medical treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Following a large frontotemporoparietal craniotomy, do not replace the bone flap when replacement would compress the brain. Secondary decompressive craniectomy is discussed for refractory ICP > 25 mm Hg.
key_toxicities: The guideline identifies decompressive craniectomy as an intervention with significant hazards when weighing escalation of ICP treatment, without specifying those hazards.
monitoring: Assess brain swelling, ICP and whether bone-flap replacement would compress the brain.

therapies_index.name: trauma craniotomy
approved_indications: Large craniotomy for evacuation of acute SDH, visualization of bleeding sources, hemostasis and the option of primary decompression.
therapies_index.administration: The cited approach uses a large bone flap of ≈ 12 × 15 cm; the document notes that 15 cm may be excessive for some smaller heads and that at least 13 cm in the vertical plane enables optimal middle-fossa decompression.
monitoring: After evacuation, assess brain swelling and whether the flap can be replaced without compression.

therapies_index.name: hematoma evacuation
approved_indications: Evacuate a large traumatic hematoma before neurological deterioration, regardless of GCS.
Promptly evacuate a hematoma causing deterioration after admission.
therapies_index.administration: A large hematoma is described as > 25 mL; a lower operative threshold may apply to posterior fossa lesions. Attempted burr-hole drainage of solid clots has no role.
monitoring: Assess neurological status and imaging for hematoma development, enlargement and mass effect.

therapies_index.name: surgical debridement and irrigation
approved_indications: Standard surgical care described for open or penetrating skull fractures.
therapies_index.administration: Accompany with perioperative antibiotics for not more than 24 hours.

therapies_index.name: tracheostomy
approved_indications: Consider early for severe TBI when liberation from mechanical ventilation within 7 days is unlikely.
Evaluate if extubation fails or cannot be safely attempted.
therapies_index.administration: Consider within 7 days of injury. Evidence is limited for choosing surgical versus percutaneous technique.
key_toxicities: Tracheostomy placement is an independent risk factor for dysphagia in injured older adults.
monitoring: Assess intracranial hypertension, hemodynamic stability and respiratory support requirements; uncontrolled intracranial hypertension, hemodynamic instability, FiO2 > 50% and PEEP > 10 cm H2O are relative contraindications.

therapies_index.name: laparoscopy
therapies_index.administration: Generally avoid, particularly early after TBI.
key_toxicities: Raises intra-abdominal pressure and induces hypercarbia.

therapies_index.name: peripheral nerve blocks
approved_indications: May have a role in providing analgesia and facilitating extracranial surgery in patients with TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Single-shot or continuous techniques are mentioned.

therapies_index.name: spinal and epidural anesthesia
therapies_index.administration: Contraindicated in patients with intracranial hypertension.

therapies_index.name: venovenous ECMO
approved_indications: Reported to have a survival benefit, compared with venoatrial ECMO, without anticoagulation in selected and monitored severe-polytrauma cases whose systemic oxygenation did not respond to conventional management.
therapies_index.administration: The cited selected cases used venovenous ECMO without anticoagulation.
key_toxicities: The effects of rescue ventilatory therapies on intracranial volumes and intracranial bleeding are a concern.
monitoring: Monitor and control effects on intracranial volumes and intracranial bleeding.

therapies_index.name: prone positioning
approved_indications: Potential rescue therapy for severe or refractory ventilatory failure, to be applied cautiously and individually because it has not been systematically studied in TBI.
key_toxicities: Potential effects on ICP and intracranial bleeding require caution.
monitoring: Monitor ICP and effects on intracranial volumes and bleeding.

therapies_index.name: endovascular therapy
approved_indications: Consider stenting or coil embolization for a BCVI-related pseudoaneurysm that does not heal or for recurrent cerebral ischemia despite antithrombotic therapy.
therapies_index.administration: Primary arterial embolization or sacrifice is often not recommended as the initial BCVI strategy. In children, consider surgery or endovascular therapy for Bifflgrade ≥ 3 injuries or progression during medical treatment.
key_toxicities: Periprocedural complications are a concern.
monitoring: Assess lesion healing and recurrent ischemic events; adjunctive antiplatelet therapy may still be required after some interventions.

therapies_index.name: inferior vena cava filters
approved_indications: Placement is indicated for a known VTE when therapeutic anticoagulation is contraindicated.
therapies_index.administration: Prophylactic placement in patients with TBI is no longer recommended, regardless of when pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis begins.

therapies_index.name: early mobilization
approved_indications: Early rehabilitation after TBI to limit complications of immobility and support functional recovery.
therapies_index.administration: Initiate mobilization activities within the first 48 hours of injury or once neurosurgical, hemodynamic and respiratory stability is achieved. Passive movement and splinting can begin earlier; out-of-bed mobilization requires stability and absence of significant intracranial hypertension.
monitoring: Monitor physiological responses and advance activity according to clinical stability.

therapies_index.name: multidisciplinary rehabilitation
approved_indications: Consider from the day of admission for patients with TBI, including some who remain medically unstable or mechanically ventilated.
Refer patients with GCS 13–15 and prolonged physical, cognitive or psychological symptoms.
Continue specialized postacute rehabilitation when medically stable and discharged from acute care.
therapies_index.administration: Coordinate care among PM&R, PT, OT, SLP, nursing, psychology/neuropsychology and social work; tailor interventions and subsequent care setting to individual needs.
monitoring: Assess function, mobility, physiological responses and progress throughout recovery.

therapies_index.name: dietary modifications
approved_indications: Listed as a treatment option to consider when individualizing management of established PTE.

therapies_index.name: neuromodulation
approved_indications: Listed as a treatment option to consider when individualizing management of established PTE.

conditions.name: Traumatic brain injury
conditions.description: Brain injury following trauma is managed as both an acute condition and a potential chronic disease. Its manifestations and recovery trajectories vary substantially, and a normal initial head CT does not exclude it.
conditions.epidemiology: In the US, TBI is associated annually with an estimated 4.8 million ED visits, 214,000 hospitalizations, and 69,000 deaths. An estimated 50 to 60 million people experience TBI worldwide each year.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Presentation may include altered mental status, loss of consciousness, PTA, focal neurological findings, changes in pupillary reactivity, or persistent physical, cognitive, behavioral, and psychological symptoms. Some survivors experience temporary or permanent disability.

subtypes.name: TBI and GCS 13–15
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A GCS sum score ≥ 13 is commonly associated with mild injury, although the score alone does not capture the full burden of injury.

subtypes.name: moderate TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A GCS sum score 9–12 is consistent with moderate injury.

subtypes.name: severe TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A GCS sum score ≤ 8 indicates severe injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess and serially document consciousness using separate eye, verbal, and motor responses; use the sum score for injury classification and group comparisons.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Throughout prehospital, ED, and subsequent care; obtain a baseline after immediate threats to life have been addressed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Record each component individually. The motor response is particularly relevant in more severe injury, while eye and verbal responses discriminate more effectively among less severe injuries. Classification by the sum alone is an oversimplification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and detection of neurological deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment and repeatedly during clinical monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New asymmetry may indicate brainstem compression and impending uncal herniation. A unilateral nonreactive pupil is consistent with a mass lesion on the same side; bilateral fixed, dilated pupils indicate a poor prognosis for functional recovery. Preexisting eye disease, surgery, medication, and orbital injury can complicate interpretation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain reproducible measurements of pupil size and light reactivity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an adjunct to repeated neurological examinations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Outputs include starting and ending diameter, percentage change, latency, and mean constriction and dilation velocities. Normal latency may vary during infancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify acute intracranial injury, hemorrhage, and fractures relevant to urgent management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For adult patients with head trauma and altered mental status, loss of consciousness, PTA, or focal deficit; apply the document's adult CT criteria and a validated pediatric decision rule for children. Repeat urgently after neurological worsening.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A negative scan does not rule out TBI. In patients with persistent altered mental status and an initially abnormal CT, the guideline's performance measures indicate repeat imaging in 6–12 hours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate injury not apparent on CT and persistent unexplained deficits or impaired consciousness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Principally when clinical concerns continue during acute or subacute care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: MRI is more sensitive than CT for small contusions, small extra-axial hematomas, microhemorrhages, and small white-matter lesions. The specified protocol includes T1, T2, T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted imaging/apparent diffusion coefficient, and SWI or conventional T2*weighted gradient echo.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help determine whether brain CT can be avoided in selected patients and provide supplementary information about structural injury and prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For patients 18 years or older with suspected TBI, GCS 13–15, a clinical indication for CT, and a clinician-assessed low but nonzero risk of traumatic ICH; FDA clearance specifies whole-blood measurement within 24 hours of injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For the iSTAT assay, GFAP less than 30 pg/mL together with UCH-L1 less than 360 pg/mL is considered nonelevated and rules out the need for CT under the specified conditions. A value exceeding either cutoff indicates CT, but does not establish that CT will be positive.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help select eligible adults with mild head injury who may avoid brain CT.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Under the cited Scandinavian guidelines, obtain a sample less than 6 hours after trauma in patients meeting the stated GCS and risk-factor criteria.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A result less than 0.10 mcg/L permits discharge without brain CT under those guidelines. S100B is not FDA-cleared for routine clinical use in the US.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and help manage seizures, including nonconvulsive seizures that may explain reduced consciousness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when seizure monitoring is clinically relevant.

diagnostic_workup.test: INR, TEG, ROTEM, and platelet function assays
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess coagulopathy and provide information about targeted reversal therapy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Early in TBI care when coagulation abnormalities or relevant preinjury medication exposure are a concern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline gives an INR goal of ≤ 1.4 in most cases. Normal routine coagulation results do not necessarily exclude clinically relevant DOAC concentrations.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Day-of-injury blood concentrations contribute to assessment of structural brain injury and, in patients with GCS 3–12, to prediction of functional recovery.
Day-of-injury blood concentrations contribute to assessment of structural brain injury and, in patients with GCS 3–12, to prediction of functional recovery.
In appropriately selected adults, a blood result below the specified threshold can support avoiding CT under the cited Scandinavian guidelines.

staging.additional_rules: GCS-based categories are approximate and should not be treated as a complete, single-dimensional measure of injury.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Individual component scores provide complementary information; the sum may aid prognostic estimation alongside other factors, but does not adequately characterize injury burden by itself.

prognostic_tools.name: Rotterdam CT score
prognostic_tools.interpretation: A score of 1 to 6 derived from CT findings predicts TBI-related 6-month mortality in patients with GCS 3–12.

prognostic_tools.name: IMPACT
components: Neurological function, including GCS score and/or pupillary reactivity
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The validated statistical model provides population-based outcome estimates with CI. It should not be used to make an exact prognosis for an individual.

prognostic_tools.name: CRASH TBI
components: Neurological function, including GCS score and/or pupillary reactivity
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The validated statistical model provides population-based outcome estimates with CI. It should not be used to make an exact prognosis for an individual.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOS-E)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: This global outcome measure has floor and ceiling effects and does not capture the full range of TBI sequelae. It is unsuitable during the initial hospitalization.

prognostic_tools.name: Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Provides additional neurological detail in patients with substantial consciousness impairment; GCS remains the preferred general ICU tool for monitoring consciousness.

follow_up.schedule: Perform standardized serial outcome assessment, ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months after injury. Individual patients may need more frequent assessment, and many may benefit from follow-up extending months, years, or longer.
recommended_tests: Multidimensional assessment of physical, cognitive, communication, behavioral, psychological, and quality-of-life outcomes
Evaluation for medical or psychiatric causes when recovery plateaus or function declines
long_term_effects: Persistent physical, cognitive, behavioral, and psychological impairments
Potential functional deterioration as well as continued recovery years after injury
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Arrange access to a clinician experienced in TBI management after acute-care discharge. Educate patients and families about recovery, persistent symptoms, available resources, and routes to further care.

conditions.name: TBI and GCS 13–15
conditions.description: This presentation spans patients with subtle deficits and normal imaging through patients with substantial intracranial pathology despite a relatively preserved GCS score.
conditions.epidemiology: Approximately 90% of patients seen annually in US EDs with suspected TBI have GCS 13–15. An estimated 50% of patients in this category who present to the ED have their TBI undetected and undiagnosed. Approximately 50% of diagnosed patients evaluated in the ED have not fully recovered by 12 months after injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms may include headache, dizziness, visual or oculomotor difficulty, cognitive and sleep problems, sensory changes, and psychological symptoms. At least half experience cognitive, somatic, or psychological symptoms that disrupt usual activities for months or years.

diagnostic_workup.test: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and neurological examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize consciousness and deficits and identify possible deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation and during reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A score of 13–15 does not exclude consequential intracranial injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify ICH and injuries potentially requiring urgent neurosurgical care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use applicable clinical decision criteria; in children, follow a validated pediatric rule such as PECARN.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Most patients in this GCS category have no traumatic intracranial lesion visible on CT, but a negative CT does not exclude TBI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help avoid unnecessary CT in eligible adults.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for patients 18 years or older who have a CT indication, GCS 13–15, and a low but nonzero assessed risk of traumatic ICH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For iSTAT, both GFAP less than 30 pg/mL and UCH-L1 less than 360 pg/mL are considered nonelevated. Elevation of either indicates CT. These biomarkers alone are not sufficiently accurate to predict functional recovery in GCS 13–15 TBI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess injuries not identified by CT when symptoms or deficits persist.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical concerns remain after initial evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess persistent symptoms and the contribution of injury and noninjury factors.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May benefit children whose symptoms persist at 3 months.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Marked day-of-injury elevation in a patient with GCS 15 indicates a risk of prolonged recovery, but the biomarker alone does not predict functional recovery accurately enough in GCS 13–15 TBI.
Marked day-of-injury elevation in a patient with GCS 15 indicates a risk of prolonged recovery, but the biomarker alone does not predict functional recovery accurately enough in GCS 13–15 TBI.

definitions.description: A sum score commonly classified as mild injury, although anatomical injury and clinical impairment may differ markedly between patients.

staging.additional_rules: Do not infer the full extent of injury from the GCS sum score alone.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

risk_groups.expected_outcome: Recovery varies; approximately 50% of diagnosed patients evaluated in the ED do not achieve full recovery by 12 months.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: A relatively high score does not reliably exclude persistent disability.

follow_up.schedule: Provide follow-up options at discharge. Symptoms persisting longer than 2 weeks postinjury may warrant targeted assessment and treatment; consider neuropsychological testing in children with symptoms persisting at 3 months.
recommended_tests: Assessment of persistent physical, cognitive, and psychological symptoms
Standardized outcome assessment ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months
Neuropsychological testing for selected children with prolonged symptoms
long_term_effects: Persistent symptoms affecting daily activities, school, or work
Possible loss of independence and reduced quality of life in older adults
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Explain the injury and expected recovery, discuss return to work, school, driving, and other activities, and direct patients with continuing difficulties toward clinicians or multidisciplinary rehabilitation services experienced in TBI.

conditions.name: moderate TBI
conditions.description: A category commonly associated with a GCS sum score of 9–12; the anatomical burden and course still require individual assessment.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may have altered consciousness, neurological deficits, or traumatic findings on imaging. Nonconvulsive seizures were reported in an estimated 25% of patients with moderate to severe TBI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Serially assess consciousness and its separate components.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Throughout acute care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A sum score of 9–12 is consistent with moderate injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify structural damage and lesions that may require intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute assessment; repeat when neurological findings worsen or according to the indicated monitoring plan.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: More than 80% of patients in the combined GCS 3–12 group have intracranial injury visible on CT.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect seizures, including nonconvulsive events.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When seizure detection and management are needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Supplement structural injury assessment and prediction of functional recovery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When measured on the day of injury in patients within the GCS 3–12 group.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Higher values are associated with more severe structural injury and a poorer prognosis; they are adjuncts, not stand-alone prognostic measures.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Day-of-injury values may supplement prediction of 6-month functional recovery in the combined GCS 3–12 population.
Day-of-injury values may supplement prediction of 6-month functional recovery in the combined GCS 3–12 population.

staging.additional_rules: GCS alone is an incomplete representation of injury burden.

prognostic_tools.name: Rotterdam CT score
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Its 1 to 6 score predicts TBI-related mortality at 6 months in the combined GCS 3–12 population.

follow_up.schedule: Assess outcomes serially, ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months after injury.
recommended_tests: Assessment across physical, cognitive, communication, behavioral, and psychological domains
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Continued rehabilitation and follow-up by clinicians experienced in TBI may be needed.

conditions.name: severe TBI
conditions.description: A severe brain injury commonly indicated by GCS ≤ 8, with substantial risk of secondary injury and long-term disability. Early clinical findings do not permit highly certain prediction of an individual's eventual outcome.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may be comatose and may have structural brain injury, intracranial hypertension, impaired cerebral oxygenation, or prolonged disorders of consciousness.

diagnostic_workup.test: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and serial neurological examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Track consciousness and neurological change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment and regularly thereafter.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: GCS ≤ 8 supports classification as severe TBI; assess eye, verbal, and motor responses separately.

diagnostic_workup.test: Head CT and serial CT imaging
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify structural injury and detect progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation and when neurological deterioration or other indications arise.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CT evidence of structural damage in a comatose patient supports ICP monitoring.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect intracranial hypertension, guide treatment, and permit calculation of CPP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Recommended for comatose patients with GCS ≤ 8 and structural brain damage on initial CT; consider other clinical indications described in the guideline.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interpret both the magnitude and duration of elevation, trends, arterial pressure, CPP, and autoregulatory responses. Monitoring does not replace neurological examination or imaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify brain tissue hypoxia that can occur even when ICP and CPP are normal.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When advanced neuromonitoring is used.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The recommended monitored target is ≥ 15 mm Hg.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and help manage seizures, particularly nonconvulsive seizures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider as part of neuromonitoring when clinically appropriate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist assessment of consciousness for prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider after factors that confound the neurological examination have been assessed and treated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline reports that standardized neurobehavioral scales can detect consciousness better than qualitative bedside examination.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Day-of-injury levels supplement assessment of injury severity and prediction of 6-month outcome in patients with GCS 3–12.
Day-of-injury levels supplement assessment of injury severity and prediction of 6-month outcome in patients with GCS 3–12.

staging.additional_rules: Assess injury and prognosis using more than the GCS sum score.

prognostic_tools.name: IMPACT
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Offers an uncertain population-based estimate rather than an exact individual prognosis.

prognostic_tools.name: CRASH TBI
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Offers an uncertain population-based estimate rather than an exact individual prognosis.

prognostic_tools.name: Rotterdam CT score
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Predicts TBI-related mortality at 6 months in patients with GCS 3–12.

follow_up.schedule: Continue reassessment during acute care and recovery; assess outcomes ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months after injury.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Meaningful recovery can occur despite prolonged early unconsciousness. Prognostic discussions should acknowledge uncertainty and incorporate the patient's values and preferences.

conditions.name: intracranial hypertension
conditions.description: Sustained ICP elevation is a measurable secondary insult after severe TBI and may compromise cerebral perfusion or lead to herniation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible warning findings include neurological decline, new pupillary asymmetry, or an unreactive dilated pupil, although physiological changes can precede an observable examination change.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure pressure and permit CSF drainage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When invasive monitoring is indicated, especially in comatose patients with structural damage on initial CT.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An EVD connected to an external strain-gauge transducer is the stated measurement standard. An initial treatment threshold of 22 mm Hg is useful; interpretation should also account for duration and trend.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor pressure when selected instead of an EVD.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When ICP monitoring is clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Provides reliable pressure measurements but cannot drain CSF.

diagnostic_workup.test: Serial neurological examinations and head CT
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess deterioration and identify evolving structural lesions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Alongside ICP monitoring or when more advanced monitoring is unavailable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Monitoring pressure alone does not replace clinical and radiographic reassessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess cerebral autoregulation and help individualize CPP goals.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when raised ICP does not respond to initial therapy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a patient with a closed cranium, rising ICP as MAP increases indicates impaired autoregulation; falling or substantially unchanged ICP indicates intact autoregulation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Continuously assess pressure autoregulation to inform CPP targets.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the required technical expertise and equipment are available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline describes PRx slope > 0.13 as impaired autoregulation and PRx slope < 0.13 as intact autoregulation.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline describes a commonly accepted treatment trigger of ICP 22 mm Hg, with a reasonable range of 20–25 mm Hg for more than 5 minutes; escalation also depends on duration, trend, injury characteristics, and treatment risks. For children, an upper limit of 20 mm Hg is recommended.

follow_up.schedule: Continue neurological, radiographic, and physiological reassessment during acute management, including when monitored patients leave the ICU for procedures.
long_term_effects: Persistently elevated ICP predicts a poor outcome.

conditions.name: acute SDH
conditions.description: A traumatic extra-axial hematoma for which a large or expanding lesion can require prompt evacuation. An acute SDH is a typical mass lesion addressed during primary decompressive craniectomy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A large hematoma may cause coma or neurological deterioration; progression can also occur after admission.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the hematoma, its size, associated injury, and potential progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute evaluation and again when the neurological examination deteriorates.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: SDH > 8 mm is a moderate-risk criterion for ICH progression in the modified Berne-Norwood criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize deterioration and guide the urgency of intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Throughout acute observation and treatment.

prognostic_tools.name: modified Berne-Norwood criteria
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Stratifies risk of intracranial hemorrhage progression rather than providing a definitive prognosis for an individual.

follow_up.schedule: Reassess clinically during acute care and repeat imaging when indicated by deterioration or the need to establish hemorrhage stability.

conditions.name: EDH
conditions.description: A traumatic extra-axial hematoma that may require urgent evacuation when large or associated with clinical deterioration.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A large lesion can contribute to coma or subsequent neurological deterioration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the lesion and reassess for progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At acute presentation and when neurological status worsens.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: EDH > 8 mm is listed among moderate-risk findings for ICH progression in the modified Berne-Norwood criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect changes that may require urgent intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute care.

follow_up.schedule: Continue neurological assessment and obtain follow-up imaging when clinically indicated.

conditions.name: traumatic intracerebral hematoma
conditions.description: An intraparenchymal traumatic lesion whose surgical management is less certain when the lesion is small; mass effect and neurological decline make the decision for intervention more straightforward.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May produce mass effect or neurological deterioration. Contusions may enlarge and contribute to intracranial hypertension.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize hematoma or contusion, mass effect, and progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation and when deterioration or reassessment of pathology warrants imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Contusion or IVH > 2 cm, or multiple contusions per lobe, are moderate-risk findings for ICH progression under the modified Berne-Norwood criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect declining function and inform management decisions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Serially during acute care.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify intracranial hypertension in patients at risk of lesion progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Carefully consider in patients with GCS > 8 and large or multiple contusions at high risk of progression.

prognostic_tools.name: modified Berne-Norwood criteria

risk_groups.criteria: Includes contusion or IVH > 2 cm or multiple contusions per lobe.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Used to stratify hemorrhage progression risk.

follow_up.schedule: Perform serial clinical reassessment and repeat imaging when progression or deterioration is suspected.

conditions.name: depressed skull fractures
conditions.description: Skull fractures with inward displacement may require a different approach according to the degree and location of depression, whether the fracture is open, and the presence of contamination or associated injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A skull deformity or suspected fracture can be evident during initial assessment.

subtypes.name: Open depressed skull fractures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually managed surgically to prevent infection; selected fractures without dural laceration, major contamination, infection, or frontal sinus injury may be considered for nonoperative management.

subtypes.name: depressed skull fractures over a dural venous sinus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually not surgically treated because uncontrolled hemorrhage is a substantial concern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify fracture characteristics and associated intracranial injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When skull fracture is suspected after head trauma.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify deformity, an open wound, possible penetrating injury, and clinical signs of associated skull-base injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During initial and subsequent trauma assessment.

long_term_effects: Posttraumatic epilepsy is associated with skull fracture and unelevated depressed skull fractures among the risk factors listed in the guideline.

conditions.name: extracranial BCVI
conditions.description: Traumatic injury of the extracranial carotid or vertebral arteries can lead to thromboembolism and ischemic stroke if it goes undetected.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported BCVI incidence is 2.7% to 7.6% among patients who underwent CT angiography after blunt trauma. The guideline cites mortality as high as 38% for untreated carotid injuries and 18% for untreated vertebral injuries.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Injury may be asymptomatic or accompanied by transient ischemic symptoms, focal deficits, or infarction. Cervical spine fractures are the strongest single predictor identified in the guideline, particularly for vertebral artery injury.

subtypes.name: carotid artery injury
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May produce cerebral ischemia; the document discusses stenting in selected injuries.

subtypes.name: vertebral artery injury
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Especially associated with spine fractures; selected injuries may be considered for stenting or embolic occlusion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for and exclude extracranial BCVI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When BCVI risk factors are present; the guideline calls for liberal screening in at-risk older adults.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The recommended radiographic screening modality. Strict application of Denver and Memphis screening criteria nevertheless misses 20% to 30% of BCVIs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess uncertain lesions or injuries potentially suitable for endovascular treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When CT angiography leaves an injury in question or endovascular treatment is being considered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify cerebral ischemia or edema in a vascular territory.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When neurological findings or injury assessment raise concern for BCVI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence of cerebral ischemia or vascular-territory edema is among the listed screening criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Stratify pediatric BCVI risk to inform dedicated vascular imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During pediatric evaluation when BCVI is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A score ≥ 3 was associated with an 18% risk of BCVI, whereas a score ≤ 2 was associated with less than 3% risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess healing.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Follow-up imaging at 3 months is described as reasonable.

staging.additional_rules: In children, the guideline advises considering surgery or endovascular therapy for higher-grade injuries, identified as Bifflgrade ≥ 3, or lesions progressing during medical treatment.

prognostic_tools.name: The Utah score
prognostic_tools.interpretation: A pediatric risk-stratification score with a maximum of 11 points.

prognostic_tools.name: McGovern modification
components: Severe injury mechanism related to motor vehicle collision: two additional points
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The modification increases sensitivity for pediatric BCVI diagnosis.

follow_up.schedule: Antithrombotic treatment generally continues for at least 3 months; CT angiography or MRI at 3 months is reasonable to assess healing.
recommended_tests: Follow-up CT angiography or MRI at 3 months
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Arrange follow-up after discharge when warranted. The guideline states that evidence is insufficient to specify a pediatric treatment duration.

conditions.name: early posttraumatic seizures
conditions.description: Seizures occurring < 7 days after TBI are associated with injury severity and with later PTE risk.
conditions.epidemiology: In the cited RCT, early PTS occurred in 14.2% of the placebo group and 3.6% of patients assigned to phenytoin.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Seizures may be convulsive or nonconvulsive. Risk is particularly high after penetrating injury and is also increased with immediate PTS, depressed skull fracture, SDH, ICH, GCS < 10, or cortical contusion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify seizure activity and changes in consciousness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute TBI care.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect nonconvulsive seizures and support seizure management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When diminished consciousness or other findings raise concern for seizures.

staging.additional_rules: Early PTS is defined by occurrence < 7 days after injury; late PTS occurs more than 7 days postinjury.

follow_up.schedule: Assess for later seizure activity during recovery and follow-up.
recommended_tests: Further diagnostic testing when potential seizure activity is identified
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Educate families about possible signs of later epilepsy, including subtle changes in consciousness.

conditions.name: posttraumatic epilepsy
conditions.description: Epilepsy arising after TBI is a clinically significant long-term complication. Its cumulative incidence increases over time.
conditions.epidemiology: Earlier population-based studies attributed about 4% of epilepsy diagnoses to TBI, while other studies cited incidence as high as 20%. The guideline reports that recurrent seizures after a first late seizure occur in as many as 86% by 2 years postinjury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Seizure manifestations can include subtle changes in consciousness. The listed risk factors include evacuated SDH, contusion with SDH, evacuation of intraparenchymal hematoma, GCS 3–8, early seizures, loss of consciousness or amnesia > 1 day, inability to follow commands for > 7 days, skull fracture, dural penetration, nonreactive pupils, parietal lesions, age > 65 years, female sex, family history of epilepsy, and history of depression.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect possible PTE during long-term follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During post-TBI follow-up, particularly in patients with PTE risk factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Potential seizure activity warrants further diagnostic assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support evaluation of suspected seizure activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical findings suggest seizures.

staging.additional_rules: A late PTS occurs more than 7 days postinjury.

follow_up.schedule: Provide ongoing seizure screening after TBI, including as patients age; arrange specialist follow-up when late seizures develop.
recommended_tests: Further diagnostic testing if seizure activity is suspected
long_term_effects: Possible additional morbidity and mortality after TBI
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Before acute-care discharge, teach families to recognize possible PTE, including less obvious changes in consciousness. The guideline notes uncertainty about how much worse outcomes reflect PTE itself rather than underlying injury severity.

conditions.name: disorders of consciousness
conditions.description: Prolonged impairment of consciousness after TBI is characterized clinically as coma, vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, or minimally conscious state.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients have sustained alterations in consciousness. The absence of regained consciousness early after injury does not by itself establish that meaningful functional recovery is impossible.

subtypes.name: coma
