subtypes.distinguishing_features: A clinical category of prolonged altered consciousness identified by examination.

subtypes.name: vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A clinical category of prolonged altered consciousness identified by examination.

subtypes.name: minimally conscious state
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A clinical category of prolonged altered consciousness identified by examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize consciousness and identify change over time.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During acute care and subsequent recovery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evaluate and address factors that can confound the examination, including sedative or analgesic medication and clinical or nonconvulsive seizures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess consciousness using a standardized neurobehavioral measure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider during prognostic evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline reports better detection of consciousness with standardized scales than with qualitative bedside examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Follow eye, verbal, and motor responses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During serial clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional neurological detail in markedly impaired consciousness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly relevant in the ICU, including when intubation prevents testing the GCS verbal component.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assesses eye and motor responses, brainstem reflexes, and respiration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate nonconvulsive seizures as a cause of impaired consciousness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When seizures may confound assessment.

prognostic_tools.name: Coma Recovery Scale–Revised
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Consider for identifying consciousness during prognostic assessment.

prognostic_tools.name: Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Offers more neurological detail than GCS in patients with greater consciousness impairment.

follow_up.schedule: Use continued treatment and observation when appropriate rather than treating an early absence of consciousness as a definitive prognosis.
recommended_tests: Evaluation for confounding medications and seizures
long_term_effects: Prolonged disability may occur, but meaningful recovery remains possible after extended unconsciousness.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline reports acceptable functional outcomes in up to 20% of patients who do not regain consciousness during the first 4 weeks after injury.

conditions.name: Paroxysmal Hyperactivity Syndrome
conditions.description: After TBI, disruption of inhibitory control over sympathetic activity can produce episodes of autonomic hyperactivity.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations may include hypertension, tachycardia, hyperpyrexia, tachypnea, and diaphoresis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize the described autonomic manifestations.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When episodic sympathetic symptoms occur after TBI.

recommended_tests: Monitor for adverse effects when BBKs are used.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline identifies bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure, and bronchospasm as BBK adverse effects that can be harmful during acute recovery.

special_populations.considerations: Low-level falls can cause significant TBI, while frailty, polypharmacy, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, age-related physiology, and preexisting conditions can reduce the accuracy of field triage. Dementia, delirium, aphasia, or ophthalmic disease may complicate interpretation of GCS or pupillary findings. A reassuring GCS score and examination do not reliably exclude intracranial injury. Anticoagulation is associated with a higher incidence of ICH. Baseline GFAP and UCH-L1 levels may rise with age or neurodegenerative disease, narrowing their ability to distinguish acute injury. Cerebral atrophy may reduce the risk of intracranial hypertension, but evidence about the outcome benefit of ICP monitoring in this population remains conflicting. Aging physiology and comorbidities can complicate interpretation of neuromonitoring and prolong drug effects. Malnutrition at admission can be as high as 62%; dysphagia adds risks of aspiration and inadequate nutrition. Older adults may have baseline oropharyngeal dysfunction and face dysphagia risks with both oral intubation and tracheostomy. Falls and comorbidities increase concern for PTE, while polypharmacy can complicate ASM use. Frailty is an important predictor of poor outcomes; age alone is not a sufficient reason to limit treatment. Persistent symptoms after TBI with GCS 13–15 can impair independence and quality of life.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider trauma-center triage and use early head CT more liberally when clinically appropriate, particularly with anticoagulation; liberal imaging and observation are often recommended for older adults with GCS 13–15. Use the medical history to interpret abnormal pupils. Individualize ICP-monitoring decisions and assess ICP-directed drug doses for toxicity or prolonged action. Screen and repeatedly assess nutritional status; the Mini Nutritional Assessment and Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index are named tools. Decisions about invasive ventilation or tracheostomy should account for individual goals of care. For VTE prophylaxis, follow the approach used for other adults, but consider altered renal function when dosing LMWH or selecting UFH. Screen liberally for BCVI when risk factors are present, including after lower-energy injury. Select an ASM for PTE with minimal cognitive adverse effects and drug interactions. Consider palliative care consultation for patients identified as frail. Plan early rehabilitation with multidisciplinary and geriatric input, emphasizing mobilization, delirium prevention, medication review, function, balance, coordination, and energy conservation.

special_populations.considerations: Children with suspected TBI benefit from assessment and transport suited to pediatric care; a caregiver-reported change from baseline behavior is a high-risk field-triage finding. CT exposes children to a greater risk of radiation-induced malignancy. Clinical examination, cerebral blood-flow physiology, and appropriate CPP vary with development; validated normative thresholds for pediatric PbtO2 and autoregulation measures are lacking. Evidence about blood GFAP, UCH-L1, and S100B for suspected pediatric TBI is insufficient. Infants may be particularly susceptible to posttraumatic seizures, while PTE is less common in children than adults except after abusive head trauma. Pediatric BCVI is less prevalent than adult BCVI, and applying the Denver criteria may overestimate its incidence. VTE is uncommon in pediatric trauma, with reported incidence of 0.09% at ages 0–12 years, 0.27% at ages 13–15 years, and 0.73% at ages 16–21 years. Children with GCS 13–15 can have persistent symptoms, and school participation and family needs are important parts of recovery. Findings from adult tracheostomy practice may not apply to infants and children under 10 years old.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Prefer a pediatric-capable trauma center when indicated; transfer may be unnecessary for selected low-risk injuries. Use pGCS for preverbal children aged 0–2 years. Base urgent head-imaging decisions on a validated pediatric rule such as PECARN, and use CT judiciously; for selected children with GCS 15, no palpable skull fracture, and no concerning basilar-fracture findings, observation for 4 to 6 hours may avoid imaging even with 1 or 2 PECARN predictors. Pediatric severe-TBI guidance recommends an ICP upper limit of 20 mm Hg; CPP goals above 50 mm Hg at ages 6 to 17 years and above 40 mm Hg at ages 0 to 5 years appear appropriate for treatment-based studies. For intracranial hypertension, supported hypertonic-saline approaches include 3% boluses of 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 20 min, a constant rate of 0.1–1 mL/kg/hour, or 23.4% at 0.5 mL/kg (up to 30 mL) over 10 to 20 minutes; evidence for mannitol is weaker. The pediatric Tier Two hypoventilation target is 28 to 34 mm Hg. Moderate prophylactic hypothermia at 32–33°C is not recommended over normothermia to improve overall outcomes, although it is suggested for ICP control. Start EN after hemodynamic stabilization, ideally within 24 to 72 hours, and attempt full supplementation within 7 days while accounting for hydration and electrolyte goals; consider PN if EN is contraindicated. A cuffed endotracheal tube is favored when intubation is required. Use a published pediatric VTE risk tool such as ROCKIT after admission: low-risk children do not require pharmacologic prophylaxis, moderate-risk children need mechanical prophylaxis at admission, and pharmacologic prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk patients. LMWH is preferred, with weight-based dosing in young children; discontinue prophylaxis once ambulatory if no other thrombogenic factors remain. For indicated PTS prophylaxis, either levetiracetam or (fos)phenytoin is appropriate for 7 days; the commonly used levetiracetam dose is 20–40 mg/kg/day in two doses. Pediatric BCVI risk stratification may use the Utah score, with the McGovern modification adding two points for a severe motor-vehicle-collision mechanism; consider surgery or endovascular therapy for Bifflgrade ≥ 3 or progression during medical treatment. Refer children after TBI to primary care for return-to-school and activity planning; consider specialty follow-up for prolonged-recovery risk and neuropsychological testing for symptoms persisting at 3 months. Refer late seizures to a clinician with pediatric and epilepsy expertise.

recommendations.statement: Transport adults and children with suspected TBI who meet a high-risk criterion promptly from the scene to the highest-level trauma center available.
recommendations.context: High-risk criteria include GCS motor score < 6, GCS total score < 13, skull deformity or suspected fracture, signs of basilar skull fracture, penetrating head injury, or a caregiver-reported change from baseline behavior in an infant or child.
recommendations.rationale: These patients may need rapid resuscitation, surgery, and critical care to prevent secondary brain injury.

recommendations.statement: During transport of patients with suspected TBI, monitor for hypotension, hypoxia, hypercarbia, and hypothermia and begin corrective measures.
Preferentially direct children with suspected TBI to centers equipped to care for pediatric patients.

Hospitals without neurosurgical services that initially resuscitate patients with TBI should have predetermined arrangements for immediate air or ground transfer to a center with continuous TBI care capability.
recommendations.context: Initial care at such a hospital may occasionally be reasonable in rural areas with long transport times; rapid transfer is particularly important with an abnormal neurological examination, displaced skull fracture, or substantial intracranial injury.

recommendations.statement: Use a standardized approach to GCS assessment and reporting, and record the eye, verbal, and motor component scores separately for each patient.
recommendations.context: Use the summed GCS score for injury classification and comparisons between patient groups.
recommendations.rationale: Component-level documentation improves communication and permits recognition of changes over time.

recommendations.statement: Assess and document pupillary light responses during neurological monitoring; consider quantitative pupillometry to obtain more consistent measurements of reactivity.
recommendations.rationale: Pupillary responses offer diagnostic and prognostic information, while quantitative measurement is more reproducible than standard clinical assessment.

recommendations.statement: Obtain a head CT in adult trauma patients with a head injury caused by an external force when altered mental status, LOC, PTA, or a focal neurological deficit is present.
Determine whether a child needs emergent head imaging with a validated pediatric decision rule, such as the PECARN decision guide.
recommendations.context: CT should be used judiciously in children because of radiation risk.

recommendations.statement: For patients 16 years of age and older with LOC or PTA, obtain a non-contrast head CT if an additional criterion listed in the CDC/ACEP clinical policy is present.
recommendations.context: The additional criteria are GCS less than 15, age greater than 60 years, visible injury above the clavicle, coagulopathy, headache, vomiting, drug or alcohol intoxication, short-term memory deficit, posttraumatic seizure, or focal neurological deficit. This recommendation is attributed to the CDC/ACEP clinical policy.

recommendations.statement: Consider head CT even without LOC or PTA when GCS is less than 15, age is 65 years and older, or coagulopathy, focal neurological deficit, severe headache, vomiting, signs of basilar skull fracture, or a dangerous injury mechanism is present.
For head CT, obtain axial, coronal, and sagittal brain images with 2.0 mm to 3.75 mm slices, together with 0.5 mm to 1.25 mm bone-algorithm images.
recommendations.rationale: The bone-algorithm images improve visualization of craniofacial fractures.

recommendations.statement: Include T1, T2, T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted imaging/apparent diffusion coefficient, and SWI in the brain MRI protocol; use conventional T2*-weighted gradient echo if SWI is unavailable.
recommendations.rationale: The susceptibility-sensitive sequences improve detection of microhemorrhages that may not appear on CT.

recommendations.statement: Blood GFAP, UCH-L1, or S100B testing can help exclude the need for brain CT in selected patients with suspected TBI.
recommendations.context: Patients must have GCS 13–15, meet clinical CT decision-rule criteria, and have a clinician-assessed low but nonzero risk of traumatic ICH; applicable assay requirements and sampling windows must be observed.

recommendations.statement: Use S100B for an imaging decision only when blood can be collected within 6 hours of injury.
recommendations.context: S100B is not FDA-cleared for routine clinical use in the US.
recommendations.rationale: Its short half-life restricts the useful sampling interval.

recommendations.statement: Under the Scandinavian guidelines, consider S100B testing in adults with mild head injury within 6 hours of trauma who have either GCS 14 without listed risk factors or GCS 15 with LOC or repeated vomiting (≥ 2) and no other risk factors; a result less than 0.10 mcg/L permits discharge without brain CT.
recommendations.context: The risk factors specified for GCS 14 include anticoagulant therapy or coagulation disorders, posttraumatic seizures, clinical signs of depressed or basal skull fracture, and focal neurological deficits. This recommendation is attributed to the Scandinavian guidelines.

recommendations.statement: For the FDA-approved iSTAT assay, brain CT is unnecessary when GFAP is less than 30 pg/mL and UCH-L1 is less than 360 pg/mL; obtain brain CT if either biomarker exceeds its cutoff.
recommendations.context: FDA clearance requires testing whole blood within 24 hours of injury. An elevated result does not establish that CT will show an injury.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients with GCS 15 and substantially elevated GFAP and/or UCH-L1 to a brain injury/concussion clinic; advise those without elevated values to seek care if symptoms persist.
recommendations.context: Biomarkers alone do not predict functional recovery accurately enough in GCS 13–15 TBI.
recommendations.rationale: Elevated values indicate a greater risk of prolonged recovery, although nonelevated values do not eliminate that risk.

recommendations.statement: Aim to maintain clinical parameters within normal physiological ranges after considering the potential benefits and risks of each intervention.
recommendations.context: The ranges in Table 4 are ideal targets, not mandatory goals to be pursued regardless of circumstances.

recommendations.statement: Use ICP 22 mm Hg as an initial treatment threshold; when escalation entails substantial risk, consider a treatment range of 20–25 mm Hg.
Target CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg, adjusting the goal to cerebral autoregulation; if PbtO2 is monitored, target ≥ 15 mm Hg.
Initially target SpO2 ≥ 94%, PaO2 80–100 mm Hg, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg, and pH 7.35–7.45 when intracranial hypertension is absent; avoid PaO2 > 100 mm Hg unless brain oximetry guides treatment.
recommendations.context: Patients with substantial pulmonary disease may need condition-specific ventilation targets while ICP is controlled by other measures.
recommendations.rationale: Excessive oxygenation may be harmful.

recommendations.statement: Monitor SBP and MAP closely and treat to achieve SBP ≥ 110 mm Hg/MAP > 80 mm Hg when ICP is not monitored.
recommendations.rationale: These targets generally support cerebral perfusion while avoiding hypotension.

recommendations.statement: Maintain normothermia at 36–37.9°C and treat fever aggressively.
Maintain serum sodium at 135–145 mEq/L, monitor it as frequently as clinically necessary, and measure osmolality when using mannitol.
recommendations.rationale: Avoiding hyponatremia helps prevent worsening cerebral edema.

recommendations.statement: Monitor serum glucose closely, targeting 100–180 mg/dL; consider more frequent checks when nutritional support begins, particularly with confirmed or suspected diabetes mellitus.
recommendations.rationale: Both low and high glucose levels may adversely affect outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Assess coagulation early using INR, with a target INR ≤ 1.4 in most cases; TEG, ROTEM, or platelet function assays may supplement evaluation for targeted reversal.
Monitor ICP in comatose patients with GCS ≤ 8 when the initial CT shows structural brain injury.
recommendations.rationale: ICP monitoring can identify intracranial hypertension and guide cerebral perfusion management.

recommendations.statement: Carefully consider ICP monitoring when structural injury has a high risk of progression despite GCS > 8, when ICP data would aid other treatment decisions, when CT findings progress or the patient deteriorates, or when surgery or necessary sedation limits neurological examination.

Generally do not place an ICP monitor in a comatose patient whose initial CT shows neither structural injury nor signs of elevated ICP; instead, observation with serial neurological examinations and CT may continue.

Use an EVD connected to an external strain-gauge transducer as the reference method for ICP measurement; an intraparenchymal transducer is another option, but subdural and epidural monitors are not recommended.
recommendations.context: An EVD also permits CSF drainage.
recommendations.rationale: Subdural and epidural monitors have lower accuracy.

recommendations.statement: For children, consider ICP monitoring with either an EVD or an intraparenchymal transducer and use 20 mm Hg as the recommended upper ICP limit.
recommendations.context: Select the monitoring method according to case-specific risks and advantages.
recommendations.rationale: Retrospective evidence did not show better outcomes with other pediatric ICP limits.

recommendations.statement: Treat sustained ICP elevation after severe TBI; use the SIBICC tiered algorithms as adaptable consensus guidance rather than as mandatory standards of practice.
recommendations.context: Relevant disciplines should review the algorithms and approve or adapt them locally.
recommendations.rationale: The tiers generally place interventions with more favorable risk-benefit profiles before those with less favorable profiles.

recommendations.statement: For ICU patients with TBI, provide SIBICC Tier Zero care irrespective of ICP, including serial neurological and pupillary examinations, head-of-bed elevation to 30–45°, fever prevention, initial CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin > 7 g/dL, avoidance of hyponatremia, and SpO2 ≥ 94%.
recommendations.context: The algorithm also lists ICU admission, intubation and ventilation, pain-directed analgesia, sedation to prevent agitation or ventilator asynchrony, core temperature measurement and treatment above 38.0°C, optimization of venous drainage, an arterial line, consideration of antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only, and central-line and end-tidal CO2 monitoring.

recommendations.statement: For SIBICC Tier One intracranial hypertension treatment, target CPP 60–70 mm Hg, intensify analgesia or sedation as appropriate, maintain PaCO2 at 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa, use intermittent mannitol 0.25–1.0 g/kg or hypertonic saline boluses, and drain CSF through an EVD when present.
recommendations.context: The algorithm also suggests considering EVD placement when an intraparenchymal probe was placed initially, antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only when appropriate, and EEG monitoring. The stated administration limits for either hypertonic saline or mannitol are sodium 155 mEq/L and osmolality 320 mEq/L.

recommendations.statement: For SIBICC Tier Two treatment, consider PaCO2 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa, neuromuscular paralysis only if a trial lowers ICP in an adequately sedated patient, and a MAP challenge to individualize MAP and CPP targets.
recommendations.context: Return MAP to baseline if autoregulation is disrupted, or consider a higher target to lower ICP when autoregulation is intact.

recommendations.statement: For SIBICC Tier Three treatment, consider pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone if testing shows ICP benefit, secondary decompressive craniectomy, or active cooling to 35–36°C.
recommendations.context: Continue barbiturates only if ICP improves; titrate for ICP control without exceeding the dose that produces burst suppression, and avoid hypotension.

recommendations.statement: Discourage continuous non-bolus mannitol infusion, scheduled hyperosmolar infusions, lumbar CSF drainage, furosemide, routine steroids, routine cooling below 35°C, high-dose propofol for burst suppression, routine PaCO2 reduction below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa, and routine CPP elevation above 90 mm Hg for severe-TBI intracranial hypertension.
recommendations.context: The SIBICC list does not rule out consideration in an individual case.
recommendations.rationale: The working group cited evidence against some treatments and insufficient supporting evidence for others; cooling below 35°C can cause systemic complications.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatments Not Recommended for Intracranial Hypertension in Severe TBI

recommendations.statement: When moving between intracranial hypertension treatment tiers, reassess the patient and potential need for CT or surgery, check for extracranial causes of elevated ICP, verify physiological targets, and consider consultation or transfer to a higher level of care.
Consider assessing cerebral autoregulation to individualize CPP targets, particularly if initial Tier One measures do not reduce ICP.
recommendations.context: A supervised MAP challenge in a euvolemic patient raises MAP by 10–15 mm Hg for no more than 20 minutes, without other simultaneous therapeutic changes.

recommendations.statement: Consider individualized treatment of brain tissue hypoxia using a tiered approach directed at its underlying physiology.
recommendations.context: The SIBICC II options include FiO2 to 60% in Tier One; PaO2 as high as 150 mm Hg, greater sedation or neuromuscular paralysis, or increased CPP with intact autoregulation in Tier Two; and PaO2 above 150 mm Hg or 1 unit of packed red blood cells when PbtO2 remains less than 20 mm Hg despite CPP optimization in Tier Three.
recommendations.rationale: Brain tissue hypoxia may occur even when ICP and CPP are normal; potential harm from hyperoxia warrants attention.

recommendations.statement: Consider neuromonitoring beyond ICP alone where resources and expertise permit, and use continuous EEG to help detect and manage seizures, particularly nonconvulsive seizures.
Evacuate a large traumatic hematoma before neurological deterioration develops, regardless of GCS score.
recommendations.context: The text identifies large hematomas as > 25 mL; patients deteriorating because a hematoma develops or enlarges require prompt evacuation.

recommendations.statement: For acute SDH evacuation, perform a large trauma craniotomy that permits bleeding control and the option of primary decompressive craniectomy; do not attempt burr-hole drainage of solid clots.
recommendations.rationale: The larger exposure facilitates identification and control of bleeding sources.

recommendations.statement: After evacuating a mass lesion, leave the bone flap out if replacing it would compress swollen brain; consider concomitant brain and extracranial injuries and the availability of ICP monitoring and ICU care when deciding whether replacement is safe.
Consider secondary decompressive craniectomy when ICP remains elevated and refractory to medical treatment at > 25 mm Hg.
recommendations.rationale: The cited RESCUEicp findings showed reduced mortality and improved outcomes over time, with functional outcomes varying among additional survivors.

recommendations.statement: Initiate EN once hemodynamic stability is achieved, ideally within 24–72 hours of injury, and aim for full nutritional support within 7 days.
recommendations.rationale: Early nutritional support is associated with fewer infections and lower mortality.

recommendations.statement: Prefer postpyloric feeding if access can be obtained promptly; begin gastric EN instead if pursuing postpyloric access would delay feeding.
recommendations.rationale: Postpyloric feeding has been associated with less pneumonia, but timely EN remains important.

recommendations.statement: Consider PN if EN is contraindicated and the contraindication is expected to delay nutritional support; when EN cannot be given, initiate PN within 72 hours postinjury.
recommendations.rationale: EN remains the preferred first-line nutritional approach.

recommendations.statement: Prefer a high-protein EN formulation after TBI and consider a fish-oil-fortified formula unless contraindicated.
recommendations.rationale: High-protein formulations better address protein targets; the cited evidence suggests possible benefits from immune-enhancing formulations.

recommendations.statement: Intubate and mechanically ventilate patients with TBI early when GCS < 9, agitation is severe, airway protective reflexes are lost, or GCS > 8 occurs with thoracic and abdominal injuries.
recommendations.rationale: Airway management aims to prevent hypoxia and aspiration and permit carbon dioxide control.

recommendations.statement: Set ventilation to maintain arterial pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg when intracranial hypertension and severe metabolic acidosis are absent, and oxygen saturation at least 94%.
recommendations.context: The stated optimal PaO2 range is 80–100 mm Hg, unless neuromonitoring supports a higher target.

recommendations.statement: Consider mild hyperventilation to PaCO2 32–35 mm Hg for elevated ICP or neurological worsening; reserve PaCO2 less than 30 mm Hg for the shortest feasible period as a rescue measure during refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation.
recommendations.context: Other interventions, including surgery, should be implemented while rescue hyperventilation is used.
recommendations.rationale: Profound hyperventilation can cause arterial spasm and reduce CBF.

recommendations.statement: Consider extubation after intracranial hypertension resolves, the latest CT shows no evolving lesions, and airway reflexes and cough are adequate.
recommendations.context: Features associated with successful extubation include GCS motor score 6, normal respiratory drive, stable intracranial status, and suctioning ≤ 2 times per hour.

recommendations.statement: Consider tracheostomy within 7 days of injury for severe TBI when rapid improvement or liberation from ventilation is unlikely.
recommendations.context: The cited BTF 4th edition guidelines assign early tracheostomy to reduce ventilation days a Level IIA recommendation; they make no claim of reduced mortality or pneumonia.
recommendations.rationale: Early tracheostomy can reduce prolonged ventilation and hospital or ICU length of stay, but a survival benefit is not established.

recommendations.statement: Balance the urgency of extracranial surgery against intracranial hypertension risk; defer non-lifesaving extracranial surgery when ICP is raised or likely to rise.
recommendations.context: Necessary time-sensitive surgery, including orthopaedic stabilization, may proceed within 48 hours of admission when monitored ICP is controlled or elevated ICP is not a concern.

recommendations.statement: Generally avoid laparoscopy in patients with TBI, particularly early after injury, and monitor carefully during general anesthesia to prevent raised ICP, hypotension, hypoxia, and hypo- or hypercarbia.
recommendations.context: When ICP is monitored during anesthesia, maintain CPP at 60 mm Hg; neuraxial anesthesia is contraindicated in intracranial hypertension.
recommendations.rationale: Laparoscopy increases intra-abdominal pressure and induces hypercarbia.

recommendations.statement: Screen for BCVI using CT angiography when indicated, and screen older adults with BCVI risk factors liberally.
recommendations.context: Formal angiography may be considered for uncertain findings or injuries potentially suitable for endovascular treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Undetected injury can delay treatment and increase stroke risk; BCVI independently predicts mortality in older patients.

recommendations.statement: After BCVI is identified, begin anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment as soon as TBI is stable, ideally within the first 24 hours when progression risk is not high and extracranial bleeding is controlled.
recommendations.context: The approach applies to symptomatic and asymptomatic extracranial BCVI.
recommendations.rationale: Antithrombotic treatment is associated with less stroke than no treatment in observational studies.

recommendations.statement: Generally continue BCVI antithrombotic therapy for at least 3 months and consider CT angiography or MRI at 3 months to assess healing.

Consider endovascular stenting or coil embolization for a pseudoaneurysm that does not heal or recurrent cerebral ischemia despite antithrombotic therapy; generally avoid primary endovascular arterial sacrifice as the initial strategy.
recommendations.rationale: Periprocedural risk and the potential for lesions to heal under antithrombotic protection weigh against routine initial embolization.

recommendations.statement: In children, consider a validated BCVI risk stratification system to identify those warranting dedicated arch-to-vertex CT angiography; individualize treatment after diagnosis according to intracranial stability and control of extracranial bleeding.
recommendations.context: Consider surgery or endovascular treatment for higher-grade injury (Bifflgrade ≥ 3) or progression during medical treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Pediatric radiation exposure and the lower prevalence of BCVI require consideration.

recommendations.statement: Provide mechanical VTE prophylaxis to all patients with TBI on admission, regardless of eligibility for pharmacologic prophylaxis.
recommendations.rationale: Patients with TBI remain at substantial VTE risk without pharmacologic prophylaxis.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: For nonoperative low-risk TBI, initiate pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis within 24 hours after injury if follow-up CT shows no intracranial injury progression.
recommendations.context: Repeat head CT within 24 hours of initial imaging is recommended before starting prophylaxis in nonoperative TBI, although minimal initial hemorrhage may be an exception.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: For nonoperative moderate- or high-risk TBI, initiate pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis within 24 to 48 hours after injury if follow-up CT shows no intracranial injury progression.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: After craniotomy or craniectomy, consider starting or resuming pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis within 24 to 48 hours after surgery when postoperative CT confirms stable ICH.
recommendations.context: If CT shows ICH progression, withhold pharmacologic prophylaxis until repeat imaging demonstrates stability, usually in another 24 to 48 hours.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely withhold pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis before placement of an ICP monitor or throughout monitoring; consider maintaining doses before monitor removal.
recommendations.context: For a patient with a monitor but no craniotomy or craniectomy, use the nonoperative TBI approach. An alternative around monitor insertion or removal is to wait one drug half-life.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: Prefer LMWH over UFH for pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in TBI, including patients with ICP monitors; begin enoxaparin at 30 mg every 12 hours and consider anti-factor Xa monitoring for subsequent adjustment.
recommendations.context: Use standard dosing if dalteparin is selected; if UFH is used, the stated best-practice dose is 5000 units every 8 hours.
recommendations.rationale: The cited evidence associates LMWH with lower VTE rates and comparable ICH progression to UFH; TBI-specific evidence for enoxaparin 40 mg every 12 hours is insufficient.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: Do not place an inferior vena cava filter solely for prophylaxis in TBI; reserve placement for known VTE when therapeutic anticoagulation is contraindicated.
recommendations.source_heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS

recommendations.statement: For pediatric trauma, use a published VTE risk assessment tool after admission; omit pharmacologic prophylaxis in low-risk children, begin mechanical prophylaxis on admission in moderate-risk children, and reserve pharmacologic prophylaxis for high-risk children.
recommendations.context: LMWH is preferred when pharmacologic prophylaxis is indicated; use weight-based dosing in young children and discontinue prophylaxis once the child is ambulatory if no other thrombogenic factors remain.

recommendations.statement: Consider ASM prophylaxis for 7 days after TBI when risk factors for early PTS are present; do not extend prophylaxis beyond 7 days to prevent late PTS.
recommendations.context: Do not routinely give seizure prophylaxis without intracranial bleeding or for isolated traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. Prophylaxis may continue for seizure activity beyond 24 hours or a preexisting seizure disorder.
recommendations.rationale: Early prophylaxis can reduce early PTS but has not prevented PTE.

recommendations.statement: Use phenytoin or levetiracetam as options for early PTS prophylaxis in patients at risk; do not use valproic acid for this purpose.
recommendations.context: Either levetiracetam or (fos)phenytoin is appropriate for the recommended pediatric 7-day course.
recommendations.rationale: Superiority between phenytoin and levetiracetam has not been established; valproic acid was associated with greater mortality than phenytoin.

recommendations.statement: When using phenytoin, monitor therapeutic levels, albumin, and free phenytoin concentrations to guide dosing; pyridoxine 50–100 mg daily may limit levetiracetam-related behavioral adverse reactions.
recommendations.context: Phenytoin monitoring is usually performed 24 hours after the initial dose and once more during the 7 days of prophylaxis.

recommendations.statement: Assess patients taking warfarin or DOACs carefully and provide medication-specific reversal when emergent surgery for life-threatening bleeding is required; do not delay urgent reversal while awaiting laboratory results in a patient at high bleeding risk.
recommendations.context: Reversal is also considered to limit hematoma expansion. If the last DOAC dose was within 8–12 hours, or INR is ≥ 1.5 with warfarin, reversal benefits are considered likely to exceed risks.

recommendations.statement: For TBI requiring emergent surgery in a patient taking warfarin, give 2.5–10 mg IV vitamin K with 4PCC according to INR or the listed fixed-dose option, and reassess INR after reversal.
recommendations.context: Table 7 specifies 15 units/kg at INR 1.5–1.9, 25 units/kg at 2–3.9, 35 units/kg at 4–6, and 50 units/kg at > 6, or 1500 units fixed-dose 4PCC. Recheck at 1 hour and 6–8 hours and provide the specified additional FFP or vitamin K if INR remains > 1.4.

recommendations.statement: For emergent reversal of rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban, consider activated charcoal if the last dose was < 2 hours earlier and use the listed andexanet alfa regimen; if unavailable, use 25–50 units/kg 4PCC or a fixed dose of 2000 units.
recommendations.context: Table 7 specifies a 400 mg IV bolus followed by 480 mg IV infusion if the last dose was > 7 hours earlier, or an 800 mg IV bolus followed by 960 mg IV infusion if it was < 7 hours earlier. Reversal may not help if the last dose was > 18–24 hours before bleeding.

recommendations.statement: For emergent dabigatran reversal, consider activated charcoal when dosing occurred < 2 hours earlier and administer two consecutive IV idarucizumab doses of 2.5 g, each infused over 10 minutes.
recommendations.context: Consider dialysis with renal failure; if idarucizumab is unavailable, 4PCC or single factor prothrombin complex concentrate PCC 50 unit/kg may be considered. Reversal may not help when the last dose was > 24 hours before bleeding.

recommendations.statement: Individualize anticoagulation restart according to bleeding and thrombosis risks and consider restarting no later than 14–90 days after TBI.
recommendations.context: The cited guidelines suggest 2 weeks or less for high-thrombotic-risk patients and 7–8 weeks for lower-risk patients, but no more than 90 days after bleeding; an earlier restart may be safe with less extensive or stable traumatic intracranial bleeding.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence does not establish an optimal restart time for patients at moderate or high thromboembolic risk.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely transfuse platelets solely to reverse preinjury antiplatelet agents in TBI; consider preprocedural platelets when a patient on antiplatelet treatment has a low platelet count and requires an invasive procedure.
recommendations.context: Platelet transfusion and desmopressin are not recommended for patients who are not candidates for invasive intervention; routine postoperative platelet transfusion is also not recommended.
recommendations.rationale: Benefit from routine reversal has not been established, and these interventions can have adverse effects.
recommendations.source_heading: Antiplatelet Agent Management in TBI Patients

recommendations.statement: Use point-of-care platelet function testing, when possible, alongside standard tests in patients with suspected dysfunction from preinjury antiplatelet therapy; do not use reversal treatment when function is normal or resistance is documented.
recommendations.context: For a patient needing neurosurgery, consider one single-donor apheresis unit of platelets and, if appropriate, desmopressin 0.4 mcg/kg IV; monitor sodium if desmopressin is given.
recommendations.rationale: Testing can help avoid unnecessary treatment and its potential thrombotic risk.
recommendations.source_heading: Antiplatelet Agent Management in TBI Patients

recommendations.statement: Consider restarting antiplatelet treatment as early as 4 days after injury after an individual assessment of bleeding and thrombotic risks.
recommendations.source_heading: Antiplatelet Agent Management in TBI Patients

recommendations.statement: Consider beta blockers, including propranolol, for adrenergic stress or paroxysmal hyperactivity syndrome after TBI while monitoring for adverse effects.
recommendations.context: Potential adverse effects identified are bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure, and bronchospasm.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence suggesting lower mortality with beta blockers is of low quality.

recommendations.statement: After addressing confounding factors, give adults in vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome or minimally conscious state amantadine 100–200 mg twice daily at 4–16 weeks postinjury.
recommendations.rationale: The intended effects are faster recovery and reduced disability.

recommendations.statement: Do not use systemic antibiotic prophylaxis during intraparenchymal ICP monitor insertion or ongoing parenchymal or ventricular drain use; use institutional insertion and maintenance protocols and consider antimicrobial-impregnated EVD catheters.
recommendations.context: Remove monitors and drains as soon as clinically feasible, minimize closed-system manipulation and unnecessary CSF sampling, and use aseptic technique.
recommendations.rationale: Unnecessary antibiotics can promote resistant organisms; the cited evidence associates antimicrobial-impregnated catheters with fewer CSF infections.

recommendations.statement: Do not give antibiotic prophylaxis for traumatic skull-base fractures with CSF leakage or pneumocephalus.
recommendations.rationale: Prophylaxis may promote growth of drug-resistant organisms.

recommendations.statement: For open or penetrating skull fractures, consider broad-spectrum antibiotics with high blood-brain barrier penetration for no more than 3 days; perform surgical debridement and irrigation with perioperative antibiotics for no more than 24 hours.

For surgical prophylaxis, select cefazolin in patients without methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or a documented severe beta lactam allergy; use clindamycin or vancomycin as alternatives for severe beta lactam allergy.
recommendations.context: Confirm reported allergy where feasible and choose agent and dose using published guidance, pharmacist input, and local ICU antibiograms.
recommendations.rationale: The guide describes cefazolin as superior to the listed alternatives when it can be used.

recommendations.statement: Use shared decision-making with families or surrogates and communicate uncertainty when discussing prognosis after severe TBI.
recommendations.context: Discuss possible best-case, worst-case, and most-likely outcomes; do not use IMPACT or CRASH TBI estimates as exact individual predictions.
recommendations.rationale: Early prognostic indicators cannot predict poor individual outcomes with high certainty.

recommendations.statement: Offer a trial of aggressive treatment for severe TBI, including necessary surgery and intensive care, when consistent with the patient's values; continue until the team and family or surrogate agree that further treatment is inconsistent with those values.
recommendations.context: Exceptions include brain death, an applicable preinjury directive, or a family or surrogate decision for comfort-focused care. Do not use age alone to limit treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Premature limitation of life-sustaining care may create a self-fulfilling poor outcome; meaningful recovery remains possible after prolonged unconsciousness.

recommendations.statement: Develop a hospital brain-death determination policy based on accepted standards and applicable local law, and use standardized criteria when assessing a patient.
recommendations.context: The document prioritizes clinical examination when its prerequisites are met.

recommendations.statement: Consider multidisciplinary rehabilitation beginning on the day of admission, incorporate PM&R into the primary trauma team, and involve PT, OT, SLP, psychology/neuropsychology, social work, and nursing.
recommendations.context: Bedside interventions can begin while medical stability is being achieved; select more intensive mobilization according to neurosurgical, hemodynamic, respiratory, and ICP status.
recommendations.rationale: Early rehabilitation may lessen complications of immobility and improve functional recovery.
recommendations.source_heading: EARLY MULTIDISCIPLINARY REHABILITATION IN ACUTE TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY

recommendations.statement: Initiate early mobilization within the first 48 hours of injury, or as soon as neurosurgical, hemodynamic, and respiratory stability allow.
recommendations.context: Simple measures such as passive movement and splinting may begin earlier even when ICP control remains necessary; defer out-of-bed mobilization until stability is achieved and intracranial hypertension is no longer a significant concern.
recommendations.rationale: Mobilization helps limit immobility-related complications.

recommendations.statement: Acute benzodiazepines and typical antipsychotics are not recommended for posttraumatic confusion or agitation; consider atypical antipsychotics or beta blockers such as propranolol when needed for safety.
recommendations.context: Use multidisciplinary behavioral approaches to reduce reliance on medication.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence suggests benzodiazepines and typical antipsychotics may prolong neurocognitive recovery.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients with GCS 13–15 and prolonged physical, cognitive, or psychological symptoms for multidisciplinary rehabilitation and follow-up.
recommendations.context: Outpatient or community-based services may support return to work, school, and usual activities.

recommendations.statement: Plan a continuous, individualized course of rehabilitation beyond emergency and acute care; start discharge planning early and refer medically stable patients to specialized postacute rehabilitation when appropriate.
Before discharge, educate families about PTE manifestations, including subtle changes in consciousness; screen for PTE during follow-up and arrange diagnostic testing when seizures are suspected.
recommendations.context: Continue screening as adults with prior TBI age, particularly when PTE risk factors are present.
recommendations.rationale: The incidence of PTE increases over time.

recommendations.statement: Treat a first late seizure after TBI with ASM and refer the patient to a clinician experienced in PTE; individualize the drug and duration according to seizure control, adverse effects, and other treatment options.
recommendations.context: Other options identified include dietary modification, neuromodulation, and surgery.
recommendations.rationale: The cited risk of recurrent seizures after the first late seizure is as high as 86% by 2 years postinjury.

recommendations.statement: Integrate decision-support tools and clinical guidelines into routine care to improve detection and appropriate management of TBI with GCS 13–15.
recommendations.rationale: An estimated 50% of these injuries go unrecognized in the hospital ED.
recommendations.source_heading: MANAGEMENT OF PATIENTS WITH GLASGOW COMA SCALE (GCS) SCORE OF 13–15

recommendations.statement: Educate patients with GCS 13–15 about their injury, expected recovery, follow-up options, and return to work, school, driving, and other activities; provide individualized care for persistent symptoms.
recommendations.context: Symptoms lasting longer than 2 weeks postinjury may warrant more targeted assessment and treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: MANAGEMENT OF PATIENTS WITH GLASGOW COMA SCALE (GCS) SCORE OF 13–15

recommendations.statement: Refer all children with TBI to their primary care clinician for return-to-school and activity management; consider subspecialty follow-up when prolonged recovery is likely and neuropsychological testing when symptoms persist at 3 months.
Assess TBI outcomes longitudinally using a global measure complemented, when possible, by measures of physical, cognitive, communication, behavioral, psychological, and quality-of-life domains.
recommendations.context: The guide identifies GOS-E as the global measure but notes that it is inappropriate during the index hospitalization.
recommendations.rationale: A global score alone cannot adequately characterize the varied sequelae of TBI.

recommendations.statement: Perform standardized serial outcome assessments after TBI, ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months following injury, and investigate clinical plateau or decline.
recommendations.context: Consider more frequent assessment for selected patients.
recommendations.rationale: Serial results help identify recovery trajectories and needs for further intervention.

recommendations.statement: Treat TBI as both an acute and a chronic condition; provide patients and families with injury education and ensure an opportunity for follow-up with a clinician experienced in TBI after acute-care discharge.
recommendations.context: Trauma centers and community systems are encouraged to establish coordinated postacute care.
recommendations.rationale: Persistent or emerging symptoms may require longer-term screening and treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY EDUCATION AND FOLLOW-UP

recommendations.statement: Have an interdisciplinary workgroup review the guideline, compare it with local TBI care, prioritize needed changes, and develop an education plan with trauma program leadership.
recommendations.context: Integrate documentation and relevant measures into existing clinical and performance-improvement processes.

recommendations.statement: Select applicable TBI care elements for monitoring through the trauma Performance Improvement and Patient Safety processes and incorporate approved elements into the existing plan.
recommendations.source_heading: IMPLEMENTATION AND INTEGRATION INTO TRAUMA CENTER PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT

artifacts.title: Box 2. Tier Zero—Basic ICU Care Interventions—SIBICC I Algorithm
artifacts.description: Step 1: For a patient with TBI admitted to the ICU, provide baseline care regardless of ICP: ICU admission, intubation and ventilation, repeated neurological and pupillary examinations, head-of-bed elevation to 30–45°, pain relief, sedation when needed to prevent agitation or ventilator asynchrony, core-temperature measurement and treatment above 38.0°C, and consideration of antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only unless continuation is indicated. Step 2: Initially maintain CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin > 7 g/dL and SpO2 ≥ 94%; avoid hyponatremia, facilitate cranial venous drainage, and continuously monitor arterial blood pressure. Step 3: Add the recommended central line and end-tidal CO2 monitoring.
artifacts.summary: Organizes expected and recommended basic ICU measures before ICP-directed treatment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Establishes baseline supportive care while distinguishing it from therapies specifically intended to lower ICP.

artifacts.title: Box 3. SIBICC I Tiers for ICP Treatment of Intracranial Hypertension for Patients with ICP Monitoring
artifacts.description: Step 1, Tier One: Target CPP 60–70 mm Hg; increase analgesia or sedation to reduce ICP; keep PaCO2 at 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa; give intermittent boluses of mannitol (0.25–1.0 g/kg) or hypertonic saline; drain CSF through an existing EVD or consider EVD placement if monitoring began with a parenchymal probe; consider antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only unless continuation is indicated, and consider EEG monitoring. For either hyperosmolar agent, recommended limits are sodium 155 mEq/L and osmolality 320 mEq/L. Step 2, Tier Two: If further treatment is needed, maintain PaCO2 at 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa; try neuromuscular paralysis in an adequately sedated patient and continue infusion only if the trial lowers ICP; perform a MAP Challenge to guide individualized MAP and CPP targets, returning MAP to baseline with impaired autoregulation or raising its target to lower ICP when autoregulation is intact. Step 3, Tier Three: If further escalation is appropriate, give pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone only if a test shows ICP benefit, titrating to ICP control without exceeding the dose producing burst suppression and avoiding hypotension; alternatively, perform secondary decompressive craniectomy or use active cooling for mild hypothermia at 35–36°C. Treatments within a tier have no prescribed rank, every lower-tier option need not be exhausted, and a tier can be bypassed when advantageous.
artifacts.summary: Describes the SIBICC I escalation options for monitored intracranial hypertension.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Structures treatment escalation according to relative risk and benefit while allowing patient-specific choices.

artifacts.title: Figure 1. Inter-Tier Recommendations
artifacts.description: Step 1: When considering progression from Tier One to Tier Two, reassess the patient and consider another CT to evaluate intracranial pathology. Step 2: Reconsider surgery for lesions that might be operable; look for extracranial contributors to ICP elevation, including intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure; and check whether basic physiological measures, including CPP and blood gases, remain in their intended ranges. Step 3: Consider consultation with a higher level of care where applicable. Step 4: Apply this inter-tier reassessment again when considering progression from Tier Two to Tier Three.
