treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients requiring acute care after TBI
decision_rules: Aim to keep physiologic measurements within the recommended ranges while weighing the risks of interventions needed to achieve them.
When ICP is not monitored, treatment targeting SBP ≥ 110 mm Hg/MAP > 80 mm Hg generally supports cerebral perfusion.
Use CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg as an initial practical target, adjusting it according to cerebral autoregulation.

recommended_regimens.name: Goal-directed physiologic management
recommended_regimens.summary: Initial targets include SpO2 ≥ 94%, PaO2 80–100 mm Hg, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg, pH 7.35–7.45, ICP < 22 mm Hg, PbtO2 ≥ 15 mm Hg when monitored, CPP 60–70 mm Hg, serum sodium 135–145 mEq/L, serum osmolality ≤ 320 mOsm, INR ≤ 1.4, temperature 36.0–37.9°C, platelets ≥ 75 × 103/mm3, glucose 100–180 mg/dL, and hemoglobin ≥ 7 g/dL. These are ideal ranges rather than goals to pursue regardless of treatment risk.

alternative_regimens.name: Individualized pulmonary targets
alternative_regimens.summary: Patients with significant pulmonary disease may need lung-directed targets, including permissive hypercapnia, while other interventions control elevated ICP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Significant pulmonary problems such as acute respiratory distress syndrome

not_recommended.name: PaO2 > 100 mm Hg
not_recommended.reason: Avoid hyperoxia unless brain oximetry guides the higher target.

response_assessment.method: Repeated assessment of blood pressure, gas exchange, temperature, sodium, glucose, coagulation, and monitored cerebral parameters
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust treatment to the patient's condition and the risks of further intervention.

supportive_care: Treat fever aggressively and maintain normothermia.
Prevent hyponatremia; monitor serum sodium frequently when indicated.
Measure osmolality when mannitol is used.
Monitor glucose more often when nutritional support begins, particularly with confirmed or suspected diabetes mellitus.
Assess coagulopathy early; TEG, ROTEM, and platelet function assays may inform targeted reversal.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: An ICP of 22 mm Hg is an initial treatment threshold; when escalation poses substantial risk, consider 20–25 mm Hg. The document reports that mortality probability rises with every 10-point SBP decrease below 119 mm Hg.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Comatose patients with GCS ≤ 8 and structural brain damage on initial CT
decision_rules: Monitor ICP when initial CT demonstrates structural injury.
Continue serial neurological examinations and imaging; ICP measurements do not replace either.
Continue ICP monitoring during transport out of the ICU for surgery, imaging, or procedures.

recommended_regimens.name: EVD
recommended_regimens.summary: An EVD connected to an external strain-gauge transducer is the preferred measurement method and also permits CSF drainage.

alternative_regimens.name: Intraparenchymal ICP monitoring
alternative_regimens.summary: Provides reliable pressure measurement but does not permit CSF drainage.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative when an EVD is not selected

alternative_regimens.name: Serial neurological examination and CT imaging
alternative_regimens.summary: Observation without an ICP device is generally appropriate if initial imaging shows neither structural damage nor signs of elevated ICP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Comatose patients without structural damage or evidence of raised ICP on initial CT

not_recommended.name: Subdural and epidural ICP monitors
not_recommended.reason: Their measurement accuracy is lower.

response_assessment.method: Interpret ICP trends alongside arterial pressure, CPP, neurological findings, and imaging
response_assessment.interpretation: Both the magnitude and duration of elevation matter; distinguish sustained increases from brief event-related elevations.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Carefully consider monitoring for patients with GCS > 8 and structural injuries likely to progress, deterioration, CT progression, or extracranial treatment or sedation that limits examination.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with severe TBI considered for ICP monitoring
decision_rules: Select the monitoring technique according to its risks and advantages for the child's clinical circumstances.
Use an ICP upper limit of 20 mm Hg in children; the document reports no improved outcomes with lower specific targets.

recommended_regimens.name: EVD
recommended_regimens.summary: A monitoring option that also permits drainage and may produce slightly lower ICP during acute care.

alternative_regimens.name: Intraparenchymal ICP monitoring
alternative_regimens.summary: May yield long-term outcomes similar to EVD monitoring.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Patient-specific technical considerations favor an intraparenchymal transducer.

response_assessment.method: ICP and age-appropriate CPP assessment
response_assessment.interpretation: Treatment-study targets described as appropriate are CPP above 50 mm Hg at ages 6 to 17 years and above 40 mm Hg at ages 0 to 5 years.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Pediatric ICP and CPP relationships vary with age; adult targets should not automatically be applied.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients admitted to the ICU, irrespective of ICP
decision_rules: Apply SIBICC Tier Zero basic care before or alongside treatment directed specifically at intracranial hypertension.
Treat the SIBICC algorithms as consensus-based suggestions, not mandatory standards of practice.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC I Tier Zero
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide ICU care with endotracheal intubation and ventilation, serial neurological and pupillary assessment, head-of-bed elevation of 30–45°, analgesia for pain, sedation to prevent agitation or ventilator asynchrony, temperature measurement and treatment above 38.0°C, initial CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin > 7 g/dL, avoidance of hyponatremia, optimized venous return, an arterial line, and SpO2 ≥ 94%. A central line and end-tidal CO2 monitoring are recommended interventions.

response_assessment.method: Neurological status, pupillary response, core temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation, and cerebral perfusion
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify deterioration or physiologic disturbances requiring targeted treatment.

supportive_care: Consider anti-seizure prophylaxis for 1 week only when no separate reason to continue exists.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The source algorithm distinguishes analgesia and sedation given for basic care from escalation specifically intended to lower ICP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe TBI and ICP monitoring who require treatment for elevated ICP
decision_rules: Begin with treatments having a more favorable risk-benefit balance, choosing within a tier according to the suspected physiologic disturbance.
An ICP of 22 mm Hg is an initial alert threshold; a sustained 20–25 mm Hg for more than 5 minutes is described as a reasonable treatment trigger.
There is no required order within a tier, no obligation to exhaust every lower-tier option, and a tier may be skipped when advantageous.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC I Tier One
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain CPP 60–70 mm Hg; increase analgesia or sedation to lower ICP; target PaCO2 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa; give intermittent boluses of mannitol 0.25–1.0 g/kg or hypertonic saline; drain CSF through an existing EVD; and consider EVD placement if monitoring initially used a parenchymal probe. Consider EEG monitoring.

not_recommended.name: Mannitol by non-bolus, continuous intravenous infusion
not_recommended.reason: The SIBICC working group discourages this approach for intracranial hypertension in severe TBI.

not_recommended.name: Scheduled infusion of hyperosmolar therapy
not_recommended.reason: Sufficient supporting evidence is lacking; the discouraged example is administration every 4 to 6 hours.

not_recommended.name: Lumbar CSF drainage
not_recommended.reason: Sufficient supporting evidence is lacking.

not_recommended.name: Furosemide
not_recommended.reason: The SIBICC working group discourages its use for this indication.

not_recommended.name: Routine use of steroids
not_recommended.reason: The working group cites evidence against this treatment.

not_recommended.name: Routine therapeutic hypothermia below 35°C
not_recommended.reason: Systemic complications are a concern.

not_recommended.name: High dose propofol to attempt burst suppression
not_recommended.reason: The SIBICC working group discourages this approach.

not_recommended.name: Routine PaCO2 below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa
not_recommended.reason: The SIBICC working group discourages routine use.

not_recommended.name: Routine CPP above 90 mm Hg
not_recommended.reason: The SIBICC working group discourages routine use.

response_assessment.method: Repeat neurological evaluation; consider CT, operability of lesions, extracranial sources of ICP elevation, basic physiology, and consultation or transfer
response_assessment.interpretation: Correct reversible problems and reassess whether a higher treatment tier is needed.

supportive_care: For either mannitol or hypertonic saline, the algorithm recommends sodium and osmolality limits of 155 mEq/L and 320 mEq/L, respectively.
Consider anti-seizure prophylaxis for 1 week only if there is no indication to continue longer.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discouraged interventions may still warrant consideration in individual cases; the list does not prohibit every possible use.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe TBI whose elevated ICP has not responded adequately to initial treatment
decision_rules: Reassess the patient and potentially correct remediable intracranial or extracranial causes before advancing treatment.
Use autoregulation findings to individualize MAP and CPP rather than assuming the same target applies to every patient.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC I Tier Two
recommended_regimens.summary: Maintain mild hypocapnia at 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa; consider neuromuscular paralysis in adequately sedated patients if it lowers ICP; and perform a MAP Challenge to assess autoregulation and guide individualized pressure targets.

response_assessment.timepoint: After a trial dose of neuromuscular paralysis
response_assessment.method: Measure its effect on ICP
response_assessment.interpretation: Proceed to a continuous infusion only if the trial demonstrates efficacy.

response_assessment.timepoint: During a MAP Challenge lasting no more than 20 minutes
response_assessment.method: In a euvolemic patient with a closed cranium, increase MAP by 10–15 mm Hg under experienced bedside supervision; record MAP, ICP, CPP, and PbtO2 before and after without making other treatment adjustments
response_assessment.interpretation: An ICP rise indicates impaired autoregulation and may favor a lower CPP goal; unchanged or falling ICP indicates intact autoregulation and may favor a higher CPP goal.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If autoregulation is disrupted, return MAP to baseline; if intact, an elevated MAP target may lower ICP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe TBI and persistently elevated ICP despite other appropriate measures
decision_rules: Base escalation on the degree and duration of raised ICP, not a momentary reading alone.
Consider whether decompressive craniectomy offers a favorable balance of potential benefit and risk.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC I Tier Three
recommended_regimens.summary: Options are pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone titrated to ICP control when effective on testing, secondary decompressive craniectomy, and active cooling to mild hypothermia of 35–36°C.

not_recommended.name: Barbiturate treatment without demonstrated ICP benefit
not_recommended.reason: The algorithm calls for continuation only when testing shows a beneficial ICP effect.

response_assessment.method: Assess ICP response, burst suppression, and blood pressure
response_assessment.interpretation: Titrate for ICP control without exceeding the dose producing burst suppression; avoid hypotension.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The SIBICC tiers are not standards of practice and may be adapted to local circumstances.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with severe TBI requiring tiered treatment
decision_rules: Use the pediatric consensus approach, which organizes escalating treatment into two tiers.
Individualize hydration and electrolyte management because fluid shifts can worsen cerebral edema.

recommended_regimens.name: hypertonic 3% saline
recommended_regimens.summary: Evidence supports a bolus of 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 20 min or administration at 0.1–1 mL/kg/hour.

alternative_regimens.name: 23.4% saline
alternative_regimens.summary: The described dose is 0.5 mL/kg (up to 30 mL) over 10 to 20 minutes.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Another supported hypertonic saline approach for pediatric severe TBI

alternative_regimens.name: mannitol
alternative_regimens.summary: The document states that pediatric evidence supporting this option is weaker than evidence for hypertonic saline.

not_recommended.name: Moderate prophylactic hypothermia (32–33°C) to improve overall outcomes
not_recommended.reason: It is not recommended instead of normothermia for improvement of overall outcomes, although it is suggested for ICP control.

response_assessment.method: Monitor ICP and the child's physiologic response
response_assessment.interpretation: Pediatric Tier Two uses a lower hypoventilation target of 28 to 34 mm Hg.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The pediatric tiered guideline was updated in 2019 and predates ADAPT results.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with impaired cerebral autoregulation or ICP that does not respond to initial therapy
decision_rules: Consider multimodal monitoring to establish patient-specific CPP goals.
For a closed cranium, interpret an ICP rise during a MAP Challenge as impaired autoregulation and unchanged or falling ICP as intact autoregulation.

recommended_regimens.name: MAP challenge
recommended_regimens.summary: In a euvolemic patient, increase MAP by 10–15 mm Hg for no more than 20 minutes using a vasopressor infusion under direct supervision while monitoring ICP; make no simultaneous therapeutic adjustments.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: no more than 20 minutes

alternative_regimens.name: PRx
alternative_regimens.summary: Continuous assessment may guide patient-specific CPP thresholds: PRx slope > 0.13 may support CPP 50–60 mm Hg, whereas PRx slope < 0.13 may support CPP 60– 70 mm Hg.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Required technical expertise, hardware, and software are available.

alternative_regimens.name: PbtO2
alternative_regimens.summary: May help assess autoregulation if systemic PaO2 is kept constant and checked with arterial blood gases before and after the challenge.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Brain tissue oxygenation is monitored.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before and after the MAP challenge
response_assessment.method: Document MAP, ICP, CPP, and PbtO2
response_assessment.interpretation: With impaired autoregulation, a lower CPP goal may help; with intact autoregulation, particularly if ICP falls, a higher CPP goal may help.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Direct CBF monitoring or transcranial doppler ultrasonography with hemodynamic challenge may also assess autoregulation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with TBI whose monitored PbtO2 indicates inadequate cerebral oxygenation
decision_rules: Consider treatment according to the cause of hypoxia, escalating through the SIBICC II tiers.
Brain tissue hypoxia can occur despite normal ICP and CPP.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC II Tier One
recommended_regimens.summary: Increase FiO2 to 60% as an initial tiered intervention for inadequate brain tissue oxygenation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: BOOST II reported a statistically significant reduction in the duration and severity of brain hypoxia with ICP + PbtO2-guided treatment compared with ICP-only treatment; it was not powered to demonstrate significant differences in clinical outcome.

response_assessment.method: Follow PbtO2, ICP, CPP, and systemic oxygenation
response_assessment.interpretation: The document gives accepted hypoxia-treatment thresholds of 15–20 mm Hg and recommends PbtO2 ≥ 15 mm Hg when monitored.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Oxy-TC did not find a difference in functional outcome between ICP + PbtO2-guided and ICP-only monitoring for nonpenetrating TBI.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistent inadequate PbtO2 after initial measures
decision_rules: Use autoregulation findings when deciding whether increasing CPP may improve oxygenation.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC II Tier Two
recommended_regimens.summary: Options include increasing PaO2 to as high as 150 mm Hg, attempting greater sedation or neuromuscular paralysis, and raising CPP when a MAP challenge indicates intact autoregulation.

response_assessment.method: Reassess PbtO2 and the relevant physiologic response
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the response to guide whether further escalation is warranted.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Consider the possible harms of hyperoxia when increasing systemic oxygenation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with ongoing inadequate PbtO2 despite lower-tier treatment
decision_rules: Escalate while weighing potential hyperoxia-related harm.
Reserve the specified transfusion intervention for PbtO2 that remains less than 20 mm Hg after CPP optimization.

recommended_regimens.name: SIBICC II Tier Three
recommended_regimens.summary: Options are PaO2 above 150 mm Hg or transfusion of 1 unit of packed red blood cells when PbtO2 remains less than 20 mm Hg despite optimized CPP.

response_assessment.method: Monitor PbtO2, CPP, and systemic oxygenation
response_assessment.interpretation: Balance the cerebral oxygenation response against potential harm from hyperoxia.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a large traumatic hematoma, including comatose patients when the hematoma is the likely cause and meaningful recovery remains possible
decision_rules: Evacuate a large hematoma before neurological deterioration, regardless of GCS.
A large hematoma is described as > 25 mL; posterior fossa lesions may warrant a lower surgical threshold.
Promptly evacuate a delayed or enlarging hematoma that causes neurological deterioration.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical hematoma evacuation
recommended_regimens.summary: Proceed immediately on arrival for an eligible comatose patient whose large hematoma is judged to cause the coma; intervene before deterioration in other patients with a large lesion.

response_assessment.method: Repeat neurological examination and assess for hematoma development or enlargement
response_assessment.interpretation: Deterioration attributable to a delayed or enlarging hematoma calls for prompt evacuation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The surgical threshold may be lower for a posterior fossa lesion.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients requiring operative evacuation of acute SDH
decision_rules: Perform a large trauma craniotomy for hematoma evacuation, identification of bleeding, hemostasis, and the option of decompression.
Following evacuation, leave the bone flap out when replacing it would compress the brain.

recommended_regimens.name: Large trauma craniotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Create a large bone flap, described as ≈ 12 × 15 cm, to expose potential bleeding sources and enable evacuation and hemostasis. A vertical dimension of at least 13 cm permits optimal middle-fossa decompression.

recommended_regimens.name: Primary decompressive craniectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Leave the bone flap out after evacuation when brain swelling is present or flap replacement could compress the brain.

alternative_regimens.name: Bone flap replacement
alternative_regimens.summary: The flap may be replaced if it does not compress the underlying brain after considering associated brain and extracranial injuries, ICP monitoring availability, and ICU resources.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No compression of the underlying brain with flap replacement

not_recommended.name: Burr hole drainage of solid clots
not_recommended.reason: The document identifies no role for attempting this approach.

response_assessment.method: Assess brain swelling and whether flap replacement causes compression
response_assessment.interpretation: Retain decompression when replacement would compress the brain.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The suggested 15 cm dimension may be excessive for some patients with smaller heads.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with hematoma, contusion, or diffuse injury and refractory ICP > 25 mm Hg without an immediate operative indication
decision_rules: Consider removal of a bone flap if medically managed brain swelling and elevated ICP remain refractory.

recommended_regimens.name: Secondary decompressive craniectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Remove a large bone flap to control refractory swelling and pressure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The RESCUEicp trial projected 21 extra survivors per 100 patients treated compared with conservative management; among those additional survivors, one-third were independent outside the home, one-third independent in the home, and one-third dependent. The document reports improved outcome over time using 24-month data.

response_assessment.method: Follow the magnitude and persistence of ICP elevation
response_assessment.interpretation: Refractory ICP > 25 mm Hg supports consideration of secondary decompression.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discuss the potential distribution of survival and functional outcomes when weighing surgery.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with mass effect and neurological decline; patients with smaller lesions require individualized consideration
decision_rules: Neurological deterioration with mass effect makes the decision to operate more straightforward.
For smaller lesions, whether early surgery prevents secondary injury remains debated.

recommended_regimens.name: Early surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider surgical intervention particularly when a traumatic intracerebral hematoma produces mass effect and neurological decline.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: STITCH (Trauma) reported improved survival with early surgery and a trend toward better functional outcome, especially with GCS 9–12; CENTER-TBI associated early surgery with improved outcomes for GCS 9–12 or isolated traumatic intracerebral hematoma.

alternative_regimens.name: Conservative treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Medical management remains an option when the lesion does not warrant immediate surgery.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No clear urgent surgical indication

response_assessment.method: Assess neurological status, lesion size, and mass effect
response_assessment.interpretation: New decline or clinically important mass effect strengthens the case for surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document describes this management decision as controversial and notes that STITCH (Trauma) ended prematurely because recruitment was slow.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with depressed skull fracture, particularly an open fracture or depression exceeding adjacent skull thickness
decision_rules: Commonly elevate a fracture when its depression exceeds adjacent skull thickness, particularly at a cosmetically important site.
Usually operate on open fractures to prevent infection.
Generally avoid surgery over a dural venous sinus because uncontrollable hemorrhage is a major risk.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical elevation
recommended_regimens.summary: Elevate appropriately selected depressed fractures; open fractures usually receive operative treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Nonoperative management
alternative_regimens.summary: May be attempted in selected open depressed fractures.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No dural laceration, gross contamination, infection, or frontal sinus injury

not_recommended.name: Routine surgery for fractures over a dural venous sinus
not_recommended.reason: The risk of uncontrolled hemorrhage is high.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hemodynamically stable hospitalized patients requiring nutritional support
decision_rules: Start EN after hemodynamic stabilization, ideally within 24–72 hours of injury.
Aim for full nutritional supplementation within 7 days.
Do not postpone EN solely to obtain postpyloric access.

recommended_regimens.name: EN
recommended_regimens.summary: Use early enteral feeding, preferably a high-protein formulation; indirect calorimetry is the preferred way to determine caloric targets. Postpyloric access is preferred when it can be obtained promptly.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies associated early nutritional support with fewer infections and lower mortality; postpyloric feeding studies in TBI reported less pneumonia without differences in other outcomes.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Initiate ideally within 24–72 hours of injury; achieve full supplementation within 7 days.

alternative_regimens.name: Gastric EN
alternative_regimens.summary: Begin through gastric access rather than delaying nutrition for postpyloric placement.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Postpyloric access would delay EN initiation.

alternative_regimens.name: Fish-oil fortified EN formulas
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider these formulations unless contraindicated.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No contraindication to a fish-oil fortified formula

response_assessment.method: Evaluate caloric and protein delivery, feeding tolerance, and glucose
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust support to reach nutritional needs and the glucose target of 100–180 mg/dL.

supportive_care: Protein delivery up to 2 g/kg/day improved nitrogen balance in the cited study of critically ill trauma patients.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document reports energy expenditure of 120% to 250% of predicted basal expenditure after TBI, while some temperature-management approaches may lower expenditure below predictions.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom EN is contraindicated
decision_rules: Consider PN if an absolute EN contraindication is expected to delay enteral support.

recommended_regimens.name: PN
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide parenteral support when enteral feeding cannot be given; EN remains the preferred first-line route when feasible.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 72 hours postinjury if EN is contraindicated.

response_assessment.method: Monitor nutritional provision and glucose
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust support according to nutrition requirements and clinical status.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For children, hydration and electrolyte targets must also be considered to avoid fluid shifts that could aggravate cerebral edema.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with GCS < 9, severe agitation, absent airway-protective reflexes, or GCS > 8 with thoracic and abdominal injuries
decision_rules: Intubate and mechanically ventilate early when the stated indications apply.
Protect the cervical spine during intubation.
Use individualized pulmonary targets when competing respiratory disease requires them while controlling ICP by other means.

recommended_regimens.name: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
recommended_regimens.summary: Prevent hypoxia and aspiration while controlling carbon dioxide. The key points specify arterial pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg without intracranial hypertension or severe metabolic acidosis, and oxygen saturation at least 94%; the ventilation discussion also gives an initial PaCO2 target of 35–40 mm Hg and a PaO2 range of 80–100 mm Hg.

response_assessment.method: Monitor oxygenation and end-tidal CO2, interpreting it in light of arterial-to-end-tidal gradients
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust ventilation to the patient's gas exchange and ICP status.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For children requiring intubation, the document favors a cuffed endotracheal tube.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Ventilated patients with refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation
decision_rules: Use profound hyperventilation only as a temporary rescue measure while other interventions, potentially including surgery, are instituted.

recommended_regimens.name: Rescue hyperventilation
recommended_regimens.summary: PaCO2 less than 30 mm Hg may be justified temporarily in refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: As short a period as possible.

alternative_regimens.name: Mild hyperventilation
alternative_regimens.summary: PaCO2 32–35 mm Hg is suggested as a SIBICC Tier-Two intervention for elevated ICP or neurologic worsening.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: High ICP or neurological worsening

not_recommended.name: Routine profound hyperventilation
not_recommended.reason: It can cause arterial spasm and reduce CBF; the SIBICC algorithm discourages routinely decreasing PaCO2 below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa.

response_assessment.method: Follow PaCO2 or end-tidal CO2 and ICP
response_assessment.interpretation: Discontinue the rescue exposure as soon as other measures allow.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: PEEP < 10 cm H2O generally can be used to maintain oxygenation in intracranial hypertension when ICP is monitored.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Mechanically ventilated patients being considered for extubation
decision_rules: Consider extubation once intracranial hypertension has resolved, the latest CT shows no evolving lesion, and the patient can protect the airway and cough.
If extubation is unsuccessful or safety criteria are absent, assess the need for tracheostomy.

recommended_regimens.name: Tracheal extubation
recommended_regimens.summary: Attempt extubation in suitable patients; favorable signs include GCS motor score of 6, normal respiratory drive, stable intracranial condition, effective protective reflexes, and endotracheal suctioning ≤ 2 times per hour.

alternative_regimens.name: Tracheostomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Evaluate when extubation cannot be performed safely or fails.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Failed extubation or absent extubation safety criteria

response_assessment.method: Assess respiratory drive, secretion burden, cough, gag reflex, swallowing attempts, and intracranial stability
response_assessment.interpretation: Reintubation may be necessary even after a carefully selected extubation attempt.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients unlikely to improve sufficiently for liberation from mechanical ventilation within 7 days
decision_rules: Consider early tracheostomy, weighing relative contraindications and the patient's goals of care.

recommended_regimens.name: Early tracheostomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider placement within 7 days of injury when prompt ventilator liberation is unlikely.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document reports shorter ICU and hospital LOS but no clear evidence of a survival benefit; the cited BTF 4th edition recommendation is Level IIA for reducing ventilation days and makes no claim of reduced mortality or pneumonia.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: within 7 days of injury

alternative_regimens.name: Percutaneous tracheostomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be safe and well tolerated, although evidence does not establish a preferred surgical or percutaneous approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Technique selected according to patient circumstances and procedural expertise

response_assessment.method: Assess ICP, hemodynamics, respiratory support, prognosis for ventilation, and goals of care
response_assessment.interpretation: Uncontrolled intracranial hypertension, hemodynamic instability, and severe respiratory failure requiring FiO2 > 50% and PEEP > 10 cm H2O are relative contraindications.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For children under 10 years old and infants, adult evidence about early timing should not automatically be extrapolated; pediatric airway anatomy and procedural risks differ.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with extracranial injuries requiring surgery
decision_rules: Balance operative urgency against intracranial hypertension and secondary brain injury.
Delay non-lifesaving extracranial surgery in patients with elevated ICP or substantial risk of it.
If ICP is controlled or raised ICP is not a concern, necessary orthopaedic stabilization or another time-sensitive operation may proceed within 48 hours of admission.

recommended_regimens.name: Individualized extracranial surgical management
recommended_regimens.summary: Prioritize resuscitation and bleeding control when hemodynamically unstable. During anesthesia, monitor closely to prevent raised ICP, hypotension, hypoxia, and abnormal PaCO2; maintain CPP at 60 mm Hg if ICP is monitored.

alternative_regimens.name: Damage control orthopaedics
alternative_regimens.summary: Initial external fixation followed by delayed definitive repair may reduce the risk of a neurologic second hit.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Definitive early orthopaedic surgery presents excessive physiologic or neurologic risk.

alternative_regimens.name: IV anesthesia
alternative_regimens.summary: Often preferable because inhalational anesthesia can adversely affect ICP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection of general anesthesia in a patient at risk of raised ICP

not_recommended.name: Laparoscopy
not_recommended.reason: Generally avoid it, particularly early, because increased intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia can result.

not_recommended.name: Spinal and epidural anesthesia with intracranial hypertension
not_recommended.reason: Neuraxial regional techniques are contraindicated in patients with raised ICP.

response_assessment.method: Repeat assessments of hemodynamics, neurological status, ICP when monitored, oxygenation, and ventilation
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust operative timing and anesthetic care to evolving physiologic status.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Lifesaving extracranial surgery remains an exception to delaying procedures for raised ICP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with diagnosed extracranial BCVI whose TBI is stable, whose extracranial bleeding is controlled, and who are not at high risk of TBI progression
decision_rules: Start antithrombotic treatment as soon as TBI stability permits, ideally within the first 24 hours.
Treat both symptomatic cerebral ischemia and asymptomatic extracranial BCVI when the stated safety conditions are met.

recommended_regimens.name: Antiplatelet agents
recommended_regimens.summary: An antithrombotic option to reduce thromboembolic stroke risk following BCVI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Large observational studies associated treatment with any antithrombotic medication with lower stroke risk than no treatment; this has not been tested in large randomized trials.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 3 months, generally.

recommended_regimens.name: Anticoagulation
recommended_regimens.summary: An alternative antithrombotic approach initiated when intracranial injury and extracranial bleeding permit.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 3 months, generally.

alternative_regimens.name: Endovascular stenting or coil embolization
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider for a pseudoaneurysm that fails to heal or recurrent cerebral ischemia despite antithrombotic treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Nonhealing pseudoaneurysm or recurrent cerebral ischemic events despite antithrombotic therapy

not_recommended.name: Primary endovascular arterial embolization or sacrifice
not_recommended.reason: Often not recommended initially because of procedural complications and the potential for lesion healing while thromboembolism is prevented.

response_assessment.method: Follow-up CT angiography or MRI
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess vascular healing and the need for further therapy.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Whether dual antiplatelet therapy is preferable to aspirin alone, or high-risk lesion features favor anticoagulation, remains unresolved. Information about direct-acting oral anticoagulants as alternatives to warfarin is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with confirmed BCVI
decision_rules: Begin antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy after considering intracranial injury stability and control of extracranial hemorrhage.
Individualize treatment; consider procedural therapy for Bifflgrade ≥ 3 or progression despite medical treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide antithrombotic treatment after diagnosis when bleeding and brain injury stability allow.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgery or endovascular therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider an intervention for higher-grade or progressive injuries.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Bifflgrade ≥ 3 or lesion progression during medical treatment

response_assessment.method: Assess lesion progression and intracranial and extracranial bleeding stability
response_assessment.interpretation: Progression may justify procedural treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence is insufficient to define a pediatric-specific treatment duration.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Hospitalized patients with low-risk nonoperative TBI and stable ICH on follow-up CT
decision_rules: Use mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission regardless of eligibility for medication.
For a nonoperative injury, repeat head CT within 24 hours of the initial study to assess stability before medication, except that minimal initial hemorrhage may not warrant repeat imaging.
Initiate pharmacologic prophylaxis within 24 hours after injury when follow-up CT shows no progression.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis for TBI. The recommended starting enoxaparin regimen is 30 mg every 12 hours; standard dosing is recommended if dalteparin is used.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Evidence summarized by the document associates LMWH with lower VTE rates and comparable ICH progression rates relative to UFH.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Start within 24 hours after injury when follow-up CT confirms stability.

alternative_regimens.name: UFH
alternative_regimens.summary: If chosen, administer 5000 units every 8 hours.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: LMWH is not selected; altered renal function may prompt UFH use.

not_recommended.name: Prophylactic inferior vena cava filters
not_recommended.reason: No longer recommended regardless of the timing of pharmacologic prophylaxis; filter placement is indicated for known VTE with a contraindication to therapeutic anticoagulation.

response_assessment.method: Repeat head CT when indicated
response_assessment.interpretation: Stable ICH supports medication initiation.

supportive_care: Apply mechanical VTE prophylaxis upon admission.
Consider anti-factor Xa monitoring to guide later LMWH doses.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Table 6 defines low risk under the modified Berne-Norwood criteria as the absence of moderate- or high-risk features.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with moderate- or high-risk nonoperative TBI and stable ICH on repeat CT
decision_rules: Begin medication within 24 to 48 hours after injury if repeat CT confirms that the hemorrhage has not progressed.
If ICH has progressed, withhold pharmacologic prophylaxis until another study demonstrates stability, usually in another 24 to 48 hours.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred pharmacologic prophylaxis, with an initial enoxaparin regimen of 30 mg every 12 hours for TBI patients.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Start within 24 to 48 hours after injury if ICH is stable.

alternative_regimens.name: UFH
alternative_regimens.summary: If selected, dose at 5000 units every 8 hours.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: LMWH is not chosen, including when renal function affects its use.

not_recommended.name: Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis during demonstrated ICH progression
not_recommended.reason: Withhold until repeat imaging confirms stability.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before starting prophylaxis and after documented progression
response_assessment.method: Repeat head CT
response_assessment.interpretation: Proceed once ICH stability is demonstrated.

supportive_care: Provide mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission.
Consider anti-factor Xa monitoring for subsequent LMWH adjustment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The modified Berne-Norwood moderate-risk features include SDH or EDH > 8 mm, contusion or IVH > 2 cm, multiple contusions per lobe, scattered subarachnoid hemorrhage, or progression at 24 hrs; its high-risk features include ICP monitor placement, craniotomy, or progression at 72 hrs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients after craniotomy or craniectomy, or patients with an ICP monitor
decision_rules: After craniotomy or craniectomy, consider starting or resuming pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis within 24 to 48 hours if postoperative CT demonstrates stable ICH.
For an ICP monitor without cranial surgery, consider prophylaxis in the same manner as for nonoperative TBI.
Do not routinely withhold prophylaxis merely because an ICP monitor will be inserted or remains in place.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred prophylactic agent, including for patients with ICP monitors; an initial enoxaparin regimen of 30 mg every 12 hours is recommended for TBI.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Consider initiation or resumption within 24 to 48 hours after cranial surgery if postoperative ICH is stable.

alternative_regimens.name: UFH
alternative_regimens.summary: If chosen, dose at 5000 units every 8 hours.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: LMWH is not selected.

not_recommended.name: Routine withholding of pharmacologic prophylaxis for ICP monitor placement or use
not_recommended.reason: The guide does not recommend withholding solely for placement or while a monitor remains in place.

response_assessment.method: Postoperative head CT
response_assessment.interpretation: Stable ICH permits consideration of prophylaxis within the specified window.

supportive_care: Use mechanical prophylaxis from admission.
Consider continuing medication without holding a dose before monitor removal; alternatively, time monitor insertion or removal after one drug half-life has passed.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If CT demonstrates ICH progression, withhold medication until repeat imaging documents stability, usually in another 24 to 48 hours.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pediatric trauma patients stratified for VTE risk after admission
decision_rules: Use a published pediatric VTE risk assessment tool, such as ROCKIT, after admission.
Do not give pharmacologic prophylaxis to low-risk children; provide mechanical prophylaxis from admission for moderate risk and reserve medication for high risk.
Apply the adult considerations concerning ICH, progression risk, and recent surgery when assessing medication contraindications.

recommended_regimens.name: LMWH
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred pharmacologic agent for children categorized as high risk for VTE; use weight-based dosing in young children.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Stop when ambulatory if no other thrombogenic factors remain.

not_recommended.name: Pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in low-risk children
not_recommended.reason: The document states that this risk group does not require it.

response_assessment.method: Pediatric VTE risk stratification and reassessment of ambulation and thrombogenic factors
response_assessment.interpretation: Reserve medication for high risk and discontinue when the specified risk no longer persists.

supportive_care: Initiate mechanical prophylaxis on admission for children at moderate VTE risk.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document reports VTE incidence of 0.09% at ages 0–12 years, 0.27% at ages 13–15 years, and 0.73% at ages 16–21 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with risk factors for early PTS, including severe or penetrating injury, immediate seizure, depressed skull fracture, SDH, ICH, GCS < 10, or cortical contusion
decision_rules: Consider ASM prophylaxis to prevent seizures occurring in the first 7 days when risk factors are present.
Do not continue prophylaxis beyond 7 days merely to prevent late PTS.

recommended_regimens.name: phenytoin
recommended_regimens.summary: An ASM option for early PTS prevention that requires concentration monitoring and attention to interactions and adverse reactions.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the cited RCT, early PTS occurred in 14.2% of the placebo group versus 3.6% of the phenytoin group; early prophylaxis did not prevent PTE.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 7 days

recommended_regimens.name: levetiracetam
recommended_regimens.summary: An ASM option with apparently similar safety and efficacy to phenytoin for early PTS in patients at risk; the studies did not establish superiority of either agent.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 7 days

alternative_regimens.name: (fos)phenytoin
alternative_regimens.summary: The document identifies this as an appropriate pediatric prophylaxis choice alongside levetiracetam.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A child for whom early PTS prophylaxis is recommended.

not_recommended.name: valproic acid
not_recommended.reason: Not recommended for early PTS prophylaxis because the death risk was higher than with phenytoin.

not_recommended.name: Prophylaxis for more than 7 days to prevent late PTS
not_recommended.reason: It is not recommended for prevention of late seizures.

not_recommended.name: Seizure prophylaxis without intracranial bleeding or with isolated traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage
not_recommended.reason: Prophylaxis is not recommended for these TBI presentations.

response_assessment.timepoint: 24 hours after initial phenytoin dosing and once more during 7 days
response_assessment.method: Assess therapeutic phenytoin concentration; monitor albumin and free phenytoin concentration
response_assessment.interpretation: Use results to guide dose adjustment.

response_assessment.method: Review clinical and EEG seizure activity
response_assessment.interpretation: Stop prophylaxis if no seizure has occurred or seizure activity occurred only within the first 24 hours; continuation may be appropriate for activity beyond 24 hours or a preexisting seizure disorder.

supportive_care: Pyridoxine 50–100 mg daily may limit behavioral adverse reactions associated with levetiracetam.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For children, the document describes levetiracetam 20–40 mg/kg/day divided into two doses per day as the most commonly used dose.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients taking warfarin before injury who require emergent surgery or have life-threatening bleeding
decision_rules: Stop the anticoagulant and consider prompt drug-specific reversal.
With warfarin-associated INR ≥ 1.5, the likely benefit of reversal generally outweighs its risks in the situation described.
Do not delay emergency reversal while awaiting laboratory results when bleeding risk is high.

recommended_regimens.name: IV vitamin K and 4PCC
recommended_regimens.summary: Table 7 specifies IV vitamin K 2.5–10 mg with 4PCC: 15 units/kg IV for INR 1.5–1.9, 25 units/kg IV for INR 2–3.9, 35 units/kg IV for INR 4–6, or 50 units/kg IV for INR > 6.

alternative_regimens.name: Fixed-dose 4PCC
alternative_regimens.summary: Table 7 gives 1500 units as the fixed-dose alternative to INR-based 4PCC dosing, alongside IV vitamin K.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A fixed-dose reversal strategy is chosen.

alternative_regimens.name: FFP
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used when 4PCC is unavailable; the document states that approximately 8–16 units of FFP are equivalent to approximately 20–50 units/kg of 4PCC.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: 4PCC is unavailable.

response_assessment.method: Recheck INR
response_assessment.interpretation: If INR is > 1.4, consider 2–4 units of FFP.

response_assessment.method: Recheck INR
response_assessment.interpretation: If INR is > 1.4, give another 2.5–10 mg of IV vitamin K.

supportive_care: Balance reversal-related thrombosis risk against bleeding risk.
Consider subcutaneous heparin or LMWH for VTE prophylaxis during the acute period off therapeutic anticoagulation when appropriate.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document suggests considering lower 4PCC doses of 10–20 units/kg at INR 1.5–1.9 because higher doses (> 2000 to 3000 units) were associated with greater VTE risk in nontraumatic ICH.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients taking rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban who require emergent surgery or have life-threatening bleeding
decision_rules: Identify the DOAC, dose, and time of last administration and stop treatment.
A last dose within 8–12 hours generally favors reversal when emergency intervention or life-threatening bleeding is present.
Normal routine coagulation results do not necessarily exclude therapeutically relevant DOAC concentrations.

recommended_regimens.name: Andexanet alfa
recommended_regimens.summary: Table 7 specifies 400 mg IV bolus followed by 480 mg IV infusion if the last dose was > 7 hours earlier, or 800 mg IV bolus followed by 960 mg IV infusion if it was < 7 hours earlier.

alternative_regimens.name: 4PCC
alternative_regimens.summary: Give 25–50 units/kg or a fixed dose of 2000 units.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Andexanet alfa is unavailable.

alternative_regimens.name: Activated charcoal
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider after a very recent dose.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Last DOAC dose was administered < 2 hours earlier.

response_assessment.method: Assess bleeding, last dose, and factors that could prolong exposure, including renal dysfunction and drug interactions
response_assessment.interpretation: If the last DOAC dose was > 18–24 hours before bleeding, reversal may not be beneficial.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Do not delay emergency reversal for laboratory testing in a patient at high bleeding risk.
