document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) has major public-health and socioeconomic effects and has the highest incidence and prevalence among neurological disorders. In the United States, it is associated annually with an estimated 4.8 million emergency department (ED) visits, 214,000 hospitalizations, and 69,000 deaths. Survivors frequently experience temporary or permanent disability. Worldwide, an estimated 50 to 60 million people sustain TBI each year, with an economic cost equivalent to 400 billion US dollars. TBI is increasingly understood as an acute injury with chronic consequences requiring continuing care. Evidence-based guidance is constrained by a shortage of high-quality studies. The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Trauma Quality Improvement Program (TQIP) first issued TBI best practices in 2015, drawing on available evidence and expert consensus where evidence was absent. At participating trauma centers, deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis among patients with TBI rose from 48% in 2014 to 71% in 2022 following introduction of that guidance; other aspects of care still need improvement. Effective neurotrauma care requires a coordinated multidisciplinary team from injury through recovery. This revision incorporates newer evidence and expands coverage to imaging, blood-based biomarkers, pharmacologic treatment, rehabilitation, and postacute systems of care. Its purpose is practical, comprehensive guidance intended to improve care and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: IMPORTANT NOTE
document_sections.content: The ACS TQP Best Practices Guidelines provide healthcare professionals with evidence-informed guidance, not an exhaustive account of prevention, diagnostic, or treatment options. They do not replace independent clinical judgment or decisions tailored to a patient's presentation.

document_sections.heading: TRIAGE AND TRANSPORT
document_sections.content: Rapidly take adults and children with suspected TBI and any high-risk criterion to the highest-level available trauma center. During transport, watch for and begin correcting hypotension, hypoxia, hypercarbia, and hypothermia. High-risk criteria are Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) motor score < 6, total GCS < 13, skull deformity or suspected fracture, signs of basilar skull fracture, penetrating head trauma, or a caregiver's report of changed baseline behavior after injury in an infant or child. Suspect TBI after a reported head impact or high-energy mechanism in trauma patients with altered mental status, a history of being found down, or neurological symptoms or signs. Maintain particular suspicion after a substantial head impact from a low-level fall, or when nonaccidental trauma is a concern, in children age < 5 years and adults age > 65 years. Prefer pediatric-capable centers for children. In prehospital care, repeatedly assess and document individual GCS components, particularly motor responses, while monitoring blood pressure, pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO2, and temperature. Initial resuscitation at a hospital without neurosurgery may be reasonable when rural transport times are long, but immediate air or ground transfer must be supported by established agreements and protocols. Transfer is especially important with an abnormal neurological examination, displaced skull fracture, or major SDH, EDH, IPH, or IVH.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: The CDC advises trauma-center triage for injured older adults when feasible. Low-energy mechanisms causing serious injury, polypharmacy, age-related physiological responses, frailty, and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use can reduce triage accuracy. Dementia, cerebral atrophy allowing initially silent traumatic hemorrhage, a concurrent stroke or syncope that may precede the injury, and chronic organ insufficiency can also complicate assessment.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Children thought to have clinically important injuries should ideally go to pediatric trauma centers or trauma centers equipped for pediatric care. Transfer to a pediatric trauma center may be unnecessary for selected children with low-energy blunt injury, no suspicion of a nonaccidental mechanism, low risk under PECARN pediatric minor-head-injury CT guidance, negative imaging, or an isolated nondisplaced skull fracture without intracranial injury. Pediatric-specific guidance and prehospital and interfacility resources are important.

document_sections.heading: BASIC ASSESSMENT
document_sections.content: A standardized GCS examination reliably assesses consciousness when its eye, verbal, and motor components are recorded and communicated separately for each patient; total scores such as 3–15 support injury classification and comparisons between groups. Pupillary responses supply diagnostic and prognostic information, and quantitative pupillometry produces measurements that are more reproducible than routine clinical assessment. Initial ED assessment follows ATLS® principles and briefly assesses GCS, pupillary reactions, and lateralizing signs. Depending on priorities, a fuller examination evaluates scalp wounds, penetrating injury, and evidence of basal or depressed skull fractures. Subsequent serial GCS and pupil examinations are central to clinical neuromonitoring. Where advanced monitoring, including ICP monitoring, is unavailable, the CREVICE approach combines clinical examinations with repeated CT. Continued evaluation and optimization of blood pressure and gas exchange are essential because the injured brain is vulnerable to physiological insults.

document_sections.heading: Assessing the Level of Consciousness: GCS and Other Tools
document_sections.content: GCS assesses eye, verbal, and motor responses across injury severities; pediatric GCS is more reliable in preverbal children aged 0–2 years. Preexisting delirium, dementia, or aphasia can confound verbal scoring in older adults, whereas motor score has the strongest association with long-term outcomes. Use a consistent assessment and reporting method throughout care, obtaining a baseline once immediate threats to life are addressed. For individual patients, document each component, for example Eye 4, Verbal 4, Motor 6. Eye and verbal responses better distinguish less severe injuries; motor responses are especially relevant in severe injury. First observe spontaneous behavior, then assess responses to speech, and, if necessary, apply and document a consistent central or peripheral stimulus. Record the response of the better arm rather than the legs. The table presents standard and pediatric GCS response categories and scores. Summed GCS can assist group comparisons, classification, and prognosis alongside other factors: ≥ 13 corresponds to mild, 9–12 to moderate, and ≤ 8 to severe injury. Classification by the total score alone oversimplifies injury burden. Posttraumatic amnesia (PTA) indicates severity but may be difficult to assess soon after injury and is more useful in rehabilitation. FOUR was designed chiefly for impaired consciousness in the ICU; it examines eye and motor responses, brainstem reflexes, and breathing, omitting a verbal component that intubation may prevent testing. In children, physicians and nurses have shown good inter-rater reliability with FOUR. It provides more neurological detail in profound consciousness impairment and can be applied in locked-in syndrome, but GCS remains preferred for general ICU assessment across injury severities.

document_sections.heading: Pupillary Reactivity and Pupillometry
document_sections.content: The pupillary light response informs diagnosis and prognosis. Some asymmetry can be normal, but newly developing asymmetry may signal brainstem compression and impending uncal herniation and requires further evaluation and intervention. Compression of third-cranial-nerve parasympathetic fibers in uncal herniation can make a pupil progressively slower to react or unreactive. A unilateral unreactive pupil is compatible with an ipsilateral mass; bilateral fixed, dilated pupils indicate a poor overall prognosis for functional recovery.

document_sections.heading: Older Adults
document_sections.content: Preexisting glaucoma, cataract disease, or previous eye surgery can complicate interpretation of pupils in older adults. Postsurgical pupils may limit some uses of quantitative pupillometry, although cataract surgery does not alter the pupillary light-reflex parameters obtained by automated pupillometry. Clinical history helps interpret abnormal light responses, anisocoria, and oculomotor palsy.

document_sections.heading: Quantitative Pupillometry
document_sections.content: Ordinary clinical estimates of pupil size and reactivity have relatively poor inter-rater and intrarater reliability. A handheld quantitative pupillometer uses visible and infrared light to measure the pupil and its light response more consistently. Its reported measures are starting and ending diameters in mm, % Change, latency in s, and average constriction and dilation velocities in mm/s. Infant myelination changes can affect normal latency and may limit predetermined pediatric thresholds. Objective measurements can reveal changes before they are evident on clinical examination and can assess reactivity when opioids or other drugs make pupils too small for easy visual assessment. Results can be entered into the electronic medical record.

document_sections.heading: IMAGING
document_sections.content: Obtain head CT for adults with externally caused head injury and altered mental status, loss of consciousness (LOC), PTA, or a focal neurological deficit. For children, use a validated rule such as PECARN to determine imaging indications. Negative CT does not exclude TBI. MRI identifies traumatic intracranial injuries more sensitively than CT, and findings on either modality contribute prognostic information.

document_sections.heading: Initial Imaging
document_sections.content: Head CT is the principal acute study because it detects acute intracranial injury and craniofacial or cervical fractures with high sensitivity and specificity. Modern multi-slice scanners acquire images in < 5 seconds, an advantage for agitated patients, polytrauma, and young children. Unlike MRI, noncontrast CT does not require screening for contraindications such as metallic implants or foreign bodies. Recommended brain reconstructions are axial, coronal, and sagittal at 2.0 mm to 3.75 mm slice thickness, supplemented by 0.5 mm to 1.25 mm bonealgorithm images to better show craniofacial fractures.

document_sections.heading: Guidelines for Imaging
document_sections.content: The CDC/ACEP policy recommends noncontrast head CT for patients aged 16 years or older with LOC or PTA when they also have any of the following: GCS less than 15; age greater than 60 years; trauma above the clavicle; a supra-therapeutic INR or thrombocytopenia; headache; vomiting; intoxication with drugs or alcohol; short-term memory deficit; posttraumatic seizure; or focal neurological deficit. Without LOC or PTA, consider CT for GCS less than 15, age 65 years and older, coagulopathy, focal deficit, severe headache, vomiting, evidence of basilar skull fracture, or a dangerous mechanism such as vehicle ejection, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, or a fall down five stairs or 3 feet or more. Published sports-concussion guidance uses similar criteria.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Imaging indications for older adults generally resemble those for younger adults, but anticoagulation increases intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) incidence and may justify more liberal early CT. Because age itself prompts CT under current rules, blood biomarkers may help identify older patients with GCS 13–15 who do not require imaging.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: When children need emergency imaging, CT is commonly selected for speed, availability, and the possibility of avoiding sedation. Use it judiciously because children are more susceptible to radiation-associated malignancy. Some centers use rapid MRI first in infants and young children who do not need sedation. Regardless of modality, follow validated pediatric rules such as PECARN. In selected children with GCS 15, neither a palpable skull fracture nor findings suggesting a basilar fracture, observation for 4 to 6 hours may avert imaging even with 1 or 2 PECARN predictors of clinically important TBI.

document_sections.heading: CT and the Incidence and Prognostic Implications of Intracranial Injury
document_sections.content: Intracranial findings on initial CT become more frequent as GCS falls; more than 80% of patients with GCS 3–12 have detectable intracranial injury. The Rotterdam CT score combines basal-cistern effacement, midline shift, EDH, IVH, and subarachnoid hemorrhage into a score of 1 to 6 that predicts TBI-related mortality at 6 months in patients with GCS 3–12. CT abnormalities are less frequent with GCS 13–15, but subarachnoid hemorrhage, contusion, and SDH are associated with incomplete recovery; IVH and/or petechial hemorrhage are associated with more severe impairment.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Role of MRI
document_sections.content: MRI is more sensitive than CT for most acute intracranial abnormalities, including small contusions, small extra-axial hematomas, microhemorrhages, and small white-matter lesions representing traumatic axonal and/or microvascular injury. Several studies at Level 1 trauma centers detected injury on MRI in more than 25% of patients with TBI whose initial CT was negative. MRI-detected injuries predict disability; a negative CT therefore does not exclude TBI. MRI is used mainly when concerns persist, including unexplained acute impairment of consciousness, continuing subacute symptoms or deficits, or suspected lesions missed on CT. A brain MRI protocol should include T1, T2, T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted imaging/apparent diffusion coefficient, and susceptibilityweighted imaging (SWI), or conventional T2*weighted gradient echo if SWI is unavailable. The latter sequences improve detection of blood products and CT-occult microhemorrhages.

document_sections.heading: BLOOD-BASED BIOMARKERS
document_sections.content: GFAP, UCH-L1, and S100B can help rule out a need for CT when suspected TBI is accompanied by GCS 13–15, clinical-rule indications for CT, and a clinician-assessed low but nonzero risk of traumatic ICH. Their elevation on the injury day helps estimate structural injury severity and contributes to prediction of functional recovery at 6 months in patients with GCS 3–12. Acute noncontrast CT identifies vascular injury, edema, tissue deformation, and patients requiring surgery, but does not adequately quantify neuronal or glial damage. Persistent disabling neurological or psychiatric symptoms can follow a negative CT. Approximately 90% of CT scans obtained during acute TBI evaluation in the United States are negative, exposing patients to potentially avoidable radiation and increasing costs and ED length of stay.

document_sections.heading: Biomarkers and Imaging Decisions
document_sections.content: Blood GFAP and UCH-L1 testing in potentially injured patients aged 18 years or older may help exclude the need for CT. FDA-authorized rapid devices include a point-of-care venipuncture test returning results in as little as 15 minutes and a laboratory test with results in 18 minutes.

document_sections.heading: S100B
document_sections.content: S100B is a glial calcium-binding protein released after glial injury and extensively studied to support CT decisions. Its diagnostic sensitivity for a likely positive CT is excellent, but its short half-life restricts recommended sampling to within 6 hours of injury. It is not FDA-cleared for routine United States use, although Scandinavian imaging guidance incorporated it in 2013. That guidance recommends testing adults with mild head injury within 6 hours of trauma if they have either GCS 14 without risk factors, including anticoagulation, coagulation disorders, posttraumatic seizures, signs of depressed or basal skull fracture, or focal deficits; or GCS 15 with LOC or repeated vomiting (≥ 2) and no other risk factors. A result less than 0.10 mcg/L permits discharge without brain CT under that guidance.

document_sections.heading: GFAP and UCH-L1
document_sections.content: GFAP is predominantly an astrocytic intermediate filament protein; UCH-L1 is abundant in neurons. Injury releases both into blood. UCH-L1 becomes detectable within 30 minutes, peaks within 8 hours, and subsequently falls; GFAP appears within 1 hour, peaks at about 20 hours, then declines. Prospective observational evidence from at least three large multicenter studies involving > 6,000 patients in the United States and Europe found excellent negative predictive value for combined injury-day measurements in excluding traumatic ICH. The table summarizes assay-specific study cutoffs and diagnostic accuracy. For the FDA-approved iSTAT assay, GFAP less than 30 pg/mL together with UCH-L1 less than 360 pg/mL is considered nonelevated and rules out the need for CT. If either exceeds its cutoff, CT is indicated; elevation does not establish that CT will be positive, and MRI can reveal structural injury despite a negative CT. FDA clearance requires whole-blood measurement within 24 hours of injury. GFAP also adds diagnostic information to clinical CT decision rules.

document_sections.heading: Biomarkers and Functional Recovery
document_sections.content: Higher biomarker concentrations are associated with greater structural injury and worse prognosis. In one study, injury-day iSTAT GFAP > 12,000 pg/mL was associated with a 6.98 times higher risk of death within 6 months than < 1200 pg/mL. Injury-day iSTAT UCH-L1 > 2000 pg/mL was associated with a 22.38 times higher risk of death within 6 months than < 360 pg/mL. Most deaths occurred in the first month. Among patients with GCS 3–12, the biomarkers discriminated independent function outside the home (GOS-E > 4) from lack of that function (C-statistic 0.89; 95% CI 0.86–0.91). Alone, they do not predict functional recovery accurately enough in GCS 13–15. Patients with GCS 15 and markedly elevated GFAP and/or UCH-L1 warrant brain injury or concussion-clinic referral because recovery may be prolonged. Even patients with nonelevated results can have persistent symptoms, although their risk is much lower; counsel them to seek care if symptoms persist.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Age and age-related neurodegenerative disease, including Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias, raise baseline GFAP and UCH-L1, narrowing the range available to distinguish acute injury. Age- or comorbidity-specific thresholds might reduce unnecessary CT, as demonstrated for S100B measured within 3 hours. The table presents injury-day diagnostic accuracy of GFAP and UCH-L1 assays in adults > 65 years old, including time-specific results.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Research links blood biomarkers to intracranial injury in children, but evidence is insufficient to establish the clinical usefulness of GFAP, UCH-L1, or S100B for suspected pediatric TBI. Validated CT decision rules such as PECARN remain the best available evaluation aids.

document_sections.heading: GOALS OF DIRECTED CARE
document_sections.content: Aim to maintain normal physiological parameters after weighing intervention risks against potential benefits. CPP, ICP, and PbtO2 are especially pertinent in ICU care, whereas SpO2 applies broadly. The table lists recommended ranges for oxygenation, ventilation, blood pressure, ICP, PbtO2, CPP, sodium, osmolality, INR, temperature, platelets, pH, glucose, and hemoglobin. These represent ideal ranges, not targets to pursue at any cost. ICP 22 mm Hg is a useful initial treatment threshold; when escalation entails substantial hazards, including decompressive craniectomy, consider 20–25 mm Hg. CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg is a practical goal adjusted for autoregulation, and monitored PbtO2 should reach ≥ 15 mm Hg. Initial targets include SpO2 ≥ 94% and PaO2 80–100 mm Hg; avoid PaO2 > 100 mm Hg unless brain oximetry guides treatment. Without intracranial hypertension, target PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg and pH 7.35–7.45. Significant lung disease may require pulmonary-specific targets such as permissive hypercapnia while other measures control elevated ICP.

document_sections.heading: Vital Signs
document_sections.content: Monitor SBP and MAP closely to prevent hypotension. When ICP is not monitored, targeting SBP ≥ 110 mm Hg/MAP > 80 mm Hg generally supports cerebral perfusion. Although no definitive blood-pressure cutoff exists, TBI mortality probability rises linearly for each 10-point SBP decrease below 119 mm Hg, suggesting that higher goals may be appropriate. Maintain normothermia at 36–37.9°C and treat fever aggressively.

document_sections.heading: Electrolyte Management
document_sections.content: Maintain sodium at 135–145 mEq/L; preventing hyponatremia is important because it can worsen cerebral edema. Frequent testing may be necessary when diabetes insipidus or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone / cerebral salt wasting syndrome develops. Measure osmolality when mannitol is used. Both high and low glucose may harm outcomes; monitor closely and target 100–180 mg/ dL. Consider more frequent glucose checks when nutritional support begins, particularly with known or suspected diabetes mellitus.

document_sections.heading: Hematology Monitoring
document_sections.content: Monitor hematologic status in TBI. Despite some variation in transfusion recommendations, the cited literature and expert consensus suggest a hemoglobin transfusion threshold of ≥ 7 g/dL. Evaluate coagulopathy early, including INR assessment of coagulation pathways; INR ≤ 1.4 is appropriate in most cases. TEG, ROTEM, and platelet-function assays may provide additional guidance for targeted reversal.

document_sections.heading: INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE MONITORING
document_sections.content: ICP monitoring supplements rather than replaces serial neurological and CT assessment. It is recommended in comatose patients with GCS ≤ 8 and structural brain injury on initial CT. Consider it carefully in patients with GCS > 8 and progressive-risk lesions such as large or multiple contusions; when ICP information would facilitate extracranial surgery or potentially ICP-raising treatments; after radiographic progression or clinical deterioration; or when urgent extracranial surgery, airway compromise, or respiratory failure necessitates sedation. It is generally not indicated for coma without structural damage or evidence of elevated ICP on initial CT; neurological examinations and serial CT can be used instead. Persistent ICP elevation predicts poor outcome. Monitoring allows calculation of CPP from MAP – ICP = CPP, supports decisions about cerebral perfusion, and may warn of lesion progression, swelling, or postoperative complications.

document_sections.heading: ICP Monitoring Role in Patient Management
document_sections.content: An elevated ICP may prompt imaging, medication, or surgery; absence of elevation may allow reduced sedation, extubation, or earlier extracranial operations. Continue established ICP monitoring when patients leave the ICU for surgery, imaging, or procedures. ACS TQIP observational data associated monitoring with lower in-hospital mortality. The international prospective observational SYNAPSE-ICU study associated it with more intensive treatment and lower mortality at 6 months in more severe cases. Monitoring-guided treatment of intracranial hypertension might therefore be considered in severe TBI, although practice varies internationally. A South American RCT found no outcome difference between care targeting monitored ICP ≤ 20 mm Hg and care guided by imaging and neurological examinations; this did not establish that monitoring should cease, but emphasized active identification and treatment of intracranial hypertension by either approach. The accepted treatment trigger is ICP 22 mm Hg, with 20–25 mm Hg for more than 5 minutes considered a reasonable range, although individual injury features may alter the appropriate threshold. The magnitude and duration of ICP elevation together may matter more than a fixed cutoff; higher ICP dose is associated with worse outcomes throughout the GOS range. Base escalation on both magnitude and duration, distinguishing sustained trends from brief elevations caused by ventilator dyssynchrony or plateau waves. Higher-tier treatment, including decompressive craniectomy, warrants a higher threshold or dose, as illustrated by RESCUE-ICP. Interpret ICP alongside arterial pressure, CPP, and autoregulation. An EVD connected to an external strain-gauge transducer is the measurement gold standard and permits therapeutic CSF drainage. An intraparenchymal transducer is reliable but cannot drain CSF. Subdural and epidural monitors are not recommended because they are less accurate.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: General indications for ICP monitoring may not fit every older adult: cerebral atrophy may lower intracranial-hypertension risk. Reported monitoring rates range from 5% to 44%, depending on the studied population. Observational findings conflict: some studies associate monitoring with lower mortality after age 65 years, whereas others associate it with severe disability, vegetative outcome, or death. Monitoring remained uncommon among older adults meeting BTF criteria at high-volume centers, and its mortality or functional benefit in this population remains unresolved.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Consensus guidance based on pooled retrospective evidence supports considering ICP monitoring in severe pediatric TBI. Studies finding no functional-survival improvement or increased morbidity and mortality could not adequately account for differences between monitored and unmonitored groups. Recent retrospective evidence suggests similar long-term outcomes with EVD and intraparenchymal transducers, although EVD drainage may produce slightly lower acute ICP. Select a technique according to clinical risks and advantages. Cerebral blood flow, autoregulation, blood pressure, ICP, and CPP vary with development; children's appropriate MAP and CPP are below adult values. CPP above 50 mm Hg at ages 6 to 17 years and above 40 mm Hg at ages 0 to 5 years appear reasonable treatment-study targets. An ICP upper limit of 20 mm Hg is recommended for children on retrospective evidence; lower thresholds have not been shown to improve outcomes, and additional research is needed.

document_sections.heading: TIERED MANAGEMENT OF INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE
document_sections.content: Treat raised ICP after severe TBI to limit secondary injury; untreated elevation can cause herniation, brainstem compression, reduced CPP, ischemia, or, in extreme cases, cessation of brain perfusion. Invasive monitors are currently preferred for accuracy and can detect expanding lesions, guide targeted treatment, calculate CPP and autoregulatory status, and provide waveform information about compliance. SIBICC developed three treatment tiers through a rigorous Delphi-based expert-consensus process to address gaps in evidence-based guidance. Treatments with more favorable risk–benefit profiles generally precede those with less favorable profiles, while clinicians retain discretion within tiers and can target suspected physiological disturbances. These algorithms are suggestions that can standardize care, not standards of practice; relevant disciplines should review and approve or adapt them locally. The full protocols cover ICP alone or ICP with low PbtO2, discouraged interventions, neurological worsening, and treatment weaning.

document_sections.heading: Tiered Treatments
document_sections.content: Tier Zero comprises basic ICU measures expected or recommended regardless of ICP; Tiers One, Two, and Three address intracranial hypertension. Treatments within a tier are unranked, not every lower-tier intervention must be tried before advancing, and a tier can be skipped when advantageous. Tier Zero expected care includes ICU admission, intubation and ventilation, serial neurological and pupil examinations, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, pain relief and sedation for comfort and ventilator synchrony rather than directed ICP control, fever prevention with core-temperature measurement and treatment above 38.0°C, and consideration of antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only unless continuation is indicated. It also includes initial CPP ≥ 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin > 7 g/dL, avoidance of hyponatremia, unobstructed venous drainage from the head, continuous arterial-pressure monitoring, and SpO2 ≥ 94%. Central-line insertion and end-tidal CO2 monitoring are recommended. Tier One includes CPP 60–70 mm Hg, more analgesia and sedation to lower ICP, PaCO2 35–38 mm Hg/4.7–5.1 kPa, intermittent mannitol boluses of 0.25–1.0 g/kg or hypertonic-saline boluses, CSF drainage through an existing EVD or consideration of EVD insertion after an initial parenchymal probe, possible antiseizure prophylaxis for 1 week only, and consideration of EEG. Recommended limits when giving mannitol or hypertonic saline are sodium 155 mEq/L and osmolality 320 mEq/L. Tier Two includes PaCO2 32–35 mm Hg/4.3–4.6 kPa; a trial dose of neuromuscular paralysis in an adequately sedated patient, followed by infusion only if ICP improves; and a MAP Challenge to assess autoregulation and individualize MAP and CPP, returning MAP to baseline if autoregulation is impaired or setting a higher target if intact autoregulation permits lower ICP. Tier Three comprises pentobarbital or sodium thiopentone when a test shows ICP benefit, secondary decompressive craniectomy, and active cooling to 35–36°C. Continue barbiturates only with demonstrated ICP improvement, titrate for ICP control without exceeding the dose producing burst suppression, and avoid hypotension.

document_sections.heading: Treatments Not Recommended for Intracranial Hypertension in Severe TBI
document_sections.content: SIBICC discourages continuous non-bolus intravenous mannitol; scheduled hyperosmolar infusions, such as every 4 to 6 hours; lumbar CSF drainage; furosemide; routine steroids; routine therapeutic cooling below 35°C because of systemic complications; high-dose propofol intended to induce burst suppression; routinely lowering PaCO2 below 30 mm Hg/4.0 kPa; and routinely raising CPP above 90 mm Hg. Its judgments reflect evidence against some interventions and insufficient supportive evidence for others; listing an intervention does not prohibit its consideration in an individual case.

document_sections.heading: Inter-Tier Recommendations
document_sections.content: Advancing tiers can indicate greater treatment resistance. Before escalation, reassess the patient and consider another CT, reconsider whether lesions warrant surgery, look for extracranial causes of elevated ICP such as intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure, and verify basic physiological targets including CPP and blood gases. Consider consultation or transfer to a higher level of care when applicable.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: When managing ICP pharmacologically in older adults, assess whether doses need adjustment to prevent toxicity or prolonged drug action. Age-related changes in volume of distribution, protein binding with hypoalbuminemia, hepatic metabolism, and renal function can increase active-drug concentrations. Dementia, stroke, other comorbidities, and medication adverse effects complicate diagnosis and treatment goals. Recovery may be slower and outcomes worse, although aggressive care and good preinjury health may mitigate these effects.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: An interdisciplinary pediatric severe-TBI consensus update in 2019 included a two-tier algorithm broadly resembling SIBICC; minor tier-placement differences do not establish evidence-based disagreement. It preceded ADAPT results. Pediatric evidence supports hypertonic 3% saline at 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 20 min or continuously at 0.1–1 mL/kg/hour, or 23.4% saline at 0.5 mL/kg (up to 30 mL) over 10 to 20 minutes. Mannitol has less supporting evidence. Tier Two recommends a lower hypoventilation target of 28 to 34 mm Hg. Moderate prophylactic hypothermia at 32–33°C is not recommended instead of normothermia to improve overall outcomes, although it is suggested to control ICP.

document_sections.heading: NEUROMONITORING
document_sections.content: Regular serial neurological examinations underpin TBI monitoring and may be supplemented with quantitative pupillometry. Techniques beyond ICP alone can help individualize targets and treatment. ICP by itself cannot identify every cerebral insult or establish whether autoregulation is intact. Pressure autoregulation maintains cerebral blood flow across a range of systemic pressures and protects against hypotensive ischemia and excessive flow that raises ICP. SIBICC recommends assessing autoregulation when initial Tier One treatment fails to lower ICP. Brain hypoxia can occur at normal or high ICP; consider physiologically targeted, tiered treatment. Continuous EEG helps identify and manage seizures, particularly nonconvulsive seizures.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of Cerebral Autoregulation
document_sections.content: For a bedside MAP challenge in a euvolemic patient with a closed cranium, start or increase vasopressor infusion to raise MAP by 10–15 mm Hg for no more than 20 minutes while monitoring ICP. An experienced bedside provider should supervise directly, without other treatment changes. Record MAP, ICP, CPP, and PbtO2 before and after. A rise in ICP suggests impaired autoregulation and possible benefit from a lower CPP goal; unchanged or falling ICP suggests intact autoregulation, with a potentially higher CPP goal, particularly when ICP falls. PRx continuously relates MAP to ICP through a regression-line slope and can inform patient-specific CPP targets. With PRx slope > 0.13, CPP 50–60 mm Hg may be considered; with PRx slope < 0.13, CPP 60– 70 mm Hg may be beneficial. PRx assessment requires specialized expertise, hardware, and software. PbtO2 can also help assess autoregulation if PaO2 stays constant, verified by blood gases before and after the challenge. Direct cerebral blood-flow monitoring during a challenge should show minimal flow change with intact autoregulation but increased flow with impairment. Transcranial doppler ultrasonography and hemodynamic challenge are other assessment options.

document_sections.heading: Research findings
document_sections.content: Multiple studies associate PbtO2 ≤ 15 mm Hg and jugular venous oxygen saturation ≤ 50% with poor outcomes; tissue hypoxia can occur despite normal ICP and CPP. In the Phase II prospective BOOST II RCT, management guided by ICP plus PbtO2 significantly reduced the duration and severity of brain hypoxia compared with ICP-guided care alone, with trends toward lower mortality and better neurological outcomes at 6 months. The trial was not powered to establish significant outcome differences. Phase III BOOST III and BONANZA trials are underway. The completed Oxy-TC trial found no difference in functional outcome between ICP plus PbtO2 and ICP-only monitoring in nonpenetrating TBI.

document_sections.heading: Brain tissue oxygen management
document_sections.content: Accepted thresholds for treating brain hypoxia lie between 15–20 mm Hg. SIBICC II options include raising FiO2 to 60% at Tier One; at Tier Two, increasing PaO2 to as high as 150 mm Hg, attempting greater sedation or neuromuscular paralysis, or increasing CPP when a MAP challenge indicates intact autoregulation; and at Tier Three, raising PaO2 above 150 mm Hg or transfusing 1 unit of packed red blood cells if PbtO2 stays less than 20 mm Hg despite CPP optimization. Autoregulation results may help individualize CPP. Consider potential harm from hyperoxia, especially with Tier Three treatment.

document_sections.heading: Electroencephalography
document_sections.content: Bedside continuous EEG assists seizure detection and management, including identifying otherwise unrecognized nonconvulsive seizures as a cause of reduced consciousness. Such seizures were estimated in 25% of patients with moderate to severe TBI and associated with worse outcomes and long-term hippocampal atrophy. Surface EEG requires an on-site technician and a physician trained in interpretation. Quantitative EEG may lessen interpretation demands but is not universally available. EEG-based detection of secondary ischemia and covert consciousness remains experimental.

document_sections.heading: Multimodal Neuromonitoring
document_sections.content: Centers with larger severe-TBI caseloads or neurocritical-care expertise may add at least one monitoring modality beyond ICP alone. Lower-volume centers may lack the resources for a full multimodal program.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Older-adult-specific evidence for multimodal monitoring is limited, and aging physiology can alter the usefulness and interpretation of findings. Published studies describe less frequent invasive ICP monitoring in older adults and/or worse observed outcomes; differences in treatment intensity or assumptions about cerebral atrophy may contribute. Other studies report an inverse relationship between age and measured ICP, suggesting normal ICP may fall with age. Arterial stiffness may reduce cerebral blood flow and increase pulsatility, impairing flow regulation; orthostasis and syncope may cause hypoperfusion. Autoregulatory capacity is nevertheless believed to persist with aging. Chronic hypertension shifts the autoregulatory curve toward higher pressures, potentially raising risk during relative hypotension. Age-related pupil changes and common baseline EEG slowing or epileptiform activity in patients with comorbidities can complicate interpretation.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Neurological examinations in children may need age-appropriate adaptations. Cerebral tissue oxygenation data are less extensive than in adults, vary with age, and lack validated normal thresholds for applying PbtO2 or autoregulation measures clinically. Continuous EEG is not routine, but broader use may be appropriate for children at particularly high seizure risk, especially infants.

document_sections.heading: SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
document_sections.content: Evacuate a large traumatic hematoma before neurological deterioration, regardless of GCS. For acute SDH, use a large trauma craniotomy that permits bleeding control and the option of leaving the bone flap out. After evacuation, assess concomitant intracranial and extracranial injuries, availability of ICP monitoring, and ICU resources before replacing the flap; do not replace it if doing so would compress the brain. Secondary decompressive craniectomy controls refractory ICP and improves longer-term outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Indications
document_sections.content: TBI surgery commonly evacuates EDH or SDH or relieves pressure from contusions or intracerebral hematomas. Take a comatose patient with a large hematoma likely causing coma directly to surgery on ED arrival if meaningful recovery remains possible. Evacuate a large traumatic hematoma (> 25 mL) before deterioration even with a relatively high GCS; posterior-fossa lesions may warrant a lower operative threshold. Delayed hematoma development or enlargement with neurological decline requires prompt evacuation. For acute SDH, a large craniotomy permits clot evacuation, identification of sources such as bridging veins, the temporal base, or superficial contusions, and meticulous hemostasis. Consistent with BTF severe-TBI guidance, a flap of ≈ 12 × 15 cm can expose parasagittal, parietooccipital, and temporo-basal bleeding and facilitate decompression. The 15 cm dimension may be excessive with a smaller head; at least 13 cm vertically allows effective middle-fossa decompression. Additional subtemporal or sphenoid-wing bone removal may improve exposure. Attempted burr-hole drainage has no role for solid clots.

document_sections.heading: Figure 2. Trauma Craniotomy
document_sections.content: The illustrated large frontotemporoparietal craniotomy improves visualization and permits primary or secondary decompression. Its reverse-question-mark incision begins 1 cm anterior to the tragus at the zygomatic root, passes above the pinna and behind the parietal prominence, then extends to the hairline while remaining 1.5–2 cm lateral to midline. Reflection of the myocutaneous flap exposes the keyhole and zygomatic root; burr holes then permit a large opening over the anterior and middle fossa floors.

document_sections.heading: Decompressive Craniectomy
document_sections.content: After a large frontotemporoparietal craniotomy, decompressive craniectomy leaves the bone flap out; its use has increased. In trauma, it has primary and secondary indications.

document_sections.heading: Primary decompressive craniectomy
document_sections.content: Primary decompressive craniectomy leaves the bone flap out after evacuation of an acute mass lesion, usually an acute SDH. It is recommended when the brain is swollen. Replacing the flap may be appropriate if it will not compress the brain, after considering associated brain and extracranial injuries and the availability of ICP monitoring and ICU facilities.

document_sections.heading: Secondary decompressive craniectomy
document_sections.content: Secondary decompressive craniectomy removes a bone flap to address swelling and ICP that remains elevated despite medical treatment. Patients without an immediate surgical indication are initially managed medically. With refractory ICP > 25 mm Hg, this operation was shown to lower mortality and improve outcomes over time, based on 24-month data. The RESCUEicp trial projected that, among 100 patients receiving the operation rather than conservative management, 21 additional patients would survive; of those additional survivors, one-third would be independent outside the home, one-third independent at home, and one-third dependent.

document_sections.heading: Other Surgical Decisions
document_sections.content: Additional operative decisions concern traumatic intracerebral hematoma, hemorrhagic contusion, and depressed skull fractures.

document_sections.heading: Traumatic intracerebral hematoma/hemorrhagic contusion
document_sections.content: Management remains disputed. Neurologic decline with mass effect makes the case for surgery clearer, whereas preventive early surgery for smaller lesions remains debatable. The STITCH (Trauma) trial ended early because recruitment was slow; it found better survival with early surgery and a tendency toward better functional outcomes, particularly at GCS 9–12. In the prospective longitudinal CENTER-TBI cohort, early surgery was associated with better outcomes for patients with GCS 9–12 or an isolated traumatic intracerebral hematoma, similarly to STITCH (Trauma).

document_sections.heading: Depressed skull fractures
document_sections.content: Surgical elevation is common when depression exceeds the adjacent skull’s thickness, particularly in a cosmetically important location such as the forehead. Open fractures are usually operated on to prevent infection. Selected fractures may be managed without surgery only when there is no dural tear, gross contamination, infection, or frontal sinus injury. Fractures over a dural venous sinus generally are not operated on because bleeding may be uncontrollable.

document_sections.heading: NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT
document_sections.content: Start EN after hemodynamic stabilization, ideally within 24–72 hours of injury, and attain complete nutritional supplementation within 7 days. Rapidly obtainable postpyloric access is preferred, but gastric feeding is acceptable if pursuing postpyloric access would delay EN. Consider PN when EN is contraindicated. Hospitalized patients with TBI risk substantial protein and energy shortfalls and loss of lean mass during critical illness; nutrition helps meet requirements, prevent malnutrition, and temper catabolism.

document_sections.heading: Nutrition Targets
document_sections.content: Metabolic disturbances can persist from 1 week to several months. Reported energy expenditure ranges from 120% to 250% of predicted basal expenditure. Muscle activity, fever, infection, and other injuries appear to increase metabolism, while normothermia protocols may lower expenditure beneath predictions. Indirect calorimetry is the optimal means of setting caloric targets. In one study of critically ill trauma patients, TBI did not increase protein requirements relative to other trauma, and protein delivery up to 2 g/kg/day improved nitrogen balance.

document_sections.heading: Initiating Enteral Feeding
document_sections.content: Studies, including a large meta-analysis, associated early nutritional support with fewer infections and lower mortality. EN started within the first two days after admission was associated with less pneumonia and a shorter hospital stay. Early EN commonly means initiation within 24 to 72 hours of injury; this timing is recommended alongside the BTF goal of full support within 7 days. The American Society for Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition gives similar guidance. High-protein EN formulas are preferred. Immune-enhancing formulas may reduce infections and improve nutritional measures. Fish oil reduced inflammatory stress and cellular injury in murine models and small human trials; consider fish-oil-fortified EN unless contraindicated.

document_sections.heading: Feeding Methods
document_sections.content: TBI-specific studies found substantially less pneumonia with postpyloric tubes, without improvement in other outcomes attributable to feeding location. Do not postpone EN to secure postpyloric access. Consider PN if an absolute EN contraindication is expected to delay feeding. EN remains first-line because it is more cost-effective and physiologically appropriate; when contraindicated, PN initiation within 72 hours postinjury is recommended.

document_sections.heading: Glycemic Control
document_sections.content: Published guidance for critically ill adults sets glucose targets at 100 to 180 mg/dL. Observational TBI studies associate both low and high glucose with worse outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Older adults with TBI have heightened nutrition-related risk. Malnutrition at admission can reach 62% and is associated with cognitive impairment, infection, depressive symptoms, delayed mobilization, longer hospitalization, and readmission. Screen and repeatedly assess nutritional status; the Mini Nutritional Assessment is most widely used, and the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index incorporates serum albumin and body mass index. Nutritional intervention aims to rebuild protein and energy stores, preserve function, and lower malnutrition-associated costs affecting length of stay, subacute care, and quality of life. Dysphagia raises aspiration and malnutrition risk; mechanical ventilation is its principal risk factor. Bedside volume-viscosity swallowing assessment can screen for it.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: In severe pediatric TBI, nutrition plans must account for hydration and electrolytes to avoid fluid shifts that worsen cerebral edema. Predictive equations may overstate energy needs: sedation, neuromuscular blockade, temperature management, and seizure control can lower expenditure below predicted basal values. Pediatric data support EN after hemodynamic stabilization, ideally within 24 to 72 hours, with an attempt at full support within 7 days. Gastric and postpyloric EN are both viable; more children reach caloric goals with postpyloric feeding, without a difference in intolerance symptoms. Consider PN if EN is contraindicated.

document_sections.heading: AIRWAY AND VENTILATION
document_sections.content: Early intubation and mechanical ventilation are recommended for TBI with GCS < 9, severe agitation, absent airway protection, or GCS > 8 with thoracic and abdominal injuries. Prescribe ventilation to keep arterial pH at 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 at 35–45 mm Hg when intracranial hypertension and severe metabolic acidosis are absent, and oxygen saturation at least 94%. Consider extubation after intracranial hypertension has resolved, the latest CT shows no evolving lesion, and the patient can protect the upper airway and cough.

document_sections.heading: Intubation and Ventilation Management
document_sections.content: Early airway support in patients with depressed consciousness, severe agitation, or lost airway reflexes aims to prevent hypoxia and aspiration while controlling carbon dioxide; protect the cervical spine during intubation. Following intubation, the described goals are arterial pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–40 mm Hg absent intracranial hypertension or severe metabolic acidosis, and saturation at least 94%. The optimal PaO2 range is 80–100 mm Hg, potentially higher when neuromonitoring supports it; without elevated ICP, optimal PaCO2 is 35–45 mm Hg. SIBICC suggests PaCO2 of 32–35 mm Hg as Tier-Two treatment for elevated ICP or neurologic worsening with uncal herniation. PaCO2 below 30 mm Hg may be justified temporarily for refractory severe intracranial hypertension or threatened or actual herniation while other interventions, including surgery, are arranged. Such profound hyperventilation is rescue treatment for the shortest feasible time because it can cause arterial spasm and reduce CBF. Continuous end-tidal CO2 can help track PaCO2, but the arterial-to-end-tidal gradient differs across patients and over time. With ICP monitoring, PEEP < 10 cm H2O usually does not further increase raised ICP and can support oxygenation. Prone positioning, neuromuscular blockers, and ECMO for severe refractory ventilatory failure lack systematic TBI study; apply them cautiously and individually while monitoring intracranial volume and bleeding. In selected monitored patients whose systemic oxygenation did not respond to conventional care, venovenous ECMO without anticoagulation showed a survival benefit compared with venoatrial ECMO.

document_sections.heading: Extubation Planning
document_sections.content: Extubation is difficult to predict in TBI. Success is more likely with GCS motor score 6, normal respiratory drive, stable intracranial status, vigorous cough and other intact airway reflexes, swallowing attempts, and endotracheal suctioning ≤ 2 times per hour. An extubation attempt may be reasonable despite possible reintubation. Evaluate tracheostomy if extubation fails or safety criteria are absent.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Ventilation decisions for an older adult with severe TBI generally follow those for younger patients while accounting for individual care goals. Hypoxia is harmful at every age; tight CO2 control through mechanical ventilation may matter less with cerebral atrophy and lower intracranial hypertension risk. Baseline oropharyngeal dysfunction may favor early intubation. Intubation and ventilation retain the same risks as in younger patients.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: No pediatric-specific post-TBI mechanical ventilation literature or guidelines are identified. A cuffed endotracheal tube is favored when a child needs intubation to optimize ventilation and reduce aspiration risk. The underlying physiologic considerations resemble those for adults.

document_sections.heading: TRACHEOSTOMY
document_sections.content: Consider early tracheostomy within 7 days of injury for every patient with severe TBI when rapid improvement is unlikely. Early tracheostomy can reduce prolonged ventilation and pneumonia risk. Prolonged ventilation may result from impaired pharyngeal protection, excess secretions, ventilator dyssynchrony, poor oxygen or CO2 exchange, severe agitation, or associated facial, airway, or chest injuries. Persistently depressed consciousness is another reason to consider tracheostomy to secure the airway and lessen ventilator-associated pneumonia and lung injury.

document_sections.heading: Early Tracheostomy
document_sections.content: Early tracheostomy reduces ICU and hospital length of stay in TBI, but clear evidence of a survival benefit is lacking. There are no absolute contraindications; relative ones include uncontrolled intracranial hypertension, hemodynamic instability, and severe respiratory failure requiring FiO2 > 50% and PEEP > 10 cm H2O. It may improve comfort, reduce oropharyngeal irritation, improve pulmonary hygiene, and accelerate ventilator liberation. A recent study reported tracheostomy in 31.8% of severe TBI patients; 41% occurred within 7 days and 26% more than 14 days after injury, with considerable variation across centers. BTF 4th edition assigns early tracheostomy a Level IIA recommendation for reducing ventilation days, without asserting reduced mortality or pneumonia. Evidence does not adequately favor surgical over percutaneous technique, though percutaneous tracheostomy can be safe and tolerated. Consider early tracheostomy when liberation within 7 days is unlikely.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Studies report that older adults receive tracheostomy less often and later than younger patients, despite an association between tracheostomy and lower in-hospital mortality in older patients. Both oral intubation and tracheostomy independently increase dysphagia risk. Weigh tracheostomy against the older patient’s goals of care.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Retrospective pediatric studies suggest early tracheostomy may reduce ICU morbidity and length of stay, but timing data for infants with abusive head trauma are scarcer. Adolescents probably benefit from approaches similar to those for adults. Benefits observed in adults and adolescents should not automatically be extended to children under 10 years old or infants, whose risks differ. Pediatric anatomy, equipment, and complications differ; percutaneous tracheostomy is uncommon, particularly under 10 years of age, and pediatric tubes are single-lumen, nonfenestrated, and variably sized.

document_sections.heading: TIMING OF EXTRACRANIAL PROCEDURES
document_sections.content: Balance operative urgency for extracranial injury against intracranial hypertension risk. Apart from lifesaving operations, delay extracranial surgery when intracranial hypertension exists or is likely. Necessary orthopedic stabilization or other time-sensitive surgery may proceed within 48 hours of admission when monitored ICP is controlled or raised ICP is not a concern. Avoid laparoscopy because it increases abdominal pressure and causes hypercarbia. During anesthesia, closely prevent elevated ICP, hypotension, hypoxia, and abnormal CO2. Head injury severity often chiefly determines mortality in polytrauma; moderate TBI doubles predicted mortality when extracranial injury coexists. Severe TBI with other injuries requires coordinated multidisciplinary management. Stable circulation may allow neurologic injury to take priority; hemorrhagic instability shifts priority to resuscitation and hemostasis.

document_sections.heading: Extracranial Surgical Procedure Planning
document_sections.content: Treatment planning aims both to prevent multiorgan failure and to limit secondary brain injury. A large cohort study found significantly worse functional outcomes at 2 weeks and 6 months among patients with CT-positive acute TBI exposed to extracranial surgery and anesthesia.

document_sections.heading: Anesthesia considerations
document_sections.content: Monitor closely to prevent hypotension, hypoxia, and hypo- or hypercarbia. A single hypotensive episode doubles mortality. Maintain CPP at 60 mm Hg if ICP is monitored. IV anesthesia is often preferable because inhaled agents adversely affect ICP. Spinal and epidural anesthesia are contraindicated with intracranial hypertension; peripheral nerve blocks may have a role in analgesia and operative care.

document_sections.heading: Timing of surgical procedures
document_sections.content: Damage control orthopedics uses early external fixation after stabilization and postpones definitive repair to lessen a potential neurologic second hit from early orthopedic intervention. Safe definitive surgery seeks a balance between that approach and early total care; repeated assessment of physiology and whether the patient is stable, borderline, unstable, or in extremis guides timing. With stated qualifications, timing of orthopedic surgery, mainly long-bone repair, does not appear to alter overall outcomes in severe TBI. Consider delaying operating-room trips during intracranial hypertension unless the procedure saves life. When necessary, open laparotomy or thoracotomy should follow principles for avoiding secondary brain injury. Laparoscopy is generally avoided, especially early, because it increases intra-abdominal pressure and causes hypercarbia, although hypercarbia’s contribution to long-term neurologic harm remains debatable. Most facial fractures are not life-threatening or urgent, but breathing may be compromised. Routine ICU procedures can occur after stabilization. Spine surgery timing may depend on instability and emergency decompression needs with spinal cord injury.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: The mean age of polytrauma patients has risen. Severe TBI and age > 65 years independently predict death during the initial hospital admission. Compared with similarly injured younger patients, older adults with polytrauma face greater injury severity, longer admission, and higher mortality; comorbidities, preexisting neurologic or psychiatric illness, and chronic antiplatelet or anticoagulant use contribute. Consider these factors when choosing extracranial procedures and their timing and extent.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Polytrauma often accompanies childhood TBI, and at least a third of children with severe TBI need extracranial surgery. TBI severity strongly affects outcome in pediatric polytrauma. No definitive evidence calls for a different extracranial operative approach from that in adults; prioritize hemodynamic stability to limit secondary brain injury.

document_sections.heading: EXTRACRANIAL BLUNT CEREBROVASCULAR INJURY
document_sections.content: When BCVI is diagnosed, begin anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment once TBI is stable, ideally within the first 24 hours. Spine fracture is the strongest single predictor, especially for vertebral arterial injury. Screen older adults with BCVI risk factors liberally because BCVI independently predicts mortality in this group. Among patients undergoing CT angiography after blunt trauma, reported BCVI incidence is 2.7% to 7.6%. Missed carotid or vertebral injury can delay treatment and increase stroke risk; untreated injuries carry mortality as high as 38% for carotid and 18% for vertebral injuries. Both vessels may be injured in patients at high stroke risk. Denver and Memphis trauma groups have proposed screening criteria. CT angiography is the recommended, sufficient, cost-effective test to exclude BCVI; formal angiography may clarify uncertain lesions or assess those suitable for endovascular treatment. Even strict use of Denver and Memphis criteria misses 20% to 30% of injuries. Several studies recommend universal screening after major trauma using WBCT: noncontrast head CT followed by a 40- or 64-slice contrast-enhanced pass from the circle of Willis through the pelvis. Some authors question universal WBCT, while ACR criteria support it for major blunt trauma.

document_sections.heading: Box 5. Recommended Screening Criteria for BCVI5–10
document_sections.content: The screening criteria include scalp degloving; severe TBI with GCS < 6; TBI with thoracic injuries; neurologic findings unexplained by imaging; transient ischemic attack, hemiparesis, vertebrobasilar symptoms, or oculosympathetic palsy/Horner syndrome; imaging evidence of cerebral ischemia or vascular-territory edema; skull-base fracture involving the carotid canal or petrous temporal bone; complex skull fracture involving, for example, sinuses or orbit; Le Fort II or III fracture; mandibular or cervical spine fracture; arterial bleeding from the neck, nose, or mouth; neck soft-tissue injury including seatbelt sign, hanging, or hematoma; near hanging with hypoxic-ischemic injury; clothesline-type trauma or seatbelt abrasion with substantial swelling, pain, or altered mental status; neck soft-tissue crepitus; cervical bruit at age < 50 years; upper rib fractures; thoracic vascular injury; and blunt cardiac rupture.

document_sections.heading: BCVI Management
document_sections.content: Treatment chiefly seeks to prevent thromboembolism and ischemic stroke. Options include antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, and endovascular procedures. Large observational studies associate any antithrombotic treatment with less stroke than no treatment, but large randomized trials have not tested this finding. Trials of cervical artery dissection, not primarily BCVI, found broadly similar performance of antiplatelet treatment and warfarin, usually bridged with IV heparin until therapeutic INR, although warfarin might have a slight advantage. Start an anticoagulant or antiplatelet as soon as TBI stabilizes, ideally within the first 24 hours when progression risk is not high and extracranial bleeding is controlled, whether BCVI is symptomatic or asymptomatic. It remains uncertain whether dual antiplatelet therapy is preferable to aspirin alone or whether thrombus or BCVI grade favors anticoagulation. Evidence on direct-acting oral anticoagulants instead of warfarin is limited. Antithrombotic treatment generally lasts at least 3 months; CT angiography or MRI at 3 months is reasonable to check healing. Consider stenting or coil embolization for nonhealing pseudoaneurysm or recurrent ischemia despite treatment. Initial arterial embolization or sacrifice is often not recommended because of procedural complications and the tendency of protected lesions to heal. Selected carotid lesions may undergo stenting and vertebral lesions stenting or embolic occlusion according to vessel and lesion characteristics, potentially with adjunctive antiplatelet therapy.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Older-adult BCVI data are sparse. Lower-energy mechanisms can lead to under-screening, although vertebral fractures and BCVI also occur after ground-level falls. Overall BCVI incidence is lower than in younger cohorts, but older adults more often have high-grade lesions, and BCVI independently predicts mortality. Screen older adults with risk factors liberally.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Screening must weigh childhood radiation exposure. Pediatric BCVI is less prevalent than adult BCVI; Denver criteria would probably overestimate its incidence. The validated Utah score classifies children into low and high risk of BCVI-related complications, and the McGovern modification adds two points for a severe motor vehicle collision mechanism to increase diagnostic sensitivity. Use of these risk systems is suggested to select high-risk children for arch-to-vertex CT angiography. Begin antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy after diagnosis according to intracranial stability and control of extracranial hemorrhage. Evidence does not yet establish a specific pediatric treatment duration. Individualize management and consider surgery or endovascular treatment for Bifflgrade ≥ 3 or progressive lesions despite medical treatment.

document_sections.content: The table assigns points for GCS ≤ 8, focal neurologic deficit, carotid canal fracture, petrous temporal bone fracture, and cerebral infarction on CT. A maximum of 11 points is possible. A score ≥ 3 carried an 18% BCVI risk; a score ≤ 2 was associated with less than 3% risk.

document_sections.heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS
document_sections.content: For low-risk nonoperative TBI, pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis is recommended within 24 hours after injury if follow-up CT shows stable intracranial injury; for moderate- or high-risk nonoperative TBI, within 24 to 48 hours under the same condition. After craniotomy or craniectomy, consider initiating or resuming it within 24 to 48 hours of surgery if postoperative CT shows stable ICH. LMWH is preferred to UFH. Trauma and particularly severe injury increase VTE risk; TBI patients remain at high risk without medication or with mechanical measures alone. Each day without medication, and missed doses, increase VTE risk. Evidence indicates pharmacologic prophylaxis lowers VTE rates and may improve TBI outcomes. Use mechanical prophylaxis for all TBI patients on admission regardless of drug eligibility. Decisions must balance thrombosis against ICH progression and account for individual coagulation disorders, prior antithrombotic use, and injury patterns. Injury severity generally correlates with progression risk. The modified Berne-Norwood criteria and Brain Injury Guidelines stratify that risk, with the latter also incorporating clinical factors.

document_sections.content: The table sets out modified Berne-Norwood low-, moderate-, and high-risk anatomic criteria for progression of intracranial hemorrhage, including lesion characteristics, documented progression, ICP monitor placement, and craniotomy.

document_sections.heading: TIMING OF PHARMACOLOGIC VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS
document_sections.content: Multiple studies and two systematic reviews suggest that, when follow-up CT confirms stable ICH, earlier prophylaxis reduces VTE without clinically significant hemorrhage progression regardless of TBI severity. Patients whose ICH progressed before prophylaxis or who underwent cranial surgery may need longer observation. This remains an evolving evidence area, and the updated advice also reflects expert consensus. For nonoperative TBI, repeat CT within 24 hours of the initial scan to check stability before medication; minimal initial hemorrhage may be an exception. Consider starting within 24 hours for hospitalized low-risk patients with stable repeat CT, or within 24 to 48 hours for moderate/high-risk patients with stable repeat CT. Patients with an ICP monitor but no craniotomy or craniectomy may be approached like other nonoperative patients. Do not routinely withhold prophylaxis before monitor insertion or while it remains in place; consider continuing it before removal, or coordinate insertion or removal after one drug half-life. After craniotomy or craniectomy, consider prophylaxis within 24 to 48 hours if postoperative ICH is stable. With documented progression, withhold medication until repeat imaging demonstrates stability, usually after another 24 to 48 hours. LMWH is preferred, including with ICP monitors; studies suggest lower VTE rates and comparable ICH progression relative to UFH after both operative and nonoperative TBI. General trauma best-practice enoxaparin dosing is 40 mg every 12 hours; because TBI-specific research on that regimen is insufficient, start TBI patients at 30 mg every 12 hours. Standard dosing is recommended for dalteparin; consider anti-factor Xa monitoring for subsequent LMWH adjustment. If UFH is chosen, best-practice dosing is 5000 units every 8 hours. Prophylactic inferior vena cava filters are no longer recommended regardless of prophylaxis timing; a filter is indicated for known VTE when therapeutic anticoagulation is contraindicated. Local improvement metrics can include time to prophylaxis, agent choice, and delayed craniotomy or craniectomy.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Older adults follow the same pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis approach as other adults. Renal impairment can change LMWH dosing or favor UFH.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: VTE is much rarer after pediatric than adult trauma. Estimated incidence is 0.09% at ages 0–12 years, 0.27% at 13–15 years, and 0.73% at 16–21 years. Risk factors include older age, higher injury severity score, lower GCS, transfusion, prolonged central venous access, and major surgery. Hospitals should adopt a published pediatric risk tool such as ROCKIT and assess risk after admission. Low-risk children do not need drug prophylaxis; moderate-risk children should receive mechanical prophylaxis on admission; reserve medication for high risk. Contraindications relating to ICH, progression risk, and recent surgery match those in adults. LMWH is preferred, with weight-based dosing in young children. Duration is insufficiently studied; stop prophylaxis once the child walks unless other thrombogenic factors remain.

document_sections.heading: PHARMACOTHERAPY FOR TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
document_sections.content: For high early-PTS risk, phenytoin or levetiracetam lowers early seizure incidence compared with no ASM. Consider ASM prevention for 7 days after severe TBI when risk factors exist, but use beyond 7 days to prevent late PTS is not recommended. Assess warfarin or DOAC exposure carefully and provide agent-specific reversal when life-threatening bleeding requires emergency surgery. Consider anticoagulant restart no later than 14–90 days according to individual bleeding and thrombosis risk. Routine platelet transfusion to reverse antiplatelet effects is not recommended; use judgment about transfusion for low platelet counts before surgery or invasive procedures. Antiplatelet therapy may resume as early as 4 days after injury after individualized assessment. Beta blockers such as propranolol may be considered for adrenergic stress or paroxysmal hyperactivity, with attention to adverse effects. Base surgical antibiotic prophylaxis on published guidance, pharmacist input, and ICU antibiograms. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for EVD or intraparenchymal monitor placement, skull-base fractures, CSF leaks, or pneumocephalus because it may favor drug-resistant bacteria.

document_sections.heading: Posttraumatic Seizure Prophylaxis
document_sections.content: Early PTS occurs < 7 days after injury, correlates with TBI severity, and is most frequent with penetrating injury. Immediate PTS, depressed skull fracture, SDH, ICH, GCS < 10, and cortical contusion also confer high risk. Early PTS is associated with morbidity, mortality, and later PTE. An RCT reported early PTS in 14.2% of placebo recipients versus 3.6% of phenytoin recipients, but early prophylaxis did not prevent PTE; a contemporary randomized study is needed. Consider ASM for 7 days when early-seizure risk factors exist; use beyond 7 days to prevent late PTS is not recommended. Prophylaxis is not recommended without intracranial bleeding or with isolated traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. The most studied agents are (fos)phenytoin, levetiracetam, and valproic acid. Phenytoin and levetiracetam appear similarly safe and effective for early prevention in at-risk patients, but low seizure incidence prevents a superiority conclusion. Phenytoin requires concentration monitoring, usually at 24 hours after first dosing and once again during the 7 days; interactions and potentially severe ADRs are concerns. Monitor albumin and free phenytoin to adjust dosing, or calculate a correction of total concentration if a free assay is unavailable. Levetiracetam has a more favorable pharmacokinetic and overall ADR profile but is associated with behavioral ADRs in children and adults, particularly with TBI; pyridoxine 50–100 mg daily may mitigate them. Valproic acid is not recommended for early prevention because mortality was higher than with phenytoin. Stop preventive ASM by 7 days when there have been no clinical or EEG seizures, or seizure activity occurred only in the first 24 hours. Continuing may be appropriate after seizures beyond 24 hours or for a preexisting seizure disorder.

document_sections.heading: Anticoagulant Management in TBI Patients
document_sections.content: Consider reversal of preinjury anticoagulation to permit emergency surgery and/or limit hematoma expansion. A specific reversal agent is generally recommended for each oral anticoagulant. If a DOAC was last taken within 8–12 hours, or warfarin-associated INR is ≥ 1.5, reversal benefits will most likely exceed risks. Some clinicians use fixed 4PCC doses of 1500 to 2500 units instead of weight-based dosing. For INR 1.5–1.9, suggested lower 4PCC doses are 10–20 units/kg; doses > 2000 to 3000 units were associated with increased VTE risk in nontraumatic ICH. When 4PCC is unavailable, approximately 8–16 FFP units correspond to approximately 20–50 units/kg of 4PCC. FFP alone can lower INR only to approximately 1.5–1.7; its mean intrinsic INR is 1.1, with a range of 0.9–1.3. Published societies provide reversal guidance for life-threatening bleeding of all causes. Acute TBI care includes stopping the anticoagulant and establishing the DOAC type, dose, last-dose timing, and implications for surgery and reversal where possible. Quantitative DOAC assays are not readily available, and no definitive therapeutic DOAC concentration range exists. Recently administered dabigatran can raise activated partial thromboplastin time; Xa inhibitors can raise prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. Normal results do not exclude therapeutic drug concentrations. Do not await laboratory results before urgent reversal in a patient at high bleeding risk. Advanced age, renal disease or dialysis, and drug interactions may prolong exposure. TEG may qualitatively assess clot strength and fibrinolysis but lacks evidence for quantifying therapeutic DOAC concentration, and massive transfusion may make its results inaccurate. Patients previously needing therapeutic anticoagulation retain thrombosis risk: consider subcutaneous heparin or LMWH prophylaxis while off anticoagulants, and weigh reversal against bleeding and underlying thrombosis risk.
