document_sections.content: The table presents agent-specific emergency-surgery reversal for warfarin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran. It includes INR-dependent IV vitamin K and 4PCC strategies with repeat INR testing and possible FFP for warfarin; time-dependent activated charcoal, andexanet alfa, or 4PCC for the listed Xa inhibitors; and activated charcoal, idarucizumab, possible dialysis, or prothrombin complex concentrate for dabigatran.

document_sections.heading: Restarting anticoagulation
document_sections.content: Evidence cannot establish the optimal restart time for patients at moderate or high thromboembolic risk but without high rebleeding risk. Consider earlier restart for mechanical valve, left ventricular assist device, or VTE within the last 3 months than for lower-risk examples such as atrial fibrillation with lower CHA2DS2-VASc scores or VTE more than 3 months earlier. Available guidelines suggest 2 weeks or less at high risk and 7–8 weeks at low risk, but no later than 90 days after bleeding. Earlier restart may be safe when traumatic intracranial bleeding is less substantial or stable on repeat CT; individual risk remains decisive. In high-risk warfarin patients, reversal vitamin K doses > 2.5 mg may delay therapeutic warfarin effect for several weeks after restarting, despite similar initial INR reduction; LMWH or unfractionated heparin is then needed until vitamin K’s effect ends.

document_sections.heading: Antiplatelet Agent Management in TBI Patients
document_sections.content: Reversing antiplatelet effects after traumatic ICH is controversial: relevant RCTs are few and results conflict. A meta-analysis of low-quality evidence found no difference in hematoma enlargement or neurosurgical intervention between single-agent users and untreated patients. Platelet transfusion and desmopressin can cause adverse effects. One traumatic-ICH study found no difference in hemorrhage progression or neurosurgery with versus without transfusion, but transfused patients had a trend toward longer ICU stay, adjusted odds ratio 1.59, 95% CI 0.74–3.40, and more in-hospital deaths, adjusted odds ratio 3.23, 95% CI 0.48–21.74. Studies of combined desmopressin and transfusion showed no benefit for progression or mortality. Patients with low platelet counts undergoing craniotomy or monitor insertion may benefit from preprocedure platelet transfusion for hemostasis. Routine postoperative transfusion is not recommended, and preinjury antiplatelet use alone is not a reason to transfuse. Consider agent properties and platelet-function findings. Irreversible agents affect platelets over approximately 8–20 days and may inhibit transfused platelets until drug clearance at about 3–5 times the agent’s half-life; clopidogrel and ticagrelor have active metabolites and longer activity. Point-of-care platelet-function assays are recommended alongside standard laboratory or coagulation assessment when preinjury therapy suggests dysfunction, potentially identifying those who benefit and avoiding unnecessary thrombosis risk. Current guidelines suggest stopping antiplatelet agents acutely. Before necessary neurosurgery, consider one single-donor apheresis platelet unit, equivalent to 6 pooled units or 1 random-donor unit per 10 kg of body weight. Desmopressin 0.4 mcg/kg IV has also been suggested alone or with transfusion for neurosurgical patients exposed to aspirin, clopidogrel, or ticagrelor; monitor and treat hyponatremia if used. Test platelet function before transfusion when possible; do not reverse if function is normal or resistance is documented. Benefit requires more study. Until then, transfusion and desmopressin are not recommended without an invasive-intervention indication.

document_sections.heading: Restarting antiplatelet agents
document_sections.content: Assess the original indication and individual thrombotic versus bleeding risk after traumatic ICH. Studies support possible restart as early as 4 days after injury; most posttraumatic hemorrhages occur within 3 days. Balance immediate and delayed ICH against potentially serious thrombotic complications.

document_sections.heading: Paroxysmal Hyperactivity Syndrome (“Dysautonomia,” “Sympathetic Storm”)
document_sections.content: Loss of inhibitory sympathetic input after TBI can produce hypertension, tachycardia, hyperpyrexia, tachypnea, and sweating. Potential treatments include BBKs, benzodiazepines, opioids, alpha-2 agonists, gabapentin, muscle relaxants, and baclofen. Low-quality evidence associates BBKs with lower mortality in severe TBI with paroxysmal hyperactivity, but mostly observational or retrospective studies vary in dose, agent, timing, patient characteristics, adverse-event monitoring, and whether treatment addressed comorbidity or TBI-related stress. Propranolol has the most supporting evidence for these indications. Monitor bradycardia, hypotension, congestive heart failure, and bronchospasm, which can be harmful acutely.

document_sections.heading: Disorders of Consciousness
document_sections.content: Prolonged altered consciousness may present as coma, vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, or minimally conscious state. After identifying and treating confounders, amantadine 100–200 mg twice daily is recommended for adults in vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome or minimally conscious state at 4–16 weeks postinjury to speed recovery and reduce disability.

document_sections.heading: Antibiotic Prophylaxis
document_sections.content: Reported monitor-related infection rates vary greatly: they are very low for intraparenchymal fiberoptic monitors but may be much higher for EVDs. Establish and follow facility insertion and maintenance protocols. Avoid systemic prophylactic antibiotics during intraparenchymal monitor insertion or while parenchymal or ventricular drains are used, to reduce resistant organisms. Recent BTF and Neurocritical Care Society guidance recommends antimicrobial-impregnated EVD catheters when available. A meta-analysis reported CSF infection of 13.7% with standard catheters versus 3.6% with antimicrobial-impregnated ones. Remove monitors and drains as soon as clinically feasible, avoid routine manipulation and unnecessary CSF sampling, and use aseptic technique. An EVD bundle can include insertion, maintenance, dressing, and CSF-sampling procedures. Avoid antibiotic prophylaxis for traumatic skull-base fracture with CSF leak or pneumocephalus because it can promote resistant organisms. For open or penetrating skull fracture, consider broad-spectrum antibiotics with high blood-brain barrier penetration for a maximum of 3 days. Surgical debridement and irrigation are standard care, with perioperative antibiotics for not more than 24 hours. For surgical prophylaxis, cefazolin is preferred when methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is absent and there is no documented severe beta lactam allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin are alternatives for severe allergy. Clarify allergy history when feasible and select drug and dose using published guidance and pharmacist consultation.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Available evidence does not suggest that older neurosurgical TBI patients have different risks of worse outcomes solely because they used anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents, although the anticoagulant selected and number of antiplatelet agents may matter. Restart timing is similar across ages. Account for age-related physiology, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics when choosing antibiotic prophylaxis or treatment and dosing to limit toxicity.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Pediatric PTS evidence broadly aligns with adult guidance. Early seizures may be more common below 24 months, with GCS < 8, and after nonaccidental injury. Evidence for levetiracetam efficacy remains limited; one observational study recorded seizures in 17% despite prophylaxis. Either levetiracetam or (fos)phenytoin is appropriate for the recommended 7-day course. Levetiracetam has a more favorable adverse-effect profile without therapeutic concentration monitoring; a common dose is 20–40 mg/kg/day in two doses. Facilities are encouraged to create multidisciplinary weight-based pediatric protocols. Individually weigh anticoagulant or antiplatelet reversal and restart. Pediatric evidence about antimicrobials beyond the EVD perioperative period is limited; extrapolated evidence supports perioperative antimicrobials only.

document_sections.heading: PROGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT AND FAMILY COMMUNICATION
document_sections.content: Meaningful independence may remain possible despite absent consciousness for the first 4 or more weeks or depressed mental status during the first weeks. Communicate prognostic uncertainty and use shared decisions with families or surrogates. Early withdrawal of life support may create a self-fulfilling poor outcome. Provide aggressive care, including indicated surgery, until the clinical team and family or surrogate agree that it conflicts with patient values and preferences. Each trauma center should develop a brain-death determination policy based on accepted standards and local law.

document_sections.heading: Prognostic Assessment
document_sections.content: Severe TBI carries high risks of death and long-term disability, but current markers cannot predict a poor individual outcome with high certainty, particularly in the first weeks. Outcomes acceptable to a patient or family can occur in up to 20% of those still unconscious during the first 4 weeks. Population-validated IMPACT and CRASH TBI models combine initial factors such as age, GCS, pupil responses, and imaging to provide estimates with CI. They are not recommended for exact individual prognostication; describe their probabilities as uncertain estimates and discuss best-case, worst-case, and most-likely possibilities. Studies across neurocritical conditions associate reflexively early do-not-resuscitate orders or life-support withdrawal with worse outcomes independently of other characteristics. Very early long-term predictions after severe TBI are often unreliable, particularly in the first days; clinician expectations and institutional practices may contribute to variable care limits and self-fulfilling poor outcomes. When consistent with patient or family goals, best practice is a trial of aggressive surgery, ICU care, and appropriate intracranial monitoring. A previously advocated minimum of 72 hours is arbitrary and lacks evidence; recovery remains possible after 4 or more weeks unconscious, so longer observation is generally needed. Exceptions include declared brain death, a contrary preinjury advance directive, and surrogate preference for comfort measures alone. Do not use age alone to limit care. Consider frailty, comorbidities, persistent bilateral pupillary nonreactivity, absent neurologic improvement, and injury severity; exclude medication or orbital-injury confounding of pupil findings and sedation, analgesia, or seizures confounding the neurologic examination. The Coma Recovery Scale–Revised reportedly detects consciousness better than qualitative bedside examination and may be considered.

document_sections.heading: Family Communication
document_sections.content: Recent ICU studies found that usual clinician communication often fails to meet surrogate needs. Unexpected TBI can leave surrogates unprepared; decisions should reflect the patient’s values. Shared decision-making combines clinical expertise with patient preferences through clinician-family collaboration, sometimes aided by palliative-care providers with time and continuity. Formal decision aids remain under clinical evaluation, although families have found them helpful. Discuss condition, treatment, prognosis, and the potential long-term care journey. Palliative and social-service expertise can help address symptoms, finances, family circumstances, pain, and disability.

document_sections.heading: Brain Death Determination
document_sections.content: State law controls brain-death determination; use standardized criteria. Prerequisites include cardiopulmonary stability and absence of sedative effects. Required findings include no central-pain response, absent brainstem reflexes, and inability to breathe independently. Prioritize clinical examination over an ancillary test such as CBF assessment unless its prerequisites cannot be met. Each hospital needs a defined policy based on accepted standards. Where relevant, collaboration with local organ procurement organizations can offer donation opportunities.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: No optimal older-adult TBI prognostic model is identified; IMPACT and CRASH TBI populations had mean ages in the 30s. Several studies identify preinjury frailty as a principal predictor of poor outcomes. ACS TQIP palliative-care guidance recommends considering consultation after a positive frailty screen to support advance planning and goals-of-care discussions.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Pediatric prognostication and family communication can be especially difficult. Pediatric-specific prediction tools perform inadequately and are not recommended clinically. Children may recover better than similarly injured adults because they have fewer comorbidities and greater plasticity, although direct comparisons are difficult. One recent study observed good recovery, GOS-E 7 or 8, in 44% of children and 59% of adolescents with severe TBI. Aggressive pediatric ICU treatment is therefore warranted for the vast majority. Guidance on discussing early prognosis with parents is limited, and prognosis after abusive head trauma may differ from unintentional injury. Clinicians influence how parents understand prognostic information and participate in shared decisions; assessing and supporting parental needs may improve parent and child outcomes and reduce parental distress. If brain death is suspected, use pediatric-specific guidelines.

document_sections.heading: EARLY MULTIDISCIPLINARY REHABILITATION IN ACUTE TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
document_sections.content: Consider multidisciplinary rehabilitation from the day of admission while planning acute care. It can be safe, feasible, and cost-effective before medical stability is achieved and during mechanical ventilation; it may reduce complications associated with immobility, critical illness, delirium, and cognitive or psychological problems. Integrate PM&R into the primary trauma team from admission and involve PT, OT, SLP, psychology/neuropsychology, social work, and nursing. Refer patients to specialized postacute rehabilitation once medically stable and ready for acute-care discharge. Patients with GCS 13–15 and lasting physical, cognitive, or psychological symptoms need follow-up and multidisciplinary rehabilitation referral. TBI can produce disturbances of consciousness and physical, cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and functional limitations. Even patients with GCS 13–15 may have symptoms that interfere with school, work, and daily function without appropriate treatment and follow-up. Critical illness following moderate or severe TBI can require prolonged ventilation and immobility; associated problems include VTE, skin damage, contractures, deconditioning, delirium, and ICU-acquired weakness, with effects potentially lasting years. ICU implementation of guidance for pain, agitation, delirium, immobility, and sleep, including the ABCDEF bundle, has been associated with lower mortality and comorbidity and better function and quality of life. Recent evidence supports early rehabilitation to limit immobility-related harm, prevent secondary complications, and improve function.

document_sections.heading: Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation Collaboration
document_sections.content: The 2022 ACS Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient calls for trauma services to have staff and resources for early multidisciplinary rehabilitation and mobilization in moderate to severe TBI. Early coordinated rehabilitation is associated with shorter LOS, lower costs and resource use, and better long-term function. Rehabilitation professionals can assess and treat patients early, measure response, monitor physiology, progress mobility and treatment intensity, support functional routines, and inform treatment and discharge decisions. Benefits are greatest when rehabilitation specialists are part of the trauma team. The team should include PM&R physicians, nurses, PT, OT, SLP, psychologists/neuropsychologists, and social workers, without being limited to these disciplines. A PM&R physician is recommended as a core trauma-team member beginning on the admission day. Early PM&R consultation is associated with greater mobility and cognitive independence and shorter acute-care LOS; these physicians can also assist with prognosis discussions.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation for GCS 3–12
document_sections.content: PT, OT, SLP, and nursing can begin bedside multidisciplinary interventions while medical stabilization continues. For severe TBI with impaired consciousness, interventions may include repeated evaluation of LOC, stimulation to optimize arousal, environmental changes, and mobilization. Early mobilization means beginning activity within the first 48 hours after injury or as soon as neurosurgical, hemodynamic, and respiratory stability allow. Evidence supports its effectiveness. ICU rehabilitation can reduce immobility-related harm and is feasible and safe. Passive movement and splinting may begin soon after admission, including during treatment for raised ICP or paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity, to preserve joint movement and limit contractures and later disability. Use caution in more severely injured patients: out-of-bed activity, for example, is appropriate only after hemodynamic and ventilatory stabilization and when intracranial hypertension is no longer a major concern. Posttraumatic confusion and agitation can accompany moderate or severe TBI; agitation affects approximately 40% of patients. Acute benzodiazepines and typical antipsychotics are not recommended because evidence suggests prolonged neurocognitive recovery. Atypical antipsychotics or beta blockers such as propranolol may instead be considered acutely when needed for patient and staff safety. Rehabilitation-based behavioral approaches can improve participation and safety while reducing dependence and medication needs. SLP and OT assessment and treatment of dysphagia and other oral-motor problems may improve intake and eating routines. These disciplines may also assess alternative or augmentative communication needs. An RCT found that self-care and ADL retraining begun during posttraumatic confusion produced faster gains in independence and shorter LOS.

document_sections.heading: Box 6. Early Mobilization Activities
document_sections.content: The listed activities span passive and active range of motion, bed movement, leg ergometry, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, upright positioning, sitting at the bedside, transfers, out-of-bed movement, walking, resistance exercise, and participation in ADLs.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation for GCS 13–15
document_sections.content: Up to 90% of people with TBI initially have GCS 13–15. Untreated symptoms may persist for months or years and cause disability. Refer patients with prolonged symptoms to multidisciplinary rehabilitation, generally through outpatient or community services, to support return to work, school, and other activities. Sports medicine, PM&R, PT, OT, SLP, and neuropsychology professionals can assess and address persistent problems.

document_sections.heading: Transition of Care Recommendations
document_sections.content: Continuing, individualized rehabilitation beyond the ED, ICU, and acute hospital is recommended, with coordination after discharge. Begin planning the next care setting soon after hospital admission. Options include long-term acute care hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, skilled nursing facilities, outpatient programs, and home- or community-based services. Many patients with moderate or severe TBI need ongoing medical and nursing care during inpatient rehabilitation. Select a discharge setting able to address their medical, functional, and neurobehavioral needs. Evidence suggests specialized postacute rehabilitation increases the likelihood of independence and continued long-term improvement. Plan the transition into outpatient and community resources so patients and families can navigate care and recovery.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: TBI-specific evidence for rehabilitation of older adults is limited. Evidence from the Acute Care for Elders (ACE) model, older adults with acute illness or hip fracture, and critical-care mobilization studies that included patients over 60 years supports early rehabilitation and mobilization for older adults with TBI. Ideally, an acute rehabilitation plan is developed with a multidisciplinary team that includes geriatric expertise. Older adults face greater risks of medical complications, extensive care needs, institutional discharge, and reduced quality of life. ACE approaches commonly combine mobilization, delirium prevention, reduction of inappropriate medications and polypharmacy, and preservation or improvement of function according to personal care goals.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Children with TBI can develop critical-illness complications associated with sedation, immobility, and delirium. A review found global dysfunction in 47% at pediatric ICU discharge and residual disability in 76% at 6 months after discharge. Pediatric multidisciplinary rehabilitation during critical care was reported to be safe with few adverse events, fewer days of mechanical ventilation, bed rest, and ICU care, less comorbidity and delirium, improved function, and reduced family or caregiver burden. Give particular attention to preinjury mental or personality conditions; behavioral health medicine can contribute nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic recommendations.

document_sections.heading: POSTTRAUMATIC EPILEPSY
document_sections.content: Before acute-care discharge, teach families to recognize PTE, including subtle changes in consciousness. Screen for PTE during follow-up and arrange diagnostic evaluation if seizure activity is suspected. Treat patients who develop PTE with ASM and refer them to an experienced clinician. Individualize ASM selection and duration according to seizure control, adverse effects, and options such as dietary changes, neuromodulation, or surgery. Because PTE incidence accumulates over time, continue screening aging adults with prior TBI, especially those with risk factors.

document_sections.heading: Incidence
document_sections.content: Earlier population studies attributed about 4% of epilepsy diagnoses to TBI; other studies reported incidence as high as 20%. Late PTS refers to seizures occurring more than 7 days after injury. ASM prophylaxis is generally not recommended to prevent late seizures because, for many patients, potential adverse effects outweigh seizure risk. PTE develops in a substantial proportion of TBI survivors and has significant morbidity and mortality. Its cumulative risk rises over time, particularly after severe and also after moderate TBI. Among patients with early seizures, reported PTE rates were higher with intracerebral hemorrhage and greater injury severity. Continue careful long-term monitoring, especially as patients age. In one population-based study, mild TBI was associated with excess seizure risk for up to 10 years relative to the general population (relative risk 2.06–3.51, increasing by age group); PTE was most frequent after more severe injuries (relative risk 4.91–12.24, depending on age group). For both mild and severe TBI, risk was highest in those > 15 years of age, and seizures tended to occur earlier after injury. High-risk patients need family education, vigilance for diagnosis, and long-term follow-up with qualified professionals.

document_sections.heading: Box 7. Factors Associated with a Higher Risk for Posttraumatic Epilepsy
document_sections.content: The listed risk factors are evacuated SDH; combined contusion and SDH; evacuation of an intraparenchymal hematoma; GCS 3–8; early seizures, particularly delayed early seizures; LOC or amnesia > 1 day; more time before following commands (> 7 days); skull fracture; depressed skull fracture that was not elevated; dural penetration; nonreactive pupil(s); parietal lesions; age > 65 years; female sex; family epilepsy history; and depression history.

document_sections.heading: Impact of PTE on Outcome
document_sections.content: Whether PTE itself worsens survival and function, rather than marking greater initial injury severity, remains uncertain. In a prospective cohort adjusted for age, presenting GCS, and imaging, participants with PTE had significantly lower GOS-E scores and worse Rivermead Cognitive Metrics and Brief Symptom Inventory-18 scores than controls. Seizures were self-identified using a National Institutes of Health stroke-related screening tool; the reported frequency in the TBI group resembled previous reports, while neither control group reported seizures. That study linked self-reported seizures with poorer function and persistent posttraumatic symptoms. Other adjusted studies reported greater mortality with TBI and PTE than with TBI without PTE. Emerging evidence therefore suggests additional morbidity and mortality associated with PTE.

document_sections.heading: Treatment Strategies
document_sections.content: Detailed ASM selection and treatment duration are outside this guideline’s scope. Begin treatment following a first late post-TBI seizure and refer to a clinician experienced in PTE; recurrent seizures after the first have been reported in as many as 86% by 2 years postinjury. Tailor ASM and treatment duration to seizure control, side effects, and individual circumstances, including possible dietary interventions, neuromodulation, or surgery.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Older adults fall more often than younger adults, and fall-related TBI has been reported to carry the greatest PTE risk regardless of injury severity. Stroke, dementia, and other comorbidities can increase seizure risk; polypharmacy can complicate ASM interactions. An ASM with the fewest cognitive adverse effects and drug interactions is recommended for older adults with PTE.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Children have a higher risk of early post-TBI seizures than adults, but pediatric PTE is less common except after abusive head trauma. ASM prophylaxis does not prevent late seizures in children. Refer a child with late seizures to a practitioner experienced in both pediatrics and epilepsy, such as a pediatric neurologist.

document_sections.heading: MANAGEMENT OF PATIENTS WITH GLASGOW COMA SCALE (GCS) SCORE OF 13–15
document_sections.content: Many patients with TBI and GCS 13–15 recover relatively quickly, but a substantial group have lasting symptoms that impair ADLs. An estimated 50% presenting to the ED after injury with GCS 13–15 have TBI that is not identified or diagnosed. Incorporating decision support and practice guidance into routine care is recommended to improve recognition, evaluation, and treatment. Apply the broader acute-care recommendations, including diagnostic assessment, individualized treatment, discharge guidance, and outcome evaluation. Educate patients about TBI, explain where to seek care for persistent symptoms, discuss return to work, school, and driving, and tailor treatment to maximize function.

document_sections.heading: Incidence
document_sections.content: Among nearly 5 million US ED presentations each year for suspected TBI, approximately 90% have GCS 13–15, historically termed mild TBI. This category also accounts for over 80% of TBI among US military personnel. Sport-related concussion affects millions of athletes worldwide each year. Practice guidance and clinical resources are available for diagnosis and management.

document_sections.heading: Detection and Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Acute ED diagnosis of TBI with GCS 13–15 relies heavily on patient-reported symptoms and signs. Reporting and history may be unreliable because of impairment, alcohol or drug intoxication, accompanying orthopaedic injury, pain treatment, or uncertainty about the injury mechanism and symptoms. Severity varies considerably within GCS 13–15: a patient with GCS 15 may have normal imaging and subtle deficits, while one with GCS 13 may show extensive imaging abnormalities and greater impairment. ED workflow may limit neurological or neuropsychological testing beyond examination and head CT. These difficulties contribute to an estimated 50% of such TBI cases going unidentified and undiagnosed in the ED each year.

document_sections.heading: Acute Management
document_sections.content: The immediate ED priority, including for GCS 13–15, is to identify patients at risk of deterioration or needing urgent neurosurgery. Most have no traumatic intracranial lesion on CT, although abnormalities are more frequent at Level 1 trauma centers and with lower GCS scores. Head CT remains the standard for detecting ICH in this group. Clinical decision rules help target imaging and avoid unnecessary scans; blood biomarkers may also contribute to evaluation.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis and Outcome
document_sections.content: Symptoms can include headache, dizziness, visual or oculomotor difficulties, cognitive and sensory dysfunction, sleep disturbance, and psychological problems. Symptoms are generally worst in the first few days and gradually improve. Many patients recover fully within days to weeks, but at least half have cognitive, somatic, or psychological symptoms affecting ordinary activities for months or years. Approximately 50% of ED-evaluated patients diagnosed with TBI and GCS 13–15 have not fully recovered by 12 months. Injury-related factors, including initial severity and CT findings, and noninjury factors, including premorbid psychiatric problems, neurological vulnerability, and social distress, increase the risk of prolonged recovery or poor function.

document_sections.heading: Follow-Up Care
document_sections.content: Give patients information about TBI, expected recovery, and follow-up options. Symptoms or difficulties lasting longer than 2 weeks postinjury may warrant symptom-specific assessment and treatment. Supportive care and rehabilitation can help restore function. Follow-up systems for this group are insufficient in the US and elsewhere; studies indicate that many receive neither useful discharge information nor later assessment and treatment despite persistent symptoms. When feasible, arrange care with TBI-experienced clinicians and use a multispecialty approach. Healthcare systems are encouraged to establish coordinated postacute TBI programs.

document_sections.heading: Resources
document_sections.content: Guidance for civilians, military personnel, and athletes with TBI and GCS 13–15 is available from ACRM, CDC, the US Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense, and the sports medicine community. Clinicians caring for these populations should know and incorporate the applicable guidance.

document_sections.heading: Box 8. Current Guidelines and Helpful Resources for Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Patients with TBI and GCS 13–15
document_sections.content: The box identifies diagnostic criteria, concussion and mild-TBI practice guidance, pediatric CDC guidance, VA/DoD guidance, a sports-concussion consensus statement, a review of TBI progress and challenges, and CDC resources for healthcare providers.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: TBI with GCS 13–15 is common among older adults, often after falls; studies report that 60%–80% of their TBIs fall within this GCS range. Evidence to guide their diagnosis and treatment remains limited. Preinjury cognition can complicate assessment, and observed GCS may differ from that of younger patients with similar structural injuries. Neither GCS nor physical examination reliably excludes substantial intracranial pathology in older adults, so liberal imaging and observation are often recommended. Most recover well, yet TBI with GCS 13–15 has been reported as an independent significant mortality risk factor in this population. Changes in self-perception or social life may persist for years and impair independence and quality of life. Consider highly specialized rehabilitation for substantial or persistent symptoms that fail to improve.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Approximately 30% of children with TBI and GCS 13–15 remain symptomatic 1 month after injury. An observational study identified factors associated with prolonged symptoms, including physician-diagnosed migraine history and slow responses to questions. Observational and interventional evidence suggests that early physical activity and return to school improve outcomes. Refer every child with TBI to their primary care clinician to manage return to activity and school. Neurology or sports-medicine follow-up may be appropriate when prolonged-recovery risk factors exist. At 3 months, persistent symptoms may warrant neuropsychological testing to assess injury and noninjury contributions and help plan return to school and ADLs.

document_sections.heading: OUTCOME ASSESSMENT AND QUALITY IMPROVEMENT
document_sections.content: Assess TBI outcomes with global and multidimensional measures covering physical, cognitive, communication, behavioral, psychological, and well-being domains. Identify individual deterioration or recovery plateaus that may signal treatable pathology, as well as improvement that further treatment or rehabilitation might support. Assess at several postinjury points, ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months. Impairments and trajectories vary among patients and may improve or worsen over many years. Evidence increasingly indicates that meaningful functional recovery may continue beyond 6 months, potentially for 10 years or more. Hospitalized patients need follow-up with TBI-experienced clinicians. TBI-related needs may continue for months or years, and lifelong follow-up may benefit many patients through screening, monitoring, treatment, and attention to brain health.

document_sections.heading: Outcome Assessment
document_sections.content: Longitudinal, multidomain assessment documents changes, identifies recovery patterns, and informs interventions. Clinicians are recommended to understand outcome measures, their uses and limitations, and how to act on findings. Monitor especially for deterioration potentially associated with posttraumatic hydrocephalus, occult seizures, endocrine dysfunction, iatrogenic sedation, major depressive disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, or neurodegenerative-spectrum conditions. Few measures apply across all TBI severities. Comprehensive assessment covers physical, cognitive, communication, behavioral, psychological, and quality-of-life domains. GOS-E is widely used for global function but has floor and ceiling effects, broad functional variation within categories, and results that differ according to whether peripheral injuries are counted. Complement it with multidimensional measures when possible. At minimum, patients across all TBI severities need serial standardized GOS-E assessment, ideally between 1 and 3 months and again between 6 and 12 months after injury; GOS-E is not appropriate during the index hospitalization. These intervals balance useful trajectory information with feasibility, and some patients need more frequent review. Plateaus or decline can prompt imaging, laboratory or neuropsychological assessment, driver reevaluation, rehabilitation, concussion-clinic care, or psychological counseling, as appropriate. Such trajectories may reflect treatable medical or psychiatric illness or adverse circumstances. Comparing observed and expected outcomes after discharge can reveal quality-improvement opportunities within and across trauma programs.

document_sections.heading: Older Adult Considerations
document_sections.content: Compared with younger patients, older adults with TBI have greater risks of longer hospital LOS, mortality, functional and cognitive decline, poorer health-related quality of life, acute-care readmission, complications, and discharge somewhere other than home. They also have high hospitalization, mortality, disability, and care-cost rates despite comparatively lower injury-severity scores. Secondary risks include VTE, hemorrhage, and neurodegeneration, including all-cause dementia and Parkinson’s disease. Functional Independence Measure motor score at hospital discharge strongly predicts later global disability measured with GOS-E. Frailty reflects biological aging and is a major predictor of poor outcomes. Screening for frailty at admission is therefore an important trauma-center quality initiative, and outcome monitoring should adjust for frailty. Screening is associated with more geriatric-service consultations and palliative-care referrals and offers an opportunity to educate patients and families about limiting functional decline. Exercise, adequate sleep, and nutrition are proposed lifestyle measures for neurocognitive outcomes; rehabilitation should emphasize function, balance, coordination, and energy conservation.

document_sections.heading: Pediatric Considerations
document_sections.content: Children need ongoing standardized postinjury assessment. Pediatric instruments include the Functional Status Scale and Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory; clinicians need training to administer, interpret, and respond to these assessments. Among hospitalized children with traumatic injuries, 3% have injuries attributed to nonaccidental trauma, and more than half of these include TBI alone or within polytrauma. Accurate diagnosis and close, comprehensive follow-up are particularly important when the child’s caregivers or home supports may change.

document_sections.heading: TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY EDUCATION AND FOLLOW-UP
document_sections.content: Manage TBI as both an acute and a chronic condition. Provide patients and families targeted information about injury, recovery, resources, and follow-up to support safety, coping, care participation, and outcomes. Clinician education can also improve care. At acute-hospital discharge, ensure every patient has an opportunity to follow up with someone experienced in TBI for continuing education, screening, surveillance, and treatment when needed. TBI is a major worldwide source of disability and may remain dynamic rather than resolve as a single event. Patients with severe TBI and coma often need long-term rehabilitation and care, yet many receive neither specialist follow-up nor any follow-up because of eligibility or benefit restrictions. US data from the early 2000s estimated that only 13%–25% of people hospitalized for moderate, severe, or penetrating TBI received inpatient rehabilitation. Fewer less-severely injured patients receive rehabilitation or access to TBI-informed clinicians, despite growing evidence of persistent impairment after GCS 13–15 TBI. Nearly 50% of this group receives no injury education at discharge and no postacute follow-up or education. Existing educational resources include CDC, Model Systems, and BrainLine; their use should be encouraged even though resources could be expanded and improved. Trauma centers should prioritize coordinated education and follow-up. Clinicians should understand that initial severity does not reliably mirror long-term outcome: severe TBI may be followed by good recovery, while so-called mild TBI may lead to lasting functional problems. Education should also address differences between sports-related and community-acquired TBI requiring trauma-center transfer. Follow-up systems are scarce in the US and worldwide, so most patients lack adequate care. Treatable problems include headache, sleep disturbance, cognitive or vestibular dysfunction, spasticity, weakness, sensory changes, and poor stamina. Outcomes improve with TBI-experienced follow-up and treatment. Trauma centers and community services are encouraged to build coordinated postacute systems; peer support groups can also help patients and families.

document_sections.heading: GAP ANALYSIS AND EDUCATION PLAN
document_sections.content: These evidence- and expert-opinion-based practices guide trauma centers caring for TBI. The TMD, TPM, trauma liaisons, registrars, and staff lead implementation, support patient care, and monitor adherence. A stakeholder workgroup directed by the TMD and trauma operations committee reviews the recommendations and compares them with current care. Leadership is responsible for sustained improvement across trauma-center designation levels, defining structures and processes that engage stakeholders. An interdisciplinary brain-injury workgroup should have identified leadership and reporting arrangements and decide on a gap analysis. Develop an education plan to implement and sustain local TBI guidance, and integrate standardized documentation into the electronic record to support reporting and outcome tracking.

document_sections.heading: Performing a Gap Analysis
document_sections.content: The interdisciplinary workgroup compares local practices against guideline recommendations to identify opportunities for alignment. A brain-injury referral center may instead review recommendations for improvement opportunities without completing the entire analysis. Together with the operations committee, the workgroup sets priorities and reports task progress. After analysis, develop or revise local guidance for the care phases the center provides. The trauma operations committee and TMD review and approve it; the committee then communicates it to trauma-care personnel.

document_sections.heading: Interdisciplinary Education Plan Development
document_sections.content: Develop an interdisciplinary plan addressing TBI-management needs in each unit and care phase. Specify expectations for professional roles and for assessment, documentation, intervention, and reassessment.

document_sections.heading: Table 8. Gap Analysis for Traumatic Brain Injury Best Practices Guidelines
document_sections.content: This gap-analysis table provides fields for whether each proposed local management element is met, partly met, or unmet, together with priority and comments. Topics include triage and transfer; standardized GCS, pupil, physiological, and imaging assessment; ICP treatment and monitoring; surgery; nutritional risk screening within 24 hours of admission; airway care and tracheostomy; mobilization and rehabilitation; associated injuries and BCVI; VTE and seizure prophylaxis; anticoagulant reversal; prognosis, brain-death policy, and behavioral support; family education; discharge coordination; standardized follow-up; and peer support.

document_sections.heading: Table 9. Educational Plan Elements for TBI Best Practices Recommendations
document_sections.content: The table provides fields to prioritize educational topics and identify staff audiences. Topics cover TBI mechanisms, epidemiology and outcomes; triage; GCS and pupil examination; resuscitation; imaging and biomarkers; physiological targets; extracranial and intracranial interventions; nutrition and pharmacotherapy; BCVI; prognosis and family communication; GCS 13–15 care; follow-up, education, and outcomes; quality indicators and support resources; and age-specific considerations.

document_sections.heading: IMPLEMENTATION AND INTEGRATION INTO TRAUMA CENTER PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENT
document_sections.content: An interdisciplinary workgroup selects guideline elements for monitoring through trauma Performance Improvement and Patient Safety (PIPS) processes. After the trauma PIPS committee approves them, incorporate those elements into the existing PIPS plan to monitor compliance, using established structures and processes.

document_sections.heading: Regional System Integration
document_sections.content: A region may establish an interdisciplinary collaborative to coordinate TBI care, including rehabilitation and psychosocial services. The collaborative sets priorities, potentially using regional TBI and outcome data. Possible regional commitments include sharing outcomes to improve prehospital triage and destination decisions, identifying available rehabilitation services to support early access, finding TBI-experienced clinicians for postacute follow-up of all patients, and mapping community psychosocial and peer-support resources.

document_sections.heading: Key Elements for the PI Processes
document_sections.content: The workgroup identifies and recommends guideline measures for integration into trauma PIPS. They apply to facility TBI admissions, including direct admissions to trauma or neurosurgical services.

document_sections.heading: Table 10. Traumatic Brain Injury Management PI Recommendations
document_sections.content: The performance-improvement table links care processes to measurable outcomes and thresholds. It specifies neurosurgical evaluation within 30 minutes of request for severe TBI (GCS < 9) with CT evidence of intracranial trauma, moderate TBI (GCS 9–12) with a possible intracranial mass on CT, or neurological deficit from possible spinal cord injury. Prehospital destination and interfacility transfer measures address high-risk neurological findings, skull injury, significant intracranial lesions, associated extracranial injury, and inability to observe for deterioration. It calls for a neurotrauma contingency plan and, when diversion occurs, at least quarterly reporting of diversion start and stop dates and times. Assessment measures cover serial documentation of individual GCS components, pupils, age-appropriate hemodynamics, and neurological findings. Worsening neurological examination warrants urgent repeat head CT; persistent altered mental status with an initially abnormal CT warrants repeat imaging in 6–12 hours. Biomarker testing to reduce unnecessary CT is considered for suspected TBI at age ≥ 18 years with GCS 13–15 within 12 hours of injury. Other monitored targets include the treatment parameters in Table 4, CPP 60–70 mm Hg, PbtO2 ≥ 15 mm Hg, and appropriate ICP monitoring and EEG use. Surgical measures include tracking delayed craniotomy when an indicated craniotomy occurs < 4 hours after arrival. Nutritional support should start within 3 days, with PN when EN is contraindicated; glucose and sodium monitoring and documented skin-protection measures are included. Early mobilization or simple movement interventions are tracked within the first 48 hours. Airway measures address intubation for GCS < 9, severe agitation, or absent protective reflexes, with possible indication at GCS > 8 in the presence of thoracic or abdominal injury; oxygenation targets include PaO2 80–100 mm Hg and PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg when ICP is not elevated. Consider tracheostomy within 7 days. BCVI measures cover vascular imaging, antithrombotic treatment, and follow-up, with therapy potentially beginning as early as 24 hours postinjury when appropriate. For stable hemorrhage on follow-up CT, the table specifies nonoperative VTE prophylaxis within 24 hours for GCS 13–15 and within 48 hours for GCS 3–12; after surgery, consider initiation or resumption 24–48 hours afterward if postoperative CT shows stable ICH. It also tracks the time and agent used for prophylaxis, anticoagulant reversal when needed, and PTS prophylaxis limited to the first 7 days. Additional measures include recording the reason, date, and time of withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment; facility brain-death guidance; psychological support and TBI education beginning at admission; postacute resources and referral criteria for GCS 13–15; rehabilitation consultation within a day of admission; inclusion of a PM&R physician in multidisciplinary care; and referral to specialized postacute rehabilitation when medically stable for discharge.

key_numeric_data.parameter: Protein delivery associated with improved nitrogen balance
key_numeric_data.context: In a study of patients with critical illness and trauma, patients with TBI had no greater protein requirements than trauma patients without TBI.
